title: Malaysian Startup Event Me Now Launches Digital Marketplace with Zero Booking Commission
bodyText:
Malaysia’s event industry is getting a new digital marketplace with the launch of Event Me Now (EMN), a homegrown platform designed to simplify event planning and help vendors manage customer enquiries, quotations and bookings.
Event Me Now Sdn Bhd officially soft-launched the platform on 1 October 2026 at St Giles Boulevard Hotel in Kuala Lumpur. The event brought together vendors, hospitality representatives, technology partners and other industry stakeholders.
The platform aims to address a common challenge for customers: finding and comparing event services across social media, websites, personal recommendations and lengthy WhatsApp conversations.
For vendors, handling enquiries across multiple channels can also take time away from running their businesses. Preparing quotations, checking availability, following up with customers and coordinating payments can create additional administrative work.
Event Me Now aims to bring these processes into one digital ecosystem, connecting customers with event vendors while allowing businesses to retain control over their services and pricing.
Event Me Now currently covers 10 key areas of Malaysia’s event industry. These include venues and event spaces, catering and beverages, decoration, entertainment, sound and lighting, photography, videography, makeup and styling, event equipment rentals, event planning, and transport and car rental.
The company plans to expand its range of services as the marketplace grows.
Unlike a traditional event agency, EMN operates as a marketplace rather than managing events on behalf of customers. Vendors decide which enquiries to respond to, set their own prices and prepare their own quotations.
The platform does not determine which vendor receives a booking. Customers can review the quotations they receive and decide which service provider best suits their needs.
“We did not want to build another platform that simply lists vendors,” said Murali Kathegesen, Founder and Managing Director of Event Me Now.
“We wanted to understand what customers actually go through when planning an event and what vendors experience while running their businesses. From there, we started building the platform around those problems.”
Event Me Now places trust, honesty and transparency at the centre of its marketplace model.
The platform introduces identity and business verification measures to promote accountability and help customers make more informed decisions when choosing event vendors.
Availability management is another key feature. Vendors will be able to manage their availability through the platform, helping customers identify suitable providers before committing to a booking.
EMN also uses a quotation-based process. Customers submit their event requirements, and vendors can choose whether to respond with a quotation. Vendors remain responsible for setting prices and presenting their offers.
The platform is also introducing milestone payments to provide a more structured way to manage payments at different stages of an event.
Together, these features are intended to make it easier for customers to compare services and coordinate bookings, while helping vendors manage the process through a central marketplace.
A key part of Event Me Now’s business model is its commitment to zero platform commission.
Rather than taking a percentage of each booking, the company plans to generate revenue through annual subscriptions paid by participating vendors.
This approach allows vendors to set their prices without having to account for an additional marketplace commission on every transaction.
“A vendor may spend years building their skills, reputation and business,” Murali said.
“We believe the price they charge should remain their decision and their earnings should remain theirs. Our role is to create the environment that helps genuine customers and genuine vendors connect.”
The company says more than 80 vendors expressed interest in joining during its early recruitment phase. These businesses represent different segments of Malaysia’s event industry.
Event Me Now has also become an Associate Member of the Malaysian Association of Hotels as it begins building relationships across the country’s hospitality and events sectors.
Public vendor registration for Event Me Now will open on 1 November 2026. The platform will offer annual subscription options for companies, enterprises and individual freelancers.
Malaysia is the company’s immediate focus, but its longer-term plans extend across the wider event economy. Potential areas of expansion include destination events, business collaboration and additional services that connect more industry participants.
For now, the company aims to establish a marketplace that customers can trust and vendors find useful.
“We are building this in Malaysia, for Malaysia first,” Murali said.
“The soft launch was an important milestone, but it is only the beginning. There is still a lot for us to prove. What matters now is building something customers can trust, vendors genuinely find useful and the industry can grow together with.”
As Event Me Now prepares to open vendor registration, its next challenge will be turning early industry interest into an active marketplace that delivers value for both customers and event businesses.

title: East Asia and Pacific Growth Hits 4.5% as AI Creates New Opportunities for Malaysia
bodyText:
East Asia and the Pacific is projected to grow by 4.5% in 2026, despite global economic uncertainty, as demand for high-tech goods supports regional growth. Malaysia is among the economies expected to perform better than previously forecast, according to the World Bank’s latest Economic Update for the region, released on 6 October.
The World Bank revised Malaysia’s 2026 growth forecast upwards by 0.7 percentage points to 5.1%. Stronger forecasts for Vietnam and Thailand also reflect the region’s growing role in manufacturing and exporting goods linked to the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
Vietnam’s growth forecast rose by 1.1 percentage points to 7.4%, while Thailand’s increased by 0.7 percentage points to 2.0%. China, the region’s largest economy, is projected to grow by 4.4%. Weak domestic demand, a soft labour market and continued adjustments in the property sector remain challenges.
Pacific Island countries face a different outlook. Their economies are projected to grow by 2.2%, 0.5 percentage points below the previous forecast. High energy prices and limited capacity to absorb external shocks continue to weigh on their prospects.
The World Bank’s report highlights a gap between producing AI-related goods and using AI across the wider economy. East Asia and the Pacific has benefited from its integration into global supply chains, particularly as worldwide investment in AI drives demand for advanced technology products.
However, many businesses across the region still face barriers to adopting AI. High implementation costs, limited technical expertise, and concerns about security and privacy can slow uptake. Adoption among individuals and firms also remains behind levels in advanced economies.
The report suggests that businesses do not need to develop entirely new AI systems to benefit from the technology. Instead, many of the region’s near-term gains could come from “Small AI” — adopting and adapting existing, accessible AI tools to improve productivity and business operations.
Carlos Felipe Jaramillo, World Bank Vice President for East Asia and Pacific, said the region must turn its strength in producing AI-related goods into broader adoption that boosts productivity and creates more and better jobs.
For Malaysian businesses, this presents an opportunity to explore practical AI applications beyond the technology sector. Wider adoption could help companies improve efficiency, strengthen competitiveness and respond to changing market demands.
AI is already changing the skills employers seek, even though its impact on jobs that can be automated remains limited. Companies increasingly value AI expertise alongside analytical thinking and social skills.
The report also identifies a gap in the types of work available across the region. Only 13% of jobs in East Asia and the Pacific involve complex thinking and judgment, compared with 39% in advanced economies.
This matters as AI tools become more widely available. Workers and businesses will need the skills to use these tools effectively, assess their outputs and apply them to tasks that require human judgment.
Sarvesh Suri, IFC Regional Vice President for Asia and the Pacific, said private investment can help accelerate AI adoption. He highlighted the importance of financing digital and energy infrastructure, expanding access to business funding and investing in workforce skills.
Small businesses may particularly benefit from affordable tools that help them improve productivity without requiring substantial investment in custom technology.
The World Bank identifies three areas where governments and businesses can act to help the region sustain economic growth and make AI more widely beneficial.
Businesses need a supportive operating environment, reliable energy and digital infrastructure, financing and workers with relevant skills. These foundations can help companies adopt AI and use it to improve productivity.
Affordable AI tools designed for local languages and conditions could help industries that employ people across different skill levels. The report highlights tourism and agribusiness as sectors where locally adapted AI could support better jobs and wider economic participation.
Governments can use AI to improve public services while developing regulations and digital foundations that support responsible adoption. Cooperation between economies can also help address shared challenges and encourage wider use of the technology.
The World Bank’s outlook points to continued growth across East Asia and the Pacific, supported in part by demand for high-tech exports. Malaysia’s revised 2026 growth forecast reflects this regional momentum.
However, sustaining that growth will require more than manufacturing the products behind the AI boom. Businesses must also find ways to apply AI across their operations, while governments and the private sector invest in infrastructure, financing and workforce development.
For Malaysia, the challenge is to turn stronger economic momentum into lasting productivity gains, more competitive businesses and better employment opportunities as AI adoption expands. Download the report

title: Sarawak Targets Startup Growth Beyond Borders with 78 Exhibitors at IDECS26 Startup Village
bodyText:
Sarawak is stepping up efforts to turn startup innovation into commercial success, with the International Digital Economy Conference Sarawak 2026 (IDECS26) placing market access, investment and regional expansion at the centre of its startup agenda.
Held at the Borneo Convention Centre Kuching on 5 and 6 October, IDECS26 marked the ninth edition of the conference. Its Startup Village brought together entrepreneurs, investors, researchers and industry players to strengthen connections across Sarawak’s digital economy ecosystem.
The initiative reflects a shift under the state’s Post-COVID-19 Development Strategy (PCDS) 2030 . After investing in digital infrastructure and entrepreneurship training, Sarawak is now focusing on helping startups validate their products, secure customers, attract investment and expand into new markets.
Yang Berhormat Dato Sri Roland Sagah Wee Inn, Sarawak’s Minister for Education, Innovation and Talent Development, outlined this direction in welcoming remarks delivered on his behalf by Yang Berhormat Datuk Dr. Annuar Bin Rapaee, who officially opened Startup Village.
“Startup Village has been created to strengthen those connections. It should be a working environment where a researcher can meet an industry partner , a founder can find a potential customer , an investor can discover an emerging company , and a promising solution can find its next route to market,” the minister said.
Between 2021 and 2025, Sarawak established nine Digital Innovation Hubs, delivered more than 800 training programmes to 28,000 participants and helped over 33,000 small businesses move online.
With these foundations in place, the state aims to connect its existing support programmes into a clearer pathway from innovation to commercialisation.
Startup Village featured 78 startup exhibitors at IDECS26, up from 54 exhibition booths the previous year. The larger showcase gives founders more opportunities to connect with prospective customers, investors and business partners.
The Sarawak Digital Economy Corporation (SDEC) has also reported progress through its startup acceleration programmes.
The SDEC Technology Accelerator (STAcc) has accelerated 47 research teams and helped 38 organisations validate their markets and technologies. Participants have secured seven external funding opportunities, while spin-off ventures have created 11 jobs.
Further along the startup pipeline, the Digital Village Accelerator (DiVA) and Sarawak SaaS Accelerator (SaSAR) have collectively supported 49 startup alumni. DiVA has generated 41 jobs and RM376,000 in partnership value, while SaSAR’s first cohort generated US$182,000 in partnership value.
SDEC has also facilitated approximately RM8.5 million in investment for startup alumni. In 2025, the corporation established the Sarawak Business Angel Network (SBAN) to strengthen connections with private investors and develop the state’s private-capital ecosystem alongside government support.
Sarawak is also expanding support for social enterprises, which combine commercial activity with social impact.
The state now has 83 enterprises registered under the Social Enterprise Malaysia (SEMy) initiative, the second-highest number among Malaysian states.
The SEHebat Catalyst Cohort 2 has onboarded 10 enterprises, building on the first cohort’s results. Participants in Cohort 1 recorded revenue growth ranging from 10% to 160%, according to the announcement.
These programmes form part of Sarawak’s wider effort to help local ventures develop sustainable business models, generate revenue and create employment while addressing social needs.
Regional collaboration is another focus of Sarawak’s startup strategy.
SDEC has established a new collaboration with the Brunei Economic Development Board (BEDB) , through the Brunei Innovation Lab, to develop a Sarawak-Brunei Hackathon and Incubation Programme.
The initiative will give entrepreneurs from both markets opportunities to develop and validate business solutions, work with mentors and industry partners, and explore cross-border commercial opportunities.
Promising ventures can also progress into SDEC’s existing SaSAR and DiVA accelerator programmes. This creates a potential pathway from early-stage ideas and prototypes to business acceleration, market access and investment.
The partnership could help Sarawak-based startups reach customers beyond the domestic market while giving entrepreneurs in both ecosystems greater access to expertise and regional networks.
Sarawak’s evolving startup strategy places greater emphasis on measurable business outcomes rather than the number of programmes delivered or pitches made.
“For Sarawak, the objective must therefore extend beyond the number of companies formed or the number of pitches delivered. We want companies that can build from Sarawak, solve real problems, generate revenue, attract investment and eventually compete in markets beyond the state ,” the minister said.
He added that the state wants more of the knowledge, intellectual property, skilled employment and entrepreneurial experience generated through business growth to remain connected to Sarawak.
By linking research, talent development, startup acceleration, private investment and regional partnerships, Sarawak aims to strengthen the pathway from innovation to commercial success.
IDECS26 was jointly organised by SDEC, the Sarawak Multimedia Authority (SMA) and Sarawak Information Systems (SAINS). The conference’s Startup Village reflects the state’s continued push to develop a digital economy in which local startups can secure investment, build sustainable businesses and compete in regional markets.

title: FCM Travel Launches Proactive Analytics to Help Businesses Control Travel Costs and Compliance Risks
bodyText:
FCM Travel has launched FCM Proactive Analytics, a new corporate travel management tool that monitors travel programmes and delivers regular spending insights to help businesses identify cost and compliance risks before they escalate.
Launched on 6 October 2026 in Singapore, the tool analyses corporate travel data around the clock and sends reports directly to customers and FCM Account Managers. It aims to reduce manual reporting work, improve cost control and help travel managers make more informed decisions.
The launch marks the second of three data capabilities that FCM Travel is developing. The company already offers interactive dashboards through its FCM Platform and plans to introduce a conversational analytics tool in the coming months.
Corporate travel managers often rely on dashboards that require manual checks or scheduled reports that may reveal problems too late. FCM Proactive Analytics aims to address this challenge by delivering insights directly to users without requiring them to log in or request reports manually.
At launch, the tool covers several areas of corporate travel spending, including hotel expenditure by city, airline costs and carrier trends, route performance, and concentrations of traveller spending. Customers can receive analysis weekly, monthly or quarterly.
By identifying spending patterns and potential compliance gaps earlier, the tool helps businesses intervene before issues affect their travel budgets. It also provides written insights that travel managers can use in management presentations, stakeholder discussions and programme reviews.
Jessica Dunderdale, Global Head of Product for FCM Travel, said the new capability strengthens the relationship between travel management technology and personalised customer support.
“A managed travel programme has always been about more than bookings – it’s about having someone in your corner who understands your business,” she said.
“Proactive Analytics strengthens that relationship: our technology does the watching, so our people can do the advising. For customers, that means a travel programme that isn’t just managed but genuinely looked after.”
FCM Proactive Analytics builds on FCM Platform, which provides businesses with interactive dashboards, governed reporting and benchmarking. Together, these capabilities give customers three ways to access and use their corporate travel data.
The first is dashboard-based reporting, which lets customers explore key performance indicators (KPIs), compare benchmarks and generate reports using agreed metric definitions.
The second is proactive monitoring through FCM Proactive Analytics. Instead of searching for information, customers receive regular analysis and recommendations directly in their inboxes.
The third capability, FCM MCP (Model Context Protocol) technology, is scheduled to launch in the coming months. It will allow customers to ask questions about their travel data in natural language through their existing AI tools, using the same defined metrics that underpin FCM’s reporting environment.
FCM Consulting can also help businesses address wider operational issues when analytics reveal opportunities for structural improvements. This approach aims to move corporate travel management beyond retrospective reporting towards more strategic, forward-looking discussions.
As businesses increasingly adopt AI-powered analytics, data governance remains an important consideration. FCM says Proactive Analytics operates within its existing governed data environment and does not use customer data to train third-party AI models.
The company also plans to introduce real-time, trigger-based alerts, allowing customers to respond more quickly when urgent travel spending or compliance issues arise.
Future developments will expand FCM MCP’s capabilities by connecting travel data with other business systems, including human resources, sales and expense management platforms. This could give companies a more connected view of their operations and help them make decisions using information from multiple departments.
With the launch of Proactive Analytics, FCM Travel is expanding its corporate travel technology offering to help businesses monitor expenditure, strengthen compliance and reduce the administrative burden of travel reporting. Its planned conversational analytics and real-time alerts will further develop this approach, supporting more proactive and data-driven travel programme management.

title: Malaysia Leads Asia in Legacy Planning, but 80% Fear Wealth Won’t Last Beyond the Next Generation
bodyText:
Malaysia leads six Asian markets in formal legacy planning, but many Malaysians still worry about passing on lasting wealth. A new Sun Life Asia survey found that 80% of Malaysians who intend to leave financial assets fear their wealth will not survive beyond the next generation.
The survey also found significant progress in inheritance planning. In 2026, 37% of Malaysian respondents had fully documented and communicated their legacy plans. That figure more than doubled from 15% in 2025. Meanwhile, the share of respondents without a legacy plan fell from 23% to just 10%.
However, only 23% of Malaysians said they felt fully prepared for their legacy. This gap highlights a key challenge: families must do more than document their wishes. They also need to prepare beneficiaries to manage and preserve inherited wealth.
Sun Life Asia published these findings in its latest report, Passing the Torch: When Legacy Means More Than Money . The study surveyed 3,073 people across Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam. Malaysia accounted for 506 respondents.
“Malaysia has made clear progress in formalising legacy plans , with more families putting their intentions in writing and discussing them with the people involved,” said Ho Teck Seng, President and Country Head of Sun Life Malaysia .
“The continuing concern about whether wealth will last shows that documentation is only one part of preparedness. Families also need to consider what they want their wealth to achieve, whether those intentions are understood and whether future beneficiaries are ready for the responsibilities they may inherit.”
Market volatility ranks as the biggest threat to long-term wealth preservation among Malaysians who worry about their legacy. Some 54% cited market fluctuations as a concern. Another 49% pointed to beneficiary preparedness, while 47% worried about potential family conflict.
Legal, regulatory and tax changes also pose challenges. Some 37% of respondents said these changes could affect their legacy plans.
Across the six Asian markets, beneficiary preparedness ranks first among wealth preservation concerns at 52%. Market volatility follows at 49%, while family conflict accounts for 44%.
Despite these concerns, Malaysians feel increasingly prepared to pass on their wealth. In 2026, 58% felt fully or somewhat prepared for their legacy, up from 47% in 2025. The share who felt fully prepared also rose, from 19% to 23%.
These findings suggest that more Malaysians are taking steps towards inheritance planning. However, economic uncertainty and family dynamics continue to challenge their confidence in preserving wealth across generations.
Malaysian Millennials face a striking contrast between concern about wealth preservation and optimism about their financial legacy.
Among Millennials who intend to leave financial assets, 90% worry their wealth will not last beyond the next generation. Gen Z respondents also share this concern, with 82% expressing similar fears. Among Gen X and Baby Boomers, the figure stands at 71% for each group.
Yet Millennials remain the most optimistic about their wealth’s long-term impact. Some 69% believe their wealth will benefit future generations. By comparison, 47% of Gen Z, 53% of Gen X and 48% of Baby Boomers share this view.
The findings highlight the importance of preparing beneficiaries alongside financial assets. Financial education, open family discussions and clear inheritance arrangements can help younger generations manage wealth responsibly.
For many Malaysians, a meaningful legacy extends beyond money. They also want to create opportunities for their children and future generations.
Education ranks as the most popular legacy priority. Some 51% of respondents placed educational opportunities among their top three priorities. Wealth came next at 49%, followed by family traditions at 44%.
Financial assets still play a central role in these plans. The survey found that 83% of Malaysian respondents intend to leave financial assets or wealth to others.
Among those planning to pass on wealth, 53% want their assets invested for long-term growth. Another 52% want their wealth to support family members during their lifetime, while 50% intend to use it to fund education.
These priorities show how inheritance planning can support more than financial security. Families can also use their wealth to fund education, preserve traditions and create opportunities for future generations.
Although more Malaysians now formalise their legacy plans, many families still struggle to communicate their intentions fully.
The survey found that 66% of Malaysian respondents said older generations had shared at least some aspects of their legacy plans. However, only 32% said their families had communicated those plans in full.
Formal family meetings remain the most common setting for legacy discussions, cited by 51% of respondents. Informal conversations follow at 40%.
Financial advisers also play a growing role. The share of respondents who reported communication about legacy plans through financial advisers rose from 16% in 2025 to 31% in 2026.
Overall, 45% of Malaysian respondents had already sought professional legacy-planning advice. Another 35% said they would like to seek advice in the future.
Even so, Malaysians believe families should lead the process. Some 32% said parents or guardians should take charge of legacy planning, compared with 18% who selected financial advisers or wealth professionals.
Trust remains essential when families seek professional help. Among those looking for advice, 57% prioritised trustworthiness and integrity when choosing an adviser. Another 50% highlighted expert knowledge.
Sun Life Malaysia has introduced its Distribution Settlement Option (DSO) to give clients more flexibility when transferring wealth to loved ones.
The feature allows clients to distribute payouts over time instead of paying the entire amount as a lump sum. Sun Life Malaysia includes DSO in its latest suite of products and plans to extend the feature to more products.
According to the company, DSO offers structured payouts without requiring a separate trust arrangement. This could help clients avoid potentially significant trust fees while giving them greater control over how and when beneficiaries receive funds.
Structured payouts can complement wider family discussions about inheritance and financial security. Families can use clear distribution arrangements to communicate their intentions and establish how beneficiaries should receive funds. They should also review their plans as family needs and circumstances change.
“Putting a plan in place is an important step, but families also need to keep the conversation going so that everyone understands what the plan is intended to achieve and how it should work as circumstances change,” Ho said.
“Features such as DSO can make structured legacy planning more accessible to Clients across all income segments, while professional advice can help families work through the financial, legal and protection considerations involved.”
Malaysia’s progress in formal legacy planning marks an important step towards better wealth preservation. Yet the survey shows that documentation alone cannot guarantee a lasting financial legacy.
Families must also communicate their intentions, prepare beneficiaries and consider how inherited wealth can support future generations. By combining clear inheritance plans with financial education and professional guidance, Malaysians can take a more considered approach to passing on their wealth.
Read the full Passing the Torch: When Legacy Means More Than Money report from Sun Life Asia for further insights into legacy planning across the region.

title: Sarawak Targets AI, Semiconductor and Space Economy Growth at IDECS26
bodyText:
Sarawak is stepping up efforts to develop its digital economy, with artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductor innovation and space technology emerging as key priorities at the ninth International Digital Economy Conference Sarawak 2026 (IDECS26).
Held at the Borneo Convention Centre Kuching on 5 and 6 October, the conference brings together participants from more than 30 countries. It aims to turn technological innovation, research and investment into practical economic opportunities for the state.
The official opening ceremony was officiated by Sarawak Premier Datuk Patinggi Tan Sri (Dr) Abang Haji Abdul Rahman Zohari bin Tun Datuk Abang Haji Openg. The event also marked 12 strategic collaborations involving technology companies, government-linked organisations and research institutions.
Jointly organised by Sarawak Digital Economy Corporation (SDEC), Sarawak Multimedia Authority (SMA) and Sarawak Information Systems (SAINS), IDECS26 carries the theme “Scaling Innovation Ecosystems for a Borderless Economy: Earth, Orbit and Beyond.”
IDECS26 supports Sarawak’s broader ambitions under the Post COVID-19 Development Strategy 2030 (PCDS 2030). The state sees digital transformation as a key driver of productivity, skilled employment and new industries.
Premier Abang Johari said Sarawak aims to build its own technological capabilities rather than rely solely on innovations developed elsewhere.
The state wants local ideas, businesses and expertise to connect with regional and global markets. This approach could also create new opportunities for investment, research and commercial development.
The conference reflects a broader shift in Sarawak’s digital economy strategy. Alongside established priorities such as AI, digital talent and future cities, IDECS26 introduces semiconductor innovation and the emerging space economy as major areas of focus.
The opening ceremony marked 12 strategic collaborations, including a Strategic Communication Instrument, 10 memoranda of understanding (MOUs) and an aerospace-related collaboration involving the Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF), Airbus Defence and Space, and the Centre for Technology Excellence Sarawak (CENTEXS).
The agreements involve organisations across technology, infrastructure, AI, telecommunications and other sectors.
Among the collaborations, SDEC signed MOUs with Huawei Technologies (Malaysia), Agibot Innovation, Airbus Defence and Space, MYTEKSI (Grab) and other partners. Sarawak Artificial Intelligence Centre (SAIC) also entered into collaborations with Global Data Centre and IBM Malaysia.
Other agreements involve Zecon Berhad, Neuronet Borneo, SAINS, Ernst & Young Consulting, the Construction Industry Development Board (CIDB) Malaysia and additional organisations.
The collaborations are intended to strengthen partnerships and create opportunities to develop, deploy and commercialise technologies in Sarawak.
The ceremony also included the handover and acceptance of two Sikorsky Nuri helicopters from RMAF to CENTEXS, supporting aerospace and defence-related collaboration.
Sarawak is targeting the launch of its first CubeSat-based nanosatellite by 2030. The planned satellite aims to collect Earth imagery, geolocation data and other strategic information from low Earth orbit.
These capabilities could support development planning, environmental monitoring and resource management. They could also help build local expertise in semiconductors, satellite systems, engineering, AI and data analytics.
The initiative forms part of a wider effort to establish a local space ecosystem. Sarawak has established the Sarawak Aerospace Advisory Council to provide strategic direction, while the planned Sarawak Space Agency is expected to coordinate sector development and partnerships.
Work on the nanosatellite is also being shaped through collaboration between the Sarawak Space Agency and i-CATS University College. The initiative includes plans for two laboratories dedicated to related research.
By investing in space technology and supporting research, Sarawak aims to develop capabilities that could create new economic opportunities beyond conventional digital services.
IDECS26 introduces the inaugural Centre of Excellence (CoE) for Digital Research Conference 2026. The platform aims to strengthen links between universities, researchers, government and industry.
The programme focuses on moving research towards real-world applications. Researchers can gain a clearer understanding of industry and public-sector needs, while businesses and policymakers can identify technologies with potential for testing, deployment and commercialisation.
This approach could help narrow the gap between academic research and market demand. It also creates opportunities for businesses to explore new technologies and work with research institutions on practical solutions.
The conference features five tracks: The Future, Future Cities, Startup Village, SHE-TECH Asia Forum 2026 and the CoE for Digital Research Conference. Together, they cover technology development, urban transformation, entrepreneurship, leadership and research commercialisation.
IDECS26 also brings back Startup Village, which connects startups with investment and business-development opportunities.
At IDECS25, seven startups received up to RM150,000 each in seed funding and business-development support. Four MOUs also covered digital agriculture, facility management, smart cities and AI-enabled biodiversity innovation.
The returning programme builds on this focus by creating further opportunities for entrepreneurs to develop solutions and connect with potential partners.
Meanwhile, SHE-TECH Asia Forum 2026 adopts the theme “From Participation to Power.” It shifts attention beyond women’s participation in technology towards their roles in leadership, decision-making and shaping emerging technologies.
The programme features international and regional experts, including former Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) astronaut Dr Soichi Noguchi, architect and urbanist Professor Jason Pomeroy, scientific futurist Dr Catherine Ball, ethical AI strategist Dr Nici Sweaney and Professor De Kai of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and the International Computer Science Institute at Berkeley.
Their participation adds international perspectives on innovation, sustainability, AI and the future of technology.
Looking ahead, Sarawak Premier Abang Johari announced that IDECS will celebrate its 10th anniversary in 2027. Kuching will also host the World Innovation, Technology and Services Alliance (WITSA) Global AI Summit 2027.
The summit is expected to bring together leaders from the global technology industry, government and innovation ecosystem. It will build on Sarawak’s partnership with WITSA through its Global AI Ecosystem Network.
The event is expected to strengthen international connections in technology, investment, research and policy.
For Sarawak, the next step is to translate the partnerships and discussions from IDECS26 into tangible outcomes. These include new investment, stronger research-industry collaboration and commercial opportunities for technologies developed and tested locally.
By connecting innovation with business growth and international markets, Sarawak aims to strengthen its position in Malaysia’s digital economy and build capabilities that can compete across the region.

title: SMEAM Urges Budget 2027 to Ease SME Costs and Boost Productivity
bodyText:
The SME Association of Malaysia (SMEAM) is urging the Government to make Budget 2027 a turning point for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), with policies that ease operating costs, raise productivity and strengthen local business competitiveness.
The call follows SMEAM’s Quick Business Survey: Minimum Wage Review 2026 , which gathered 333 responses from businesses across manufacturing, services, retail, wholesale and trading, food and beverage, technology and other sectors. Businesses employing 50 people or fewer accounted for 73.3% of respondents.
The findings highlight mounting pressure on businesses. Some 61.6% of respondents said conditions had worsened or worsened significantly compared with 12 months ago.
SMEAM National President Dr Chin Chee Seong said the results should not be interpreted as employers opposing better wages. Instead, businesses want wage growth to align with productivity, company performance and broader economic conditions.
The survey found that 45.9% of respondents disagreed or strongly disagreed with a potential increase in the minimum wage from RM1,700 to around RM2,000.
Another 21.3% supported higher wages in principle but believed the increase should be deferred until business and economic conditions improve. Meanwhile, 15.3% said wages should primarily reflect market conditions, skills and productivity.
A further 9.6% would support an increase if it were linked to productivity or business performance. Only 6.6% directly supported raising the minimum wage to around RM2,000 at this time.
SMEAM acknowledged the importance of improving workers’ incomes and living standards. However, it argued that sustainable wage increases depend on stronger businesses and higher productivity.
The impact of a minimum wage increase could extend beyond the additional RM300 per employee.
According to the survey, 92.8% of respondents expect some pressure to adjust salaries for employees already earning above the proposed minimum. Employers may need to preserve reasonable pay differences between entry-level workers and experienced employees, technicians or supervisors.
This could create a cascading effect across salary structures and increase overall labour costs.
Businesses also identified several potential consequences of higher operating expenses:
These figures reflect respondents’ concerns and anticipated actions, rather than confirmed future outcomes. Nevertheless, SMEAM said policymakers should take them seriously when assessing the cumulative cost of doing business.
When asked what should guide future minimum wage adjustments, 63.7% of respondents selected employee productivity. Overall economic conditions ranked second at 56.2%, followed by a company’s ability to pay at 54.4%.
SMEAM said Malaysia should aim to create higher-skilled, better-paying jobs rather than remain a low-wage economy. Achieving that goal requires businesses to become more productive, innovative, automated and competitive.
The association wants Budget 2027 to support this transition through stronger investment in technology, workforce capabilities and business development.
Its proposals are outlined in Strengthening SME Competitiveness and Building Future Malaysian Champions , which calls for a shift from announcing funding allocations to measuring their actual impact on businesses.
SMEs face several cost pressures at once, including labour, utilities, financing, sales and service tax (SST), e-Invoicing, licensing and regulatory compliance.
While individual changes may be manageable, their combined impact can weaken cash flow, reduce margins and limit investment, recruitment and expansion.
SMEAM proposes a Cumulative SME Cost and Regulatory Impact Assessment before the Government introduces major policies that increase business costs.
The assessment would consider the combined impact on different sectors and company sizes. It would also involve meaningful SME consultation, better sequencing of policy changes and reasonable transition periods.
In this context, SMEAM is calling for any further increase to the RM1,700 minimum wage to be deferred for now. It wants the Government to prioritise productivity, automation, workforce development and business expansion.
SMEAM argues that businesses at different growth stages need different types of financing.
A microbusiness seeking working capital has different requirements from a manufacturer investing in automation or a company preparing to expand overseas.
The association proposes an SME Life-Cycle Financing and Investment Framework. It would cover working capital, machinery, automation, digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives, commercialisation, exports and international expansion.
The framework would combine grants, guarantees, debt, equity, co-investment and private capital according to each company’s needs and stage of growth.
Budget 2027 should strengthen support for SMEs adopting automation, robotics, AI, cloud technology, data analytics, cybersecurity and smart manufacturing.
However, SMEAM stressed that assistance should extend beyond purchasing equipment. Businesses also need help with software, systems integration, implementation, technical skills and workforce training.
Support should deliver measurable improvements in productivity, operating costs, production capacity, quality, revenue and market access.
By helping SMEs produce more value, the Government can also strengthen their ability to offer better salaries and higher-skilled jobs.
SMEAM supports continued efforts to attract high-quality foreign direct investment (FDI). However, it believes Malaysia must do more to ensure local businesses benefit from multinational companies’ presence.
The association wants policymakers to measure how many Malaysian SMEs become suppliers, how much technology and knowledge transfer takes place, and how much domestic procurement is generated.
It proposes a Supplier Development, Localisation and Procurement Programme to connect capable Malaysian SMEs with multinational corporations (MNCs), government-linked companies (GLCs) and Government procurement opportunities.
The proposed pathway is straightforward: Match, Upgrade, Qualify, Procure and Scale.
The goal is to move beyond business introductions and help Malaysian SMEs secure actual contracts and build lasting supply-chain relationships.
SMEAM said Malaysia should not rely solely on foreign investment to drive economic growth. Malaysian-owned companies must also have the support to reinvest, automate, innovate and expand internationally.
It is calling for stronger domestic direct investment (DDI), backed by suitable financing, guarantees, equity and co-investment.
Government-linked companies (GLCs), government-linked investment companies (GLICs) and institutional investors could also support capable Malaysian businesses through strategic partnerships, co-investment and growth capital where commercially appropriate.
The broader objective is to help local companies grow into stronger domestic and regional competitors.
Although Malaysia already offers grants, financing, digitalisation initiatives, ESG programmes and market-access assistance, SMEs may struggle to identify the right support.
Businesses may not know which agency to approach or what assistance they need as they grow.
SMEAM proposes an integrated SME Development Gateway to coordinate existing programmes without creating another agency.
Its proposed model is: One SME, One Profile, One Diagnostic, One Development Pathway.
The gateway would connect businesses with relevant financing, technology, ESG, skills, certification, supplier-development and export programmes. This would give SMEs a clearer route from their current challenges to their next stage of growth.
SMEAM wants the Government to assess SME assistance based on measurable business outcomes rather than the amount of money allocated.
Key indicators could include higher productivity, increased automation, more skilled employment, new supply contracts, export growth and the development of Malaysian intellectual property.
The association also wants progress to be measured by how many businesses grow from micro to small, small to medium, and medium-sized enterprises into Malaysian mid-tier or regional companies.
This approach would help policymakers identify which programmes deliver results and where further improvements are needed.
SMEAM welcomed the Government’s recognition of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) as a priority in preparing Budget 2027. It urged policymakers to create conditions that help businesses become stronger, more productive and more competitive.
The association’s priorities include reducing unnecessary costs, supporting automation and AI adoption, improving workforce training, expanding access to appropriate financing, and helping Malaysian companies commercialise innovations and enter international markets.
SMEAM framed its proposed development journey as Survive, Formalise, Transform, Scale and Globalise.
Ultimately, the association believes a stronger SME sector will also benefit workers. More productive and profitable businesses are better positioned to create quality jobs and raise wages sustainably.
Its broader ambition is for Malaysia to do more than attract successful global companies. The country must also build its own business champions.

title: INTAC’26 Welcomes 155 Exhibitors From 35 Countries to Boost Malaysia’s Tourism Industry
bodyText:
The International Tourism, Arts and Culture Exhibition and Conference 2026 (INTAC’26) opened at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre (KLCC), bringing together 155 exhibitors from 35 countries to strengthen global tourism partnerships and promote Malaysia’s arts and cultural heritage.
The three-day event, which runs from 2 to 4 October, expects around 5,000 trade visitors. It aims to create business opportunities across tourism, arts, fashion and culture while supporting Malaysia’s Visit Malaysia 2026–2027 campaign.
Mr Mohd Akbal Setia, Deputy Director General (Promotion) of Tourism Malaysia and Head of the Visit Malaysia 2026–2027 Secretariat, officiated the opening on behalf of Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Yang Berhormat Dato Sri Tiong King Sing.
Mohd Akbal highlighted the tourism sector’s economic contribution, which accounts for more than 15% of Malaysia’s gross domestic product (GDP). He noted that tourism supports businesses throughout the value chain, including hotels, e-hailing services, local artisans and family-owned restaurants.
Malaysia recorded 21.1 million international visitor arrivals between January and June 2026, marking a 2.5% increase compared with the same period in 2025.
“This performance reflects the continued appeal of Malaysia as a tourism destination and the importance of strengthening our international tourism partnerships ,” he said.
Organised by WEX Malaysia Sdn Bhd with co-organiser Warisan AD, INTAC’26 returns for its second edition under the theme “Bridging Cultures, Inspiring Trade”.
The exhibition aims to connect tourism, arts and culture practitioners while creating opportunities for international collaboration and business development.
Mohd Akbal said Malaysia’s multicultural heritage, cuisine, festivals, natural attractions and creative communities form an important part of the country’s “Malaysia, Truly Asia” identity.
He added that platforms such as INTAC can help industry players develop joint promotions and create tourism experiences that benefit local destinations and communities.
WEX Malaysia Chief Executive Officer Dr Leena Mujahed said the event aims to establish INTAC as a global hub for tourism, arts and culture.
She highlighted how tourism connects people, art shares cultural stories, and trade turns these connections into lasting partnerships.
Across three days, INTAC’26 features a range of exhibitions and activities for industry professionals, businesses and visitors.
Highlights include tourism showcases, destination presentations and displays by artisans, fashion designers and artists. The programme also features the Fashion Tourism Forum and the Journey in Style international fashion showcase.
In addition, industry pocket talks, youth-focused activities and a virtual conference will explore tourism, culture and innovation.
These activities aim to encourage knowledge sharing, showcase creative talent and build connections between local and international industry players.
The conference segment also connects tourism professionals with academic researchers through industry development and research initiatives.
According to the organisers, the INTAC’26 conference received recognition from ASEAN RECORDS for being the first international tourism, arts and culture exhibition and conference to combine licence-renewal education points for tourist guides with an academic research conference.
The programme includes six sessions offering six Continuing Tourism Related Education (CTRE) points approved by the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture Malaysia (MOTAC) for tourist guides. It also incorporates the 6th International Conference on Languages, Education and Tourism (ICLET 2026).
GEO Training Studio Sdn Bhd and MOTAC supported the initiative.
INTAC’26 receives support from MOTAC, Tourism Malaysia and the Malaysia Convention & Exhibition Bureau (MyCEB).
Its strategic partners include the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Environment Sabah, the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL). JGL Worldwide serves as the main sponsor and logistics partner.
During the opening, Mohd Akbal encouraged exhibitors and participants to use the platform to showcase their offerings, establish business connections and explore new partnerships.
He expressed hope that the event would generate new tourism products, visitor experiences and lasting commercial opportunities beyond the exhibition.
By bringing together international exhibitors, tourism professionals, creative practitioners and policymakers, INTAC’26 aims to strengthen Malaysia’s global tourism connections and support the continued development of its tourism, arts and culture sectors.
The event is held in support of Visit Malaysia 2026–2027, with the broader goal of turning cultural exchange into stronger industry partnerships and sustainable tourism opportunities.

title: Pos ArRahnu Gold-i: You Don’t Have to Wait Until You’re Rich to Own Gold
bodyText:
For many Malaysians, gold needs little introduction. Growing up, Aisyah associated it with something tangible and valuable—something bought carefully and kept for the future. But owning gold herself always seemed like something for later: when she earns more, when the business gets bigger, or when she has a few hundred, perhaps a few thousand, ringgit she can comfortably put aside.
But what if the starting point was RM10?
Pos ArRahnu Gold-i is a Shariah-compliant digital gold service that allows Malaysians to start owning gold digitally from as little as RM10. Customers can buy, sell and accumulate gold, cash out their holdings or convert their digital gold into physical gold. For someone like Aisyah, RM10 is significant. Gold ownership no longer has to begin with a large amount of money.
Pos ArRahnu offers physical gold wafers and bars for savings, gifting and long-term holding. Pos ArRahnu Gold-i introduces digital gold ownership, enabling customers to start from RM10 and accumulate gold progressively according to their financial capacity. It brings a familiar asset into a format that fits increasingly digital financial habits.
The lower starting point addresses one of the practical barriers to gold ownership: the perception that buying gold requires a substantial amount of money. For first-time owners, digital gold can seem unfamiliar or technical, particularly when it comes to understanding how the gold is held, how buying and selling work, and how accumulated gold can eventually be converted or cashed out.
Pos ArRahnu Gold-i allows customers to buy and accumulate gold digitally before selling, cashing out or converting their holdings into physical gold. This gives someone like Aisyah the flexibility to begin with an amount she is comfortable with rather than waiting until she has a large sum available.

The digital gold is backed by real physical gold, with recognised verification and certification such as LBMA, SIRIM and NMIM. The service is Shariah-compliant and offered in collaboration with Go Capital Growth Sdn Bhd, Pos ArRahnu’s appointed gold provider. The service sits within Pos ArRahnu’s wider gold ecosystem, which includes Shariah-compliant gold pawn-broking and physical gold wafers and bars.
For Aisyah, these details put substance behind the digital transaction. She may be accumulating gold through a digital platform, but that ownership is backed by physical gold. The amount she starts with may be small, but understanding what it represents remains important. Another consideration is the spread, the difference between the price at which gold is bought and the price at which it can be sold.
For example, if gold were bought at RM500 per gram and the corresponding selling price was RM480 per gram, the RM20 difference would be the spread. A smaller spread means a narrower gap between the buying and selling prices. Pos ArRahnu Gold-i is positioned as having one of the lowest gold spreads in the market, with the lower spread intended to offer better value and make gold saving more cost-efficient and less intimidating.
A lower spread, however, does not guarantee a return. Gold prices can change, and the price at which someone eventually sells may differ from the price at which the gold was purchased. Gold ownership should therefore not be approached with the assumption that its value will always rise.
For Aisyah, the more useful consideration may not be how quickly gold can make money, but something closer to everyday life: What am I putting something aside for? It could be education, a holiday, an emergency, or simply the desire to gradually build an asset rather than letting every ringgit earned flow back into everyday spending. For entrepreneurs, small traders, gig workers and people earning income from more than one source, the challenge of putting money aside can be particularly familiar.

Running a business has a habit of absorbing available cash. There is always stock to replenish, equipment to replace, marketing to pay for or another operational expense around the corner. A good month can quickly become the funding needed for the next month’s business. Aisyah experiences much the same thing. Her side business may generate additional income, but that money can quickly return to the business or go towards household commitments.
Building personal assets alongside those responsibilities does not necessarily have to begin with a large financial decision.

It can begin progressively, with an amount that fits within existing commitments. How much to set aside, how frequently to do so and which asset to choose remain personal decisions. The important shift is recognising that building something for the future does not always have to wait for a large surplus of money.
Back to Aisyah. Nothing dramatic needs to happen. She does not suddenly put thousands of ringgit into gold. Her first RM10 does not become the beginning of an overnight fortune, nor does she ignore the other financial priorities competing for her income.
What changes is much smaller but more meaningful. “Nanti bila ada duit lebih” no longer must mean waiting indefinitely for the month when everything has been paid, and there is somehow plenty left over. Aisyah can start with an amount she is comfortable with and build up gradually.
Behind the digital service is a physical network of more than 60 Pos ArRahnu outlets located within post offices, supported by more than 600 Pos Malaysia touchpoints nationwide. The proposition connects something familiar with a new way to access it: physical gold and an established physical presence, complemented by the ability to start accumulating gold digitally from RM10 at one’s own pace.
For Aisyah and others who have always thought of gold as something to consider only when they have more money, this shift signals greater economic inclusivity. You do not have to wait until you are rich to start. But when you do start, understand what you own. To learn more about Pos ArRahnu Gold-i, how it works and how to get started, visit posarrahnugold.ace2u.com

title: What Will Keep Malaysia Cool? Reimagining HVAC&R for a Smarter, Hotter Future
bodyText:
By Aileen Anthony, Executive Editor, MALAYSIA SME

The sector’s economics are changing too. Malaysia’s HVAC market was estimated at US$1.17 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach US$1.47 billion by 2030. More significantly, the Energy Commission said electricity demand reached new peaks in 2025, driven partly by data centre expansion, electrification and economic growth.
CHAT MALAYSIA SME spoke with Peter Tan , Immediate Past President of the Malaysian Air-Conditioning & Refrigeration Association (MACRA) at the recent MARVEX, about that transformation, the opportunities emerging for SMEs and his ambition for Malaysia to become an ASEAN HVAC&R knowledge and innovation hub.
Peter Tan likes to challenge one of the industry’s most basic assumptions, that air conditioning is simply about making a room cold. “If God has created atmosphere, humans have actually created what I call an indoor curated atmospheric air solution,” he said.  His reasoning is straightforward. As people spend more time indoors, HVAC&R has to do considerably more than provide cooling. Temperature, humidity, ventilation, filtration and moisture control increasingly have to work together.
Peter describes air conditioning as contributing a “fifth element” to how people use spaces. We work, live and play indoors. But the additional question, he argued, is how long people are comfortable enough to stay there. “Once this is complete, human probability will go indoor more and more,” he said, while quickly adding that people should still venture outdoors whenever possible.  The larger point is that HVAC&R is evolving from a mechanical product into an environmental solution.
Technology is accelerating that evolution. AI-enabled systems can monitor equipment, control settings and identify potential problems before maintenance is required. Even household air-conditioning systems can increasingly be managed through smartphones. Peter does not believe this removes the technician from the equation. Instead, technology gives technicians and users better information.
“My one word: embrace technology,” he said, “because it will help.” He envisages systems eventually becoming intelligent enough to recognise different temperature requirements among occupants, correlate the information and automatically regulate the indoor environment.  But smarter cooling also requires smarter behaviour.

Peter is particularly clear that energy efficiency should not simply mean reducing air-conditioning usage. An efficient machine can still waste electricity when it is used irresponsibly. “When you own the aircon, use it wisely,” he said. “Just like use your money wisely, spend it wisely, responsibly.” Efficiency, Peter alluded, is becoming both a behavioural and technological issue.

Nowhere is that equation more apparent than in data centres. Cooling is mission-critical to data centre operations, and Malaysia’s rapid emergence as a digital infrastructure location is creating an entirely new market for HVAC&R expertise. Peter describes the relationship between cooling and data centres as inseparable, almost like a body and its soul. “In order for data centres to run, they need cooling,” he said.  That creates an important downstream opportunity.
Peter shared that Malaysia has the foundations to participate. “Malaysia in ASEAN has a very good, strong engineering faculty strength,” he said, pointing also to the country’s pool of servicing and maintenance talent. From installation and design to engineering, “we have” the capability.  The challenge is ensuring local businesses gain access to the opportunities. Large data centre operators often arrive with established supply chains. Peter believes greater participation by Malaysian companies can help translate data centre investment into wider economic value.
That makes skills increasingly important. At MARVEX, visitors can watch students and practitioners install air-conditioning systems live through a skills competition. Peter sees this as a way of making previously invisible expertise visible. Installation requires specialised tools, precision, safety practices and adherence to manufacturers’ specifications. “Your (the technician’s) skill is how we are able to enjoy full comfort,” he said.
Peter also sees another possibility: making technical careers more inclusive. He noted that more women are entering the field and believes female technician teams could become a viable part of the industry. And he emphasised, professionalism matters because installation is ultimately a safety issue. “Make sure it’s done professionally. Make sure you get the right accredited person,” he stressed.

For SMEs, the opportunity extends far beyond selling air-conditioning units. The ecosystem includes installers, contractors,engineers, distributors, maintenance specialists and technology providers. But Peter cautions entrepreneurs against entering the sector without understanding its technical foundations.
An SME owner, he said, should know something about air conditioning and surround the business with experienced technical people.  Customers will increasingly require more specialised solutions. A luxury home, for example, may require humidity control to protect artwork or leather goods. Families sensitive to allergens may need better filtration and fresh-air solutions. Data centres require precision cooling and increasingly sophisticated technologies such as liquid cooling.
“Air conditioning is no longer just heat and cold,” Peter said. It should be viewed as part of supporting indoor lifestyles and well-being.  The SME opportunity, therefore, may lie increasingly in solving specific environmental and performance problems rather than merely installing equipment.

Peter explained that MACRA’s vision goes beyond growing individual businesses. For more than a decade, MACRA has worked to position Malaysia as an ASEAN HVAC hub. His larger aspiration is for Malaysia to become an ASEAN research and development centre . “Why we do that? So that we can actually allow this area to be housed by the best technologies, the latest innovations,” he said.
R&D brings knowledge. Knowledge supports training. And training can turn Malaysia into a destination for regional talent. Instead of talking constantly about losing skilled Malaysians overseas, Peter reframes the possibility: “Malaysia will not be losing talent, but Malaysia will be exporting talent.”  Peter explained that this is the push behind the newly introduced MARVEX INTERNATIONAL EXCELLENCE AWARD DINNER (MIEAD 2026), aimed at honouring excellence, leadership, innovation, and contributions across the HVAC&R, engineering, and built-environment sectors.

Regional collaboration is already part of that ambition. Peter said Malaysian and Vietnamese industry counterparts have discussed establishing a federation of HVAC associations, potentially bringing countries including Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines into a broader ASEAN platform.
Asked about MACRA’s greatest responsibility, Peter’s answer is simple: “Of the industry, by the industry, for the industry.” The same philosophy underpins his advice to SMEs. Too many businesses, he believes, see another company’s success as their loss. He advocates the opposite: mentorship, collaboration and knowledge sharing. “If you’re going to perform 100 per cent, I have to perform 110 per cent,” he said. Better competitors can force everyone to elevate their game.  It is a philosophy that could be described simply as prosper thy neighbour .
Because Malaysia’s HVAC&R future will not be shaped by air-conditioning equipment alone. It will be shaped by intelligent buildings, energy efficiency, data centres, skilled technicians, digital technologies and an ecosystem capable of bringing them together. The opportunity is therefore larger than keeping Malaysia cool. It is about building the skills, businesses and knowledge that could help Malaysia determine how the region cools next .
