title: Aventra Group Achieves ISO 42001 Certification to Strengthen AI Governance
bodyText:
Aventra Group has achieved ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS), strengthening its AI governance framework across its operations, technology infrastructure and core business applications.
The international standard provides a structured framework for managing the risks and opportunities associated with artificial intelligence. Aventra Group said the certification places it among the early adopters of AI governance in Malaysia and among fewer than 400 organisations worldwide holding the certification.
By embedding the framework across its operational footprint, Aventra Group has brought its existing ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II frameworks together with its AI governance approach.
The company said the unified governance baseline is designed to address concerns around data liability, AI risks and evolving regulatory requirements that can slow enterprise technology adoption.
Corporate procurement, legal and risk teams can spend months carrying out detailed risk assessments before approving new software, particularly when dealing with emerging technologies such as AI.
Aventra Group said its certified framework is intended to reduce this friction by providing enterprise customers with an established compliance foundation when evaluating its technology solutions.
The company said this can help organisations reduce lengthy vendor review processes and remove some of the operational barriers that can prevent APAC businesses from adopting technology and expanding into highly regulated international markets.
“The primary barrier to enterprise AI scaling across the Asia-Pacific region isn’t a lack of technological innovation; it is a profound trust deficit,” said Mohan Vasudevan, Group Chairman at Aventra Group. “Corporate leaders want the efficiency gains of automation and AI but cannot compromise on institutional risk or data safety. By anchoring our foundational operations to the world’s most rigorous AI operational framework, we have institutionalised trust, giving regional enterprises a pre-vetted runway for rapid cross-border scale globally.”
The ISO/IEC 42001 certification forms part of Aventra Group’s broader move towards a borderless digital ecosystem, with the company developing AI-ready solutions for enterprise clients through its AG ONE Marketplace.
Its solutions include the AG ONE Intelligent Workforce Management (IWM) Suite, an AI-native enterprise platform designed to bring workforce processes and talent management into a single ecosystem.
The platform is designed to automate operations while incorporating data privacy, governance and compliant AI adoption into its enterprise offering.
Aventra Group’s second highlighted solution is AG ONE Safe, an enterprise governance, risk and compliance (GRC) solution designed as an “Agentic OS for Cyber Resilience”.
The platform aims to provide autonomous risk protection and continuous security compliance, complementing the group’s broader focus on AI governance and enterprise technology risk.
Together, the solutions form part of Aventra Group’s strategy to provide enterprises with technology that combines automation and artificial intelligence with governance, security and compliance requirements.
The company said its ISO/IEC 42001 certification is intended to provide enterprises with greater confidence as AI adoption expands across the Asia-Pacific region.
By combining AI management with existing information security and compliance frameworks, Aventra Group aims to help businesses address procurement and risk concerns while adopting AI-enabled technologies and pursuing international growth.
For more information, visit the AG ONE Marketplace .

title: EY Malaysia and SAINS Partner to Advance Digital and AI Transformation in Sarawak
bodyText:
Ernst & Young Consulting Sdn. Bhd. (EY Malaysia) and Sarawak Information Systems Sdn. Bhd. (SAINS) have formalised a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to collaborate on digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI) and innovation initiatives supporting Sarawak’s long-term development ambitions.
The MoU was announced during the International Digital Economy Conference Sarawak (IDECS) 2026 in Kuching, which brought together industry, government, investors, researchers and technology leaders to explore the future of Sarawak’s digital economy.
The agreement was exchanged by Adrian Chew, EY Asean Consulting AI & Data Co-leader, Malaysia Technology Consulting Leader and Partner at EY Malaysia, and Busiai Bin Seman, Chief Executive Officer of SAINS, on behalf of their respective organisations.
The collaboration combines EY Malaysia’s global experience in business transformation, digital strategy, AI, governance and industry expertise with SAINS’ understanding of the public sector and longstanding track record in delivering digital solutions to support Sarawak’s development agenda.
Through the MoU, the two organisations will explore opportunities to support digital transformation, AI adoption, capability building, innovation and governance across the public sector and broader state-linked ecosystem.
EY Malaysia said the collaboration comes at an important point in Sarawak’s digital transformation journey, as organisations increasingly look beyond technology investment towards measurable outcomes.
“EY Malaysia is honoured to work with SAINS at a pivotal time in Sarawak’s transformation journey,” said Adrian Chew. “Technology is moving quickly, but organisations are under pressure to monitor that it delivers real results. Digital platforms, data and AI each have a role to play, but lasting impact comes from getting the fundamentals right, building capability, strengthening governance and embedding change.”
Chew added that EY Malaysia looks forward to working with SAINS to help organisations take practical steps towards Sarawak’s long-term digital ambitions.
The collaboration aligns with Sarawak’s aspirations under the Post COVID-19 Development Strategy 2030 (PCDS 2030), which envisions the state as a thriving, high-income economy driven by data, innovation and technology.
As organisations across the public sector continue to modernise, digital technologies and AI are becoming increasingly important to improving productivity, efficiency and decision-making while supporting sustainable economic growth.
The wider direction is also reflected in IDECS 2026, which focused on emerging technologies including AI, semiconductors, digital talent and the emerging space economy as part of Sarawak’s next phase of digital development.
Mohd Husin, EY Asean Government and Public Sector Consulting Leader and Partner at EY Malaysia, said the focus should be on translating technology investments into meaningful economic and societal value.
“As Sarawak advances its digital economy ambitions, the focus becomes how we can translate technology investments into meaningful economic and societal value,” he said. “Through this initiative, we aim to support efforts that strengthen digital capabilities, promote responsible AI adoption and help build the foundation for a resilient, innovative and future-ready economy.”
For Sarawak, strengthening local digital capabilities and developing talent will be increasingly important as the state expands its participation in advanced technology and emerging industries.
Busiai Bin Seman said Sarawak had already built strong momentum in its digitalisation journey, supported by a clear vision and commitment to innovation.
“We look forward to exploring opportunities with EY Malaysia that support capability building, innovation and the continued advancement of the state’s digital economy,” he said.
As Sarawak continues to pursue its development goals, the collaboration between EY Malaysia and SAINS reflects a shared commitment to accelerating digital transformation, strengthening governance and supporting the adoption of emerging technologies.
The partnership will focus on helping organisations build the capabilities needed to turn digital and AI investments into practical outcomes, while contributing to a resilient and future-ready economy in Sarawak.

title: OCBC Expands Cross-Border Payments to 67 Currencies for Malaysian Businesses
bodyText:
As Malaysian businesses diversify their supply chains and expand into new markets across ASEAN, North Asia and the Middle East, OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Berhad (OCBC Bank) has expanded its cross-border payment service, OCBC World Transfer, to support payments in 67 currencies, up from 26 previously.
The enhancement gives businesses greater flexibility when managing international transactions, allowing them to pay overseas suppliers directly in their preferred local currencies.
The expanded currency offering includes currencies such as the Vietnamese Dong, South Korean Won and United Arab Emirates Dirham, supporting trade, procurement and other commercial activities across key growth markets.
The expansion comes as the international business activities of OCBC’s customers continue to diversify.
While China, Singapore and Hong Kong remain among the bank’s key overseas payment destinations, customers are increasingly conducting transactions across a wider range of markets.
The enhanced OCBC World Transfer service is designed to help businesses pay suppliers in their preferred local currencies, reducing foreign exchange friction and streamlining cross-border payment processes.
The bank said this can also support stronger relationships between Malaysian businesses and their overseas suppliers.
The increased demand for cross-border payment solutions comes alongside greater adoption of digital banking among OCBC’s business customers.
Digital overseas transfers by OCBC customers grew 50% year-on-year as at June 2026, with transactions extending to a broader range of international markets.
“Businesses today are expanding well beyond traditional trade corridors. They are sourcing from new supplier markets, entering new customer segments and managing increasingly complex cross-border payment requirements,” said Jeffrey Teoh, Head of Wholesale Banking, OCBC Bank. “We are seeing this trend reflected in our customers’ activities, with digital overseas transfers growing 50% year-on-year and extending to a broader range of markets.”
He added that the expansion of supported currencies is intended to make it easier for businesses to pay and be paid across more countries.
“Together with our regional network across ASEAN and Greater China, we are well-positioned to support customers as they deepen existing trade relationships and pursue new opportunities overseas,” he said.
Businesses using OCBC World Transfer can also benefit from competitive foreign exchange rates and real-time payment tracking, providing greater visibility over international transactions.
OCBC Network Transfer enables customers to send funds to OCBC beneficiaries in six currencies at preferential pricing, with the full amount received by the beneficiary.
Together, OCBC World Transfer and OCBC Network Transfer form part of the bank’s broader digital banking ecosystem available through OCBC Velocity.
OCBC Velocity allows companies to manage their accounts and foreign currency positions, perform foreign exchange conversions, manage collections and access trade-related banking services through a single digital platform.
The growing adoption of digital banking is reflected in the fact that more than 90% of OCBC’s cross-border payments are conducted through OCBC Velocity.
With Malaysian businesses increasingly looking beyond traditional trade corridors, OCBC said its expanded currency coverage and digital banking capabilities are intended to support companies as they manage international payments, strengthen overseas supplier relationships and pursue new opportunities in global markets.

title: 59% of Malaysians Could Not Use SARA Aid at Their Preferred Retail Stores
bodyText:
A survey of 1,000 Malaysians has found that 59% of SARA users could not use their Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) assistance at their preferred retail channel over the past year, highlighting gaps in access to eligible retailers and essential products.
The Survey of the SARA Effect on Purchasing Behaviour, conducted one year after SARA for All was rolled out in August 2025, found that the government aid initiative has influenced how and where Malaysians shop for everyday essentials.
According to the survey, 72% of respondents changed their usual shopping store because SARA was not accepted at their preferred outlet, while 44% said they had travelled further to access a retailer where SARA could be used.
The findings have prompted the Malaysia Retail Chain Association (MRCA) to call for convenience stores and pharmacies to be included in the SARA retail network to provide recipients with greater choice and more equitable access to their benefits.
Neighbourhood proximity remains a key consideration for Malaysians when purchasing everyday essentials.
The survey found that visiting a store near home was cited by:
However, access to SARA-eligible retailers has affected these usual shopping patterns.
Among respondents who could not use SARA at their preferred outlet, the most commonly cited reason was that the outlet did not accept SARA (35%), followed by the item they wanted to purchase being ineligible under the programme (29%).
The findings suggest a gap between where Malaysians typically purchase essential goods and the retail outlets currently qualified to accept SARA.
The survey also highlighted gaps in the types of products that can be purchased using SARA assistance.
Some of the most commonly purchased fresh food items included fresh vegetables and fruit (69%), as well as fresh meat, poultry, seafood and eggs (68%).
With the exception of eggs, fresh vegetables, fruits and meat are currently not covered by SARA, despite being among the items respondents most wanted to see included in the programme.
The survey also found that Malaysian households rely on a range of retail formats for their daily essentials, including:
Convenience stores, pharmacies and wet markets are currently not included as eligible SARA merchant channels.
The survey found particularly strong support for expanding the SARA retail network.
Among respondents:
The support comes alongside significant usage of these retail channels and evidence that SARA acceptance can influence consumers’ usual shopping behaviour.
The MRCA said the findings indicate strong demand for greater choice in where eligible Malaysians can use their SARA benefits.
“The high level of rakyat support, together with the significant usage of these channels and the impact of SARA acceptance on consumers’ usual shopping behaviour, indicates strong demand for greater choice in where eligible Malaysians can utilise their SARA benefits,” the association said.
The findings come as Malaysia continues to expand the SARA merchant network.
The Ministry of Finance announced in February 2026 that it was targeting 10,000 small grocery shops as SARA merchant partners by the end of 2026, while in June it reported that more than 13,500 shops nationwide were already registered.
The MRCA said the merchant network remains critical to ensuring accessibility and convenience for SARA recipients, and called for a level playing field that would allow convenience store chains and pharmacies to participate in the programme.
“The rakyat should be able to utilise their SARA benefit at any place at their convenience – be it convenience stores, pharmacies, mini markets or supermarkets etc.,” said Dato’ Liew Bin, President of MRCA.
The independent survey was conducted by Ipsos in Peninsular Malaysia and commissioned by MRCA to examine how SARA has affected purchasing behaviour.
The Social & Economic Research Initiative (SERI) subsequently analysed the independent survey findings and produced policy briefs aimed at identifying ways to strengthen the initiative, which benefits 22 million Malaysians and supports the local economy through its multiplier effect.
The findings provide an evidence base for consideration in the next stage of SARA’s development, with the survey showing that the initiative has a tangible influence on where recipients shop.
Two key recommendations have been put forward.
The first recommendation is to broaden SARA eligibility to include selected fresh foods, including fresh vegetables and fruit, as well as fresh meat, poultry and seafood.
According to the findings, expanding coverage to these food categories could help Malaysians access more nutritious food as part of a balanced diet.
The second recommendation is to qualify convenience stores, pharmacies and wet markets as additional SARA outlets, given their role as important retail touchpoints for recipients.
The current retail framework creates an uneven environment between retailers that accept SARA and those that do not.
Expanding both the range of eligible products and the network of participating retailers could make it easier for recipients to use their assistance at the outlets where they already shop for household essentials.
The survey findings point to the importance of convenience, proximity and product relevance in determining how effectively recipients can use their SARA benefits.
For the MRCA, addressing these access and eligibility gaps would allow SARA to better reflect the everyday shopping habits of Malaysians while giving recipients greater flexibility in choosing where to purchase essential goods.
As the SARA merchant network continues to expand, the association said these considerations should remain central to the programme’s next phase.

title: Beyond Another Podcast: How TEJ Is Building a Trusted Journal of Malaysian Entrepreneurship
bodyText:
By Aileen Anthony
It is a fair question. Podcasts have multiplied across almost every subject, from finance and personal development to entertainment, health and business. With microphones, cameras and digital platforms becoming increasingly accessible, almost anyone can start one. Gene Loo and Steven Fong, however, did not set out to create another casual conversation filmed around a table.
From the beginning, they wanted The Entrepreneur Journal , better known as TEJ, to feel closer to a cinematic business documentary. Every episode would have structure, emotional build-up and a carefully produced opening that worked almost like a film trailer. The intention was to draw viewers into an entrepreneur’s journey rather than simply record a discussion.
“We want people to feel like they are watching a movie. There is a hook, a build-up and then the actual episode. User experience is key to the production,” Gene explained. That ambition shows in TEJ’s production choices. Its emerging market position may also be driven by something deeper: the two people asking the questions have lived through many of the realities they are exploring.

Steven’s entrepreneurial journey has been anything but linear. Trained in interior architecture, he began working for himself shortly after college, building businesses across the entertainment and technology spaces he has always been passionate about.  Over the years, he founded several companies. Some he built and grew. Not every bet paid off. He has lived through failed partnerships, cash flow crises and hard pivots, but each experience sharpened his sense of what it actually takes to keep a business alive. “When a guest speaks about debt, shareholder conflict, hiring difficulties, cash flow or the collapse of a partnership, I don’t have to imagine the pressure; I know it,” Steven shared.
Gene arrived at TEJ through a different route. He began as an animator and game designer before joining what was then a games and animation studio, where he spent two decades. During that time, he progressed from junior artist to team lead, production manager and eventually head of production. He helped restructure divisions, build teams and grow the organisation to around 500 people. Yet after years in the industry, Gene began questioning what should come next. That transition arrived sooner than expected when the company was acquired  and Gene found himself caught between competing visions. Steven, meanwhile, was dealing with challenges of his own. The two met and their conversation sparked ideas and that led them to build something they were both passionate about.
Interestingly, the podcast was not their original business idea. Gene and Steven initially explored developing a functional beverage for entrepreneurs and high-performing individuals. They invested in research and formulation, but the economics proved challenging. Bringing the product to market would have required high manufacturing volumes and capital. They put the beverage on the back burner, for now.
The media component, however, could begin immediately. Their thinking for TEJ should be was inspired by the use of storytelling to build communities rather than simply promote products. More importantly, it could address a problem Steven had experienced personally: finding a suitable business mentor was difficult. TEJ could not replace direct mentorship, but it could make the experiences of many entrepreneurs accessible in one place.
“We wanted a platform where CEOs and business owners could sit down and answer the difficult or relevant questions that someone starting or running a business may have,” Steven said. “You may not have a mentor, but through TEJ, you could learn from many founders who have walked that path before you.”

The name of the podcast would aptly reflect that purpose. Both founders admired the cinematic treatment of interview programmes and began considering what could represent a broader business journey. The answer was a journal. A diary is often private, they shared, but a journal can be documented and revisited. Each TEJ episode, they felt, could become another page in a growing collection of entrepreneurial experience.
TEJ’s recent audience research offered the founders a welcome indication that their strategy is working. According to findings by Vodus Research, TEJ is tied as the second most preferred channel for business content among respondents in Malaysia, alongside other popular podcast channels . The survey showed that TEJ is reaching a concentrated and relevant business audience. The findings also pointed towards the qualities viewers associate with the platform: real entrepreneurial stories, useful business insights and a strong emotional connection with its guests.
“We believe the findings can be attributed to viewer experience,” Gene shared. For Steven, it is also about the willingness to continually improve by studying performance and audience response. Both, however, agree that authenticity matters. The objective is to create the warmth of a conversation between people who understand business while retaining the discipline necessary to produce a useful and engaging programme.
The survey also gave TEJ a clearer picture of what its audience appreciates. TEJ’s guests have included founders of small, lean enterprises, established SMEs and publicly listed companies. They come from different communities, industries and stages of development. For Steven and Gene, Malaysian entrepreneur stories must reinforce the value of local experiences drawn from across the country’s business community.
A company with a small team may generate millions in revenue. A large organisation may have impressive turnover but thin margins, heavy borrowings or little available cash. Entrepreneurship does not automatically mean wealth, just as employment does not automatically mean financial limitation. These are precisely the realities Gene and Steven want TEJ to reveal.
“The audience wants to understand how it relates to them. We need to drive the conversation towards business strategy, how someone improved sales, got out of debt or ran a campaign that tripled the business.” Not every entrepreneur will disclose profit margins or precise financial data, but TEJ encourages guests to share meaningful indicators, such as revenue, growth stages or the economic consequences of important decisions.

TEJ’s polished appearance conceals a production process that stretches across eight to ten weeks. Before filming, the team identifies and evaluates potential guests. Gene and Steven often meet them for a preliminary conversation. The team then conducts research, prepares questions and schedules filming.
The studio operates with multiple cameras recording in 4K, professional lighting and dedicated audio equipment. The material then moves to a post-production team for editing, colour grading, sound processing and subtitles. Post-production is part of the storytelling, not an afterthought. “Our editors understand TEJ’s visual language, particularly its signature opening trailers,” Gene explained.
For added reach, the podcast is repurposed into short-form videos, vertical trailers, thumbnails, captions and platform descriptions. “A crew of people are involved across the different stages of production, editorial, visual, audio and marketing expertise,” Steven said. “This commitment to quality is part of TEJ’s competitive positioning.”

TEJ is an intellectual property developed under Horizen Media Sdn. Bhd., the parent company Gene and Steven established. Their ambition extends well beyond operating a single podcast. The name itself captures that intent. Horizen, intentionally spelt with an ‘e’ instead of an ‘o’, brings together the ideas of horizon and zen — paired with mindfulness, balance and patience. It reflects the attitude the founders try to live by and the message they want to share: aim wide, but stay grounded and deliberate in how you get there. Under that banner, Horizen Media is developing channels across fitness and wellness.
TEJ’s editorial content also extends beyond YouTube. According to the founders, TEJ is available in more than 40 hotels, MyTV and TV Sarawak, giving the programme access to audiences outside conventional podcast platforms. Future plans include programmes in Mandarin or Cantonese and, eventually, regional editions for markets such as Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines.
Gene and Steven ultimately want TEJ to become a household name in the business niche, a ‘place’ people visit when they want to understand entrepreneurship, learn from leaders or hear questions rarely answered publicly. The positioning reveals entrepreneurship through a collective mentorship experience.
The Entrepreneur Journal may have started as one component of a larger business idea. But audience acceptance suggests it is now becoming the idea itself , a growing capture of what Malaysian entrepreneurship actually looks like, one difficult, instructive and occasionally triumphant ‘mike moment’ at a time.

title: Perak Entrepreneurs Set to Strengthen Export Readiness at Hari Eksport Perak 2026
bodyText:
The Perak State Government, through the Perak State Entrepreneur Secretariat (STeP), in collaboration with the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), will organise Hari Eksport Perak 2026 on 14 October 2026 at Hotel Kinta Riverfront, Ipoh.
The free forum is designed specifically for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), cooperatives and product- and service-based social enterprises in Perak, providing practical guidance to help local businesses assess their potential, strengthen export readiness and expand their reach into international markets.
Participation is limited to two representatives per company.
The initiative brings together MATRADE’s national export development expertise with the expertise of the Majlis Pembangunan Usahawan Perak (MPUP) and the Subcommittee on Market Expansion and Entrepreneurial Services Cluster, with support from key players within Malaysia’s export ecosystem.
Running from 8.30am to 5.30pm, Hari Eksport Perak 2026 will feature six main forum sessions involving government agencies, financial institutions, logistics providers and experienced exporters.
The sessions will cover key areas including:
The programme places emphasis on three key areas for Perak entrepreneurs: building a strong foundation of export knowledge, improving financial literacy for international trade, and understanding international economic and geopolitical dynamics.

title: Why WhatsApp Leads Go Quiet After the First Reply
bodyText:
By Vishesh Jain, Founder of Nudge
A customer messages a clinic in Kuala Lumpur during lunch: “Hi, how much is a consultation, and do you have a slot this week?”
The team replies quickly with the price. Then the conversation stops.
Nobody asks which day works, nobody checks the calendar, and nobody follows up when the customer goes quiet.
This is an illustrative example, not a customer case study. Yet it shows why response speed alone does not solve the problem. A fast first reply is useful, but it is only the beginning of the customer journey. What converts an enquiry is a clear next step, carried through reliably.
For many Malaysian SMEs, WhatsApp is already the front door. Customers use it to ask about prices, availability, locations and appointments. The problem is that the process behind the chat is often informal.
An owner replies from one phone, an employee checks another calendar, and a third person assumes somebody else will call back.
Leads are not always lost because nobody cared. They are lost because the business had no operating system after the first message.
A useful first reply does three things: it answers the immediate question, asks for the minimum information needed, and tells the customer what will happen next.
“A consultation is RM___” answers only one part of the enquiry.
“A consultation is RM___. Which branch and day would suit you? I can check the available times” moves the conversation forward.
Every new enquiry should also become one record with a simple status such as new, qualified, appointment offered, booked, not ready or closed.
It should have one owner and one next-action time.
This prevents duplicate replies and the more common problem: everybody assuming somebody else is handling it.
Qualification should make the customer’s decision easier, not turn the chat into a form.
A clinic may need the service, preferred branch and suitable day. A training provider may need the course, intended start date and whether the person prefers online or classroom learning. A home-service company may need the location, problem and urgency.
Three relevant questions are usually better than ten generic ones.
Sensitive, unusual or high-risk questions should go to a qualified person. The customer should also be able to say, “Please let me speak to someone,” and reach a human without repeating the whole conversation.
The most important step happens outside the chat.
If the customer wants an appointment, the business should check its real calendar, offer genuinely available times and record the confirmed booking in the system the team already uses.
A time selected in WhatsApp should not be treated as booked until the calendar accepts it.
The confirmation should make the next step obvious: date, time, branch, reference and any preparation instructions.
The same principle applies beyond appointments. A payment request should use the approved payment process. A site visit should appear in the employee’s calendar. A support request should enter the correct queue.
The conversation and the operating system must agree.
Interested customers do not always reply immediately.
They may be comparing options, checking with a family member or simply distracted. A good follow-up removes a specific piece of friction.
For example:
Repeating “just following up” several times adds no value.
The timing and type of message also matter. Under WhatsApp’s current Business Messaging Policy, a business may reply without a message template during the 24-hour customer-service window opened by the user’s latest message.
Outside that window, messages on the WhatsApp Business Platform must use an approved template. Businesses must also have the required permission to contact people, respect opt-outs and comply with applicable local law.
A template is a delivery format, not a licence to pester people.
A sensible follow-up sequence is short, relevant to the original enquiry and stopped as soon as the person replies, books, declines or opts out.
The purpose is to help a real customer complete the next step, not to keep a dormant conversation alive forever.
Automation is useful for routine steps, but it should stop when judgement matters.
Complaints, refunds, special pricing, sensitive information, repeated misunderstanding and direct requests for an employee are clear handover points.
A good handover includes the conversation history, answers already collected and action already attempted. The employee should not ask the customer to start again.
Once a person takes control, automated follow-ups should pause.
They should also stop after a booking, an opt-out, a wrong-number response or any change that makes the original message irrelevant.
Before automating more messages, an SME can strengthen its process by checking the following:
The strongest WhatsApp process is not the one that sends the most messages.
It is the one that leaves the fewest genuine enquiries without a useful outcome.
For a small business, that means making ownership visible, connecting the chat to real calendars and systems, following up with context, and bringing in a person at the right moment.
Software can support this process, but it cannot rescue a confused workflow.
Malaysian SMEs should first decide what a successful enquiry looks like, who owns each stage and when the system must stop. Once those rules are clear, automation becomes a practical employee aid rather than another inbox the team has to manage.

title: Mohamad Nizar Najib Drives Pahang’s Push for AI and Smart Agriculture
bodyText:
Pahang is taking steps to strengthen its agricultural and technology ecosystem through a new public-private collaboration aimed at bringing artificial intelligence (AI), emerging technologies and smart agriculture closer to local communities.
The initiative was launched through the Smart Harvest Series: Durian Meets AI Agri-tech Summit, initiated by YB Dato’ Mohamad Nizar bin Dato’ Sri Mohamad Najib, Pahang State Exco for Investments, Industrial Development, Science, Technology and Innovation.
The summit, held in Pekan on 1 October 2026, focused on how AI and emerging technologies can be responsibly applied to empower communities, improve public sector efficiency and address real-world challenges in agriculture.
For YB Dato’ Mohamad Nizar, the initiative also reflects a commitment to grooming anak Pahang by giving local communities greater access to technology, knowledge and opportunities to participate in the state’s digital transformation.
At the centre of the initiative is a public-private collaboration involving the Pusat Khidmat DUN Peramu Jaya, Universiti Malaysia Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah (UMPSA) and Global Renaissance Sdn Bhd.
Ms Jane Teo, Managing Director of Global Renaissance, unveiled plans to build a dedicated Pahang Tech Community by connecting local talent with proven technologies, international experts and innovation models from overseas, including Silicon Valley.
The initiative aims to give Pahang’s SMEs and students access to local technology sandboxes where they can test, validate and refine technologies against real-world challenges.
By creating an environment where technologies can be experimented with locally, the collaboration seeks to bridge the gap between international technology models and the needs of Pahang’s communities and industries.
The summit brought together experts from academia, agriculture, technology, business and professional services to discuss how digital transformation can move beyond theory and into practical applications.
Professor Chm. Dr Mohd Hasbi bin Ab Rahim, Deputy Vice-Chancellor of UMPSA, highlighted the need for stakeholders to move beyond theoretical concepts towards tangible and commercialised solutions.
The importance of real-world testing was reinforced by Muhammad Adlan bin Ma’arup, General Manager of Tanah Makmur Berhad, who discussed the challenges involved in adopting technology at farm level. He also offered a 95-acre segment of a farm as a testing ground for developers.
This creates an opportunity for technology providers and researchers to evaluate solutions under actual agricultural conditions rather than relying solely on demonstrations or controlled environments.
The summit also explored how emerging technologies could intersect with sustainability and the circular economy.
Assoc. Prof. Dr Chen Kai Hsien from Sinetics Accreditation International Ltd introduced a circular economy model linking local grain production with the creation of Sustainable Aviation Fuel.
Meanwhile, Alvin Tan Keng Yi, Senior Legal Associate of Daljit Singh Partnership, highlighted the legal considerations surrounding technology adoption and foreign investment.
He stressed the importance of robust contracts and urged local players to protect their data and intellectual property when engaging with foreign technology investors.
These discussions highlighted that smart agriculture is not simply about adopting new technology. Successful implementation also requires consideration of commercial, legal, data and intellectual property issues.
The role of AI in creating practical business value was another key focus of the summit.
John Pang, Solutions Engineer from Galaxy Software Services, demonstrated how AI needs to be incorporated into verifiable workflows and systems of record to generate meaningful business value while maintaining human accountability.
The summit also featured an Agentic AI Masterclass led by Thu Ya Kyaw, Senior DevRel Engineer from Google, who focused on building and simplifying generative AI solutions for developers and technology builders.
The masterclass introduced multimodal AI models and demonstrated how custom AI agents could be developed to address specific problems, including applications such as identifying durians using AI agents.
While AI can offer new capabilities for agriculture, the summit also highlighted the importance of having reliable data to support those systems.
Assoc. Prof. Ir. Ts. Dr Roshahliza Binti M Ramli of UMPSA’s Center for Bioaromatic Research emphasised that AI cannot be effective without high-quality data from the field.
She advocated controlled pilot testing of Internet of Things (IoT) systems before large-scale deployment, reinforcing the importance of validating agricultural technologies under real operating conditions.
Professor Madya Dr Mohamed Ariff bin Ameedeen, research fellow of UMPSA’s Centre for Artificial Intelligence & Data Science, meanwhile shared practical experiences from the digital transformation journeys of startups.
His presentation demonstrated how academic research can be translated into deployable industry applications, strengthening the connection between research institutions and businesses.
The summit also introduced an Agricultural Industry Reverse Pitching Session, allowing industry players to communicate their operational challenges directly to researchers and technology providers.
Rather than technology developers presenting solutions without first understanding industry needs, the reverse pitching approach gives agricultural businesses an opportunity to explain the problems they are actually facing.
The aim is to encourage researchers, developers and businesses to build solutions around genuine market requirements.
Affandi bin Mohd Isa, CEO of Pahang Go and representative of YB Dato’ Nizar, reinforced this approach by stressing that research and technology should move beyond demonstrations and be actively implemented to solve real industry bottlenecks.
The various initiatives presented during the summit reflect a broader ambition to build local technological capabilities alongside agricultural innovation.
Through the proposed Pahang Tech Community, local SMEs and students can gain opportunities to experiment with technologies, engage with international expertise and develop solutions for local challenges.
The collaboration between the Pusat Khidmat DUN Peramu Jaya, UMPSA and Global Renaissance provides a framework for connecting these local capabilities with international technology networks.
By combining YB Dato’ Mohamad Nizar’s state-level vision with Jane Teo’s international experience and networks, the initiative aims to give anak Pahang a more direct role in developing the technologies that could shape the state’s agricultural future.
The Smart Harvest Series ultimately positioned technology as a means of addressing practical agricultural and economic challenges rather than an end in itself.
From AI agents and IoT systems to field testing, academic research and international technology partnerships, the summit brought together different parts of the innovation ecosystem around a common objective: developing solutions that can work in the real world.
The public-private partnership is intended to help make Pahang’s agricultural economy smarter, more connected and more technology-driven, while creating opportunities for local students, SMEs, researchers and technology providers to participate in that transformation.
For Pahang, the ambition is not simply to adopt technologies developed elsewhere, but to give its own communities the opportunity to test, adapt and eventually build solutions around the challenges they understand best.

title: IRGCE 2026 Generates Over RM6 Billion in Potential Rubber Glove Business
bodyText:
The 12th International Rubber Glove Conference & Exhibition 2026 (IRGCE 2026) concluded with strong international participation and significant business prospects, reinforcing Malaysia’s position within the global rubber glove industry.
Organised by the Malaysian Rubber Glove Manufacturers Association (MARGMA) together with co-host Malaysian Rubber Council (MRC), the event was held from 8 to 10 September 2026 at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre (KLCC).
Post-event feedback indicated potential business sales of more than US$1.48 billion, equivalent to over RM6 billion, over the next six months, highlighting the commercial opportunities and business connections generated through the event.
IRGCE 2026 attracted nearly 9,000 visitors from 75 countries, with 215 exhibitors from 17 countries occupying 605 exhibition booths.
The conference also drew approximately 600 delegates from 22 countries, bringing together participants from across the global rubber glove ecosystem.
MARGMA President Mr Oon Kim Hung said the strong participation reaffirmed IRGCE’s role as an important global platform for the rubber glove industry.
“IRGCE is more than an exhibition and conference. It is where the industry comes together to exchange ideas, understand market developments, explore new technologies and create new business opportunities and partnerships.”
Held under the theme “Synergising Innovation: Redefining the Future of the Rubber Glove Ecosystem,” the event brought together manufacturers, buyers, suppliers, technology providers, researchers, regulators and other industry stakeholders.
The conference examined key developments shaping the future of the rubber glove industry, including global trade and market access, automation, artificial intelligence, advanced materials, sustainability, regulatory requirements and talent development.
The exhibition, meanwhile, gave participants opportunities to explore new technologies and solutions, reconnect with existing business partners and establish new commercial relationships.
The programme featured international and Malaysian experts including Dr Robert G. Hamilton of Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Dr Zhaomin Hou of RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science, Prof Dato’ Dr Adeeba Kamarulzaman of Monash University Malaysia, Prof Alex Routh of the University of Cambridge and Prof Dr Yeah Kim Leng of the Jeffrey Cheah Institute on Southeast Asia.
The breadth of topics and expertise reflected the increasing importance of technology, innovation and cross-sector collaboration to the future competitiveness of the rubber glove industry.
Mr Oon said the industry’s continued competitiveness would increasingly depend on its ability to innovate, improve productivity and create greater value.
“Our future cannot depend only on scale. It must depend on how well we operate, how quickly we adapt, how effectively we innovate and how much value we can create.”
The emphasis on productivity and innovation comes as manufacturers face an increasingly competitive global market and the need to move towards higher-value production.
MARGMA said continued investment in innovation, technology, productivity and higher-value manufacturing will be important to strengthening Malaysia’s position in the global rubber glove market.
The Malaysian rubber glove industry continues to make a significant contribution to the country’s exports.
In the first half of 2026, rubber gloves generated more than RM7 billion in export revenue, accounting for approximately 66% of Malaysia’s total rubber product exports.
The Malaysian Rubber Council has also projected global glove consumption to reach approximately 405 billion pieces in 2026, compared with around 290 billion pieces in 2019.
The projected growth reflects continued demand for rubber gloves across healthcare, industrial, cleanroom and other applications.
For Malaysian manufacturers, the outlook reinforces the importance of maintaining competitiveness while responding to evolving market requirements and investing in technology and productivity.
Beyond its role as an industry conference and exhibition, IRGCE provided a platform for businesses across the rubber glove ecosystem to develop commercial relationships.
The more than US$1.48 billion in potential business sales indicated through post-event feedback highlights the scale of opportunities generated through the event.
With manufacturers, buyers, suppliers, technology providers and other stakeholders gathered in Kuala Lumpur, the event also provided opportunities for participants to explore new markets, technologies and partnerships.
MARGMA expressed its appreciation to the Malaysian Rubber Council as co-host, along with supporting ministries and agencies, sponsors, supporting organisations, exhibitors, speakers, delegates and industry partners for their contributions to IRGCE 2026.
Following the conclusion of this year’s event, MARGMA announced that the 13th International Rubber Glove Conference & Exhibition will return to the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre from 5 to 7 September 2028.
“We look forward to building on the momentum of IRGCE 2026 and welcoming the global rubber glove community back to Kuala Lumpur in 2028,” Mr Oon said.
With Malaysia continuing to play a major role in the global rubber glove industry, the next edition is expected to provide another platform for manufacturers, technology providers, buyers and industry stakeholders to explore new business opportunities and developments across the sector.

title: What Will Keep Retail Relevant? Reimagining the Rules of Malaysia’s Retail Growth
bodyText:
By Aileen Anthony, Executive Editor, MALAYSIA SME

The scale of commerce flowing through Malaysia is equally significant. Wholesale and retail trade recorded RM163.7 billion in sales in December 2025 alone, an increase of 7.6 per cent year-on-year, while retail trade grew 6.9 per cent. For the full year, the volume index for wholesale and retail trade expanded 4.8 per cent. Yet behind the numbers, the economics of running a retail business are becoming considerably more complex.
Consumers can compare products across multiple platforms without entering a store. Online marketplaces have widened choice and intensified price competition. Retailers are simultaneously dealing with higher rentals, manpower costs, utilities and other operating expenses, while technology and artificial intelligence (AI) are changing how products are discovered, marketed and purchased.
CHAT MALAYSIA SME spoke with Dato’ Liew Bin, President of the Malaysia Retail Chain Association (MRCA),  about the changing economics of retail, why physical stores continue to matter, the role of AI and data, the advantage smaller retailers may now possess, and why Malaysia’s culture could ultimately become one of the industry’s strongest competitive assets.

Dato’ Liew traces much of retail’s transformation back to the internet and, subsequently, the smartphone. What started as another channel has progressively altered consumer behaviour. Today, the customer standing in a store is no longer comparing that retailer only with the shop next door. The comparison can involve multiple platforms, sellers and countries.
“Spending did not change. People still buy what they need to buy,” he said. What has changed is how consumers decide where to spend. Previously, online shopping was often used to find something unavailable locally. Today, particularly among younger consumers, comparing online has become an ordinary part of purchasing.

“Anything I buy, I compare all platforms,” Dato’ Liew said. Consumers can compare prices “anytime, any minute” before deciding where to buy. The result is greater transparency for consumers but considerably more competition for retailers. That pressure is also contributing to retailers’ dependence on promotions, vouchers and discounts. But price cannot be the only answer. The physical store still has a role.
Dato’ Liew shared that the advantage of the physical store is something digital commerce struggles to replicate. “First, you’ve got a human touch. Second, you can touch and feel the product.” But the role of physical retail he said is becoming broader than the transaction itself.  Malaysia’s malls remain social destinations where people meet, shop and spend time together.  In Dato’ Liew’s view, this shift in consumer behaviour will need retailers to increasingly compete on experience, interaction and relevance, rather than simply availability.

The changing environment also challenges one of retail’s oldest growth equations. “Traditionally, when you talk about growth, you open more chain stores,” said Dato’ Liew. But as shopping centres multiplied, retailers expanded alongside them and several outlets within the same catchment can end up serving essentially the same population.
Dato’ Liew shared, “Growth may not necessarily follow by opening more outlets,” he said, adding that even when revenue increases, net income and profitability may not follow. Retailers therefore need the discipline not only to decide where to open, but when an existing outlet no longer makes economic sense. “You must decide whether you want to close or not. That’s a very important decision for the retailers.”

Technology could help retailers make those decisions better. For Dato’ Liew, one of AI’s most practical applications is understanding the data businesses already possess. Retailers can use technology to analyse stock, sales and customer demand, giving management greater visibility over what is selling, what is not and who their customers are. The advantage comes from translating information into better decisions on inventory, customers, marketing and operations. Dato’ Liew’s message is succinct: “If you don’t adapt to it, you lose out.”

Interestingly, Dato’ Liew opined that the changing landscape may create opportunities for smaller retailers. “The bigger the chain store you are, you could be facing bigger challenges,” he said. Smaller businesses can possess a different advantage: agility. “When you are small, you’ve got a lot of personal touch.”
Owners can stay closer to customers, respond faster and make decisions without multiple management layers. This can be particularly powerful in F&B and specialist retail, where customers may return because of a product, personality, recipe, craft or experience associated with one particular business.
Dato’ Liew shared that being small should not automatically be interpreted as being less successful. A highly profitable single outlet can be a stronger business than a larger network burdened by escalating costs.
“A Home for Retailers” is a philosophy that shapes Dato’ Liew’s direction for MRCA. When he assumed the presidency, he wanted the association to become what he calls a “home” for retailers, not only established chains, but smaller and emerging businesses. “The big brands may not need us as much as the smaller brands,” he said. At the same time, he emphasised, established brands provide experience and mentors who can help younger retailers. “Big and small, we need to move together, grow together.”

Looking towards 2030, Dato’ Liew believes one of Malaysia’s strongest retail advantages may be something competitors cannot easily reproduce: culture. He opined that Malaysia’s multicultural population, languages, food and hospitality create an experience he believes can become a commercial asset.
“This is something that nobody can take from us,” he said. And that advantage does not have to remain within Malaysia. “As retailers, we can export our culture.” For Malaysian F&B and retail brands, international expansion can be more than exporting products. It can be about taking a recognisably Malaysian experience into other markets.

Dato’ Liew’s closing message, however, returns to the independent retailer. Across Malaysia are businesses handed from grandparents to parents and then to the next generation. Some are now struggling with rising costs and changing consumer behaviour. He believes they must change with what he calls the “disruptive economy”. Working hard is no longer enough; retailers also have to work smart. But adaptation does not mean discarding what made the business special.
“Focus on that one tradition that makes your business special.” And for the retailer operating only one outlet , his message is particularly poignant. “Do not feel discouraged. Sometimes small is beautiful.”

Because ultimately, success in the next chapter of Malaysian retail may not be determined simply by how many outlets a business can open. It may depend on understanding what customers cannot easily find anywhere else and having the discipline to preserve it. As Dato’ Liew put it: “You are not keeping a shop. You are keeping a legend.”
Sources for Opening Statistics
Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), Gross Domestic Product 2025; and Performance of Wholesale & Retail Trade, December 2025.

title: What Am I Investing In? Building the Business Before Building the IPO
bodyText:
By Aileen Anthony, Executive Editor, MALAYSIA SME
Malaysia’s Initial Public Offering (IPO) market has gathered considerable momentum. In 2025, Bursa Malaysia recorded 60 new listings, up from 55 in 2024 and the highest annual number since 2005. Eleven companies listed on the Main Market, 44 on the ACE Market and five on the LEAP Market. Together, the new listings raised RM6 billion and added RM27.4 billion in IPO market capitalisation. Malaysia also recorded the highest number of IPOs among ASEAN exchanges for the second consecutive year. The numbers reflect the capital market’s broader role in enabling home-grown companies to access capital, expand, and move into their next stage of growth.
CHAT MALAYSIA SME spoke with Dato’ Lock Peng Kuan, Managing Partner, Audit & Assurance at Baker Tilly Malaysia, about what companies need to get right long before they embark on an IPO, the gaps that emerge when businesses begin that journey, and why a credible equity story must ultimately answer the question every investor is asking.
When companies approach Baker Tilly about a potential IPO, one of the first questions is why. “A lot of companies, when they come to us, they say, ‘I have hit the number, I have the size, so I am prepared to list.’ From my experience, most owners can’t clearly articulate their intention for listing; they’re there simply because they hit the threshold. So the next natural step is to go for listing,” shared Dato’ Lock.
Reaching a certain size does not automatically make an IPO the right next step. The business first needs to establish what it intends to achieve with the capital it plans to raise.
“If you are successful in your listing, how would you utilise your proceeds? Is it to buy machinery? Is it going for regional expansion? Is it to strengthen your balance sheet?”

The motivation, Dato’ Lock explained could be various including, expansion, succession planning, or institutionalising the business for its next chapter. Depending on the objective, alternatives such as private equity, peer-to-peer financing or equity crowdfunding may also be appropriate. “Very importantly, the owner must know what the motivation is before they start the IPO process.”
Once an IPO becomes the chosen destination, Dato’ Lock emphasised that preparation should begin years in advance. “Ideally,  the preparation should start three years before,” said Dato’ Lock. In practice, however, many companies tend to begin considerably later. “When an IPO case comes in one year before the submission, that compresses years of audit, compliance and preparation into a much shorter period.”
Companies that prepare earlier approach the journey differently. “They have the end in mind. They may not have decided when would be the best time to list, but they are  building the company in a way that they are prepared to assume the role as a public company.” This includes progressively strengthening financial reporting and developing a much deeper understanding of the business behind the accounts.
“It’s not just about having audited numbers. Management must understand why revenue grows from year to year, why margins have changed, where the better profit margins are coming from, which particular line of service or product drives profitability, and what happens to working capital and cash flow, among other considerations.”
Because, Dato’ Lock emphasised,  “Management will eventually need to explain how the company arrived at its current position and a business that consistently tracks its performance is not forced to reconstruct its history when the IPO process begins.”

A company may be profitable, growing and seemingly ready for the capital market. Yet the weaknesses uncovered during IPO preparation are often fundamental. According to Dato’ Lock, gaps emerge in documentation, data extraction, account closures, reporting processes, regulatory compliance and the internal resources available to support the IPO.
“They are numbers, but they (the numbers) may be all over the place. Data  needs to be compartmentalised in the right context.” This is why preparation cannot be treated as a last-minute exercise.  Closing  gaps takes time and   newly introduced processes must prove that they work. “You need time actually to put in the processes, but you also need time to test again to see whether the newly implemented processes hold water,” cautioned Dato’ Lock.
“Besides numbers accuracy, businesses should be looking at the timely closure of financial numbers.”  Management must understand cash flow, debtor turnover, stock ageing  and its balance sheet. It  needs reliable accounting systems, internal controls, clear approval processes and defined responsibilities.
The same applies to data. “Data quality is important.” The reason goes beyond operational efficiency. Clean, properly organised data allows management to understand the business and explain its performance. It becomes the evidence behind the story the company eventually takes to investors.
Another critical transition is reducing excessive dependence on the founder. “Most entrepreneur-driven businesses in Malaysia are founder-driven. The success of the company is very much tied to the success of the founders.” That influence may have driven the company’s success, but a business seeking external investors must show it can operate beyond one individual.
“It doesn’t mean that we dilute the impact of the founders . It’s more about putting the founder’s decisions into the process, system and, importantly, the governance.”
This means addressing related-party transactions, potential conflicts of interest and management override of controls. It also means establishing professional management, accountability and clear decision-making authority.
“Suppose the founders go away for three months or six months. The business should continue.” The objective is to build “the system, process and the people to safeguard the business” while allowing the founder to focus increasingly on strategic direction and future growth.
The same principle applies to systems. Informal practices may work when the company is small, but eventually they reach their limit. “It gets you to a certain size, but from there, how do you actually scale?” IPO readiness is therefore closely connected to institutional readiness. The company has to demonstrate that its people, governance, information and processes can support the scale it is promising investors.
This is where, Dato’ Lock explained, the business story has to evolve. “The business story and the product story are about how the business operates. But as we move into the equity market, commonly known as the stock market, we need to build the equity story. A company may have very strong products or services and good sales, but investors are not only looking at what the company is doing today.”
Instead, they (investors) ask two fundamental questions. “‘What am I investing in?’ and ‘What could this company become over the next few years?’”

A credible equity story answers those questions across four areas. The first is market opportunity . “What is the market opportunity? Is the industry still growing? Is there a clear demand for the products that you are selling?” The second is competitive position . What is the competitive position of the company? Why is this business so different from your competitor? What is the barrier to entry into your industry?”
The third is growth . Investors need to understand whether future growth will come from increased capacity, new markets, overseas expansion, new products or acquisitions. The fourth is management . “Does the management team have the ability and capacity to embrace the growth?”
Together, market opportunity, competitive positioning, identifiable growth drivers and management capability turn the business story into an investment proposition. “The equity story is all about credibility.” And that credibility is built from evidence, not aspiration. “The best test is based on what you have achieved in the past, because the past fortifies the future”
Dato’ Lock added, “Managing perception ahead of an IPO is not simply about generating greater visibility. It is about helping investors understand the company behind the product, how it has created value, what has brought it to its present position and why that track record gives credibility to what it says it can become.”

Sustainability, Dato’ Lock said, has also become part of that assessment of future value. “Sustainability has evolved from a good-to-have initiative to a must-have initiative because investors nowadays are not only looking at the hard financial numbers.” It is increasingly connected to “business strategy, governance, risk management and operational resilience. Investors want to see whether the company understands the environmental, social and governance factors that could impact future performance.”

For an SME that might consider listing five or ten years from now, Dato’ Lock’s advice is clear. “They should be looking at the following, financial reporting processes, robust internal controls, even as basic as hiring professionally qualified accountants, forming a capable team and having a sustainable growth strategy.”
“The companies that start early have more options, more flexibility and a smoother journey when the opportunity for IPO arises.” His final advice brings the journey back to its starting point. “Don’t wait until you have decided to list but build a business today that has potential to be listed tomorrow.”

Baker Tilly (Malaysia) is the 6 th largest accounting and advisory firm in Malaysia, with 80 Partners and Directors, 14 offices across Malaysia and a staff force of 1000 professionals.

title: Malaysian Companies Generate RM305.62 Million at CAEXPO 2026
bodyText:
Malaysian companies generated RM305.62 million in sales at the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) 2026, surpassing the initial RM275 million target by 11.1%.
Coordinated by the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), Malaysia’s participation at CAEXPO took place from 17 to 21 September 2026 at the Nanning International Convention & Exhibition Center (NICEC) in Guangxi, China.
A total of 67 Malaysian companies participated, with the majority comprising small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The companies represented a range of high-value and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sectors, including artificial intelligence (AI), medical devices, household products, food and beverages, agricultural produce, personal care and cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and tourism.
The results highlight the ability of Malaysian SMEs to connect with international buyers, explore new market opportunities, expand global business networks and convert these engagements into business deals.
To maximise business outcomes for participating companies, MATRADE organised a series of targeted business and promotional activities throughout CAEXPO.
These initiatives were designed to facilitate direct engagement between Malaysian exhibitors and potential buyers and strategic partners, while strengthening the visibility of Malaysian brands in the China and ASEAN markets.
Activities included B2B business matching sessions with China Construction Bank (CCB), as well as engagements under the 2026 China-ASEAN Silk Road E-Commerce Promotion Event.
Malaysian exhibitors also took part in pitching sessions, product selection programmes with selected buyers, live-streaming sessions with key opinion leaders (KOLs) and a market visit to Sam’s Club, among other supporting activities.
The initiatives aimed to help Malaysian SMEs better understand market demand, identify potential distribution channels and establish business connections that could support sustained export growth.
MATRADE Chief Executive Officer YBhg. Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof said empowering SMEs to compete on the global stage remains a central priority for the organisation.
“The multi-pronged tools and platforms have proven effective with the outcomes achieved. It is a clear testament to the resilience, quality and export capability of our SMEs. CAEXPO serves as a vital springboard for smaller, high-potential Malaysian enterprises to scale beyond domestic borders. MATRADE’s structured business matching and digital outreach strategies ensure that our SMEs do not just exhibit, but establish concrete, long-term commercial partnerships in China and ASEAN,” he said.
He added that MATRADE would continue to strengthen capability-building programmes and market access platforms to help more Malaysian SMEs transition into global exporters.
Malaysia’s participation at CAEXPO 2026 also received recognition, with MATRADE presented with two awards: Best Exhibition Organiser and Special Contributor for Trade and Investment Promotion.
The awards recognised MATRADE’s contribution to CAEXPO and its efforts to promote trade and investment.
The latest results build on Malaysia’s longstanding participation in the China-ASEAN trade platform. Since CAEXPO was established, more than 2,400 Malaysian companies, predominantly SMEs, have participated in the exhibition.
Malaysia’s continued participation reflects sustained interest among local businesses in using CAEXPO as a platform to access the China market, build regional networks and explore opportunities across ASEAN.
MATRADE had previously highlighted CAEXPO as a platform for Malaysian exporters to connect with buyers, distributors and business partners while strengthening their visibility and competitiveness in China and ASEAN.
The 2026 results further demonstrate the role of international trade exhibitions and structured business matching in helping Malaysian SMEs identify overseas opportunities, develop commercial partnerships and expand their presence beyond the domestic market.

title: What Southeast Asia’s Next Generation of Industrial Talent Needs to Learn
bodyText:
By Atlas Copco
For decades, the skills expected of industrial employees were relatively easy to define. Engineers understood machines. Technicians knew how to diagnose faults. Service teams maintained equipment, while sales professionals understood products and customer requirements.
That is changing.
Industrial environments across Southeast Asia are becoming increasingly connected, automated and data-driven. Equipment can generate real-time performance data, remote monitoring can identify unusual behaviour before a breakdown occurs, and digital technologies can help anticipate problems. AI-supported systems can also turn operating data into recommendations on maintenance, uptime and energy use.
The next generation of engineers, technicians, service professionals and even commercial teams will therefore need more than mechanical knowledge or digital literacy in isolation. They will need to understand how the two work together.
Consider the changing role of a service engineer.
Historically, much of the job centred on inspecting equipment, identifying a physical problem and repairing or replacing the affected component. Those skills remain essential, but the information available to engineers is changing.
Connected industrial equipment can now provide data on operating conditions, energy consumption, maintenance requirements and potential abnormalities before a technician arrives on site.
For example, Atlas Copco Malaysia’s SMARTLINK monitoring technology captures live data from compressed air equipment and translates it into insights on uptime, energy efficiency and equipment health. Its remote diagnostics capabilities use smart algorithms and expert analysis to identify deviations at an early stage, supporting proactive troubleshooting.
This changes the skill set required of the person responsible for the machine.
Operations professionals need to interpret dashboards as well as understand production processes. Engineers need to understand sensors, connectivity and automation alongside mechanical systems. Technicians increasingly need to combine physical inspection with information gathered remotely.
The industrial worker is consequently becoming a hybrid professional, combining traditional technical expertise with digital capabilities.
There is a danger, however, in interpreting this shift as a requirement for every industrial employee to become a programmer or AI specialist.
What industrial companies increasingly need is applied data literacy: the ability to interpret information within the context of equipment, processes and customer operations.
Employees do not necessarily need to build AI models. They increasingly need to understand what digital information is telling them about equipment performance, maintenance, energy efficiency and customer operations.
The strongest industrial talent will not necessarily be those who know the most about software. It will be those who can connect digital information with engineering judgement.
Technical education has traditionally rewarded knowing the correct answer. Modern industrial environments increasingly reward knowing how to investigate a problem.
As equipment becomes more complex and interconnected, employees will need stronger diagnostic and systems-thinking capabilities.
This is where human judgement becomes more valuable, not less.
AI and remote diagnostics can narrow the field of possibilities, but experienced people still need to understand the operating environment well enough to determine what happens next. Technology can provide more information, but people still need to interpret that information and make decisions based on the circumstances.
Malaysia offers a useful illustration of the scale of this challenge.
The country’s industrial sector is moving towards more sophisticated and technology-intensive activity. Malaysia recorded RM131.3 billion in approved manufacturing investments in 2025, with the investments expected to create 109,950 new jobs. Nearly half, or 46.3%, of these positions fall within managerial and technical categories, highlighting the growing demand for higher-skilled industrial talent.
Talent development therefore needs to keep pace with industrial transformation.
Research by TalentCorp into the impact of AI, digitalisation and the green economy similarly found that approximately 620,000 employees across the sectors it studied could be significantly affected by technological and economic shifts. The research identified 60 emerging roles and mapped hundreds of skills required to support workforce transitions.
That requires deeper collaboration between employers, universities and technical institutions.
There are already examples of this model. Atlas Copco Malaysia’s Compressed Air Service Academy operates as a regional training hub for Southeast Asia, providing competency development for service employees, distributors and customer operations and maintenance teams.
Its training programmes combine equipment fundamentals with maintenance, troubleshooting, monitoring and control systems. Courses cover areas such as equipment operation, maintenance procedures, basic troubleshooting, energy saving and monitoring, showing how technical training can incorporate both traditional engineering knowledge and newer digital capabilities.
As companies expand teams in areas such as service, sales and marketing, these programmes point to a broader reality: industrial capability development is no longer confined to engineering departments.
Industrial sales and marketing roles are becoming more technically demanding because the products themselves are increasingly sold as part of a broader operational solution.
A commercial team needs enough technical fluency to understand a customer’s operation, identify the problem and communicate how the technology addresses it.
The traditional boundary between the “technical” and “business” sides of an industrial company is therefore becoming less useful.
Sales professionals do not need to become engineers, just as engineers do not need to become salespeople. But both increasingly benefit from understanding how technology creates value for the customer.
This could mean understanding equipment performance, energy efficiency, automation, maintenance requirements or the operational impact of downtime.
Perhaps the biggest change employers need to make is abandoning the idea that industrial education largely finishes when someone enters the workforce.
Training cannot be treated as an occasional intervention when new equipment arrives. It has to become part of the operating model.
That means giving employees time to learn, providing structured technical and digital training, and creating career pathways that reward employees for building skills beyond their original discipline.
This is particularly important as technologies continue to evolve. The skills required to operate and maintain industrial equipment today may not be the same as those required several years from now.
Continuous learning therefore needs to become part of how industrial careers are structured, rather than something employees are expected to pursue separately from their jobs.
Southeast Asia has spent much of the past decade positioning itself as an increasingly important manufacturing and industrial region.
The encouraging part is that technology does not eliminate the need for traditional industrial expertise. Instead, it can make that expertise more valuable when combined with new capabilities.
Consider the engineer who understands machinery and data.
The technician who can combine remote diagnostics with physical inspection.
The salesperson who understands both customer economics and industrial technology.
The operations professional who knows when to trust an algorithm and when to question it.
These are the hybrid capabilities likely to define Southeast Asia’s next generation of industrial talent.
The question for employers and educators is whether workforce development can evolve quickly enough to produce them.
As industrial technology continues to advance, the competitive advantage may not simply belong to companies with the most sophisticated equipment or software. It may increasingly belong to those with people capable of understanding, applying and adapting that technology.

title: IDECS26 Brings Five Tracks Together to Turn Technology Ambitions into Industry Opportunities
bodyText:
As Sarawak expands its ambitions in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and space technology, the next challenge is not simply building these capabilities, but turning them into solutions that industries can use, businesses can build around and communities can benefit from.
This challenge will run across five interconnected tracks at the ninth International Digital Economy Conference Sarawak (IDECS26), bringing together different parts of the ecosystem needed to move technology from potential to application.
The five tracks are The Future, Future Cities, Startup Village, SHE-TECH Asia Forum 2026 and the inaugural Centre of Excellence (CoE) for Digital Research Conference.
Taking place from 5 to 6 October at the Borneo Convention Centre Kuching (BCCK), IDECS26 is hosted by the Sarawak Government and jointly organised by the Sarawak Digital Economy Corporation (SDEC), Sarawak Multimedia Authority (SMA) and Sarawak Information Systems (SAINS).
This year’s conference carries the theme “Scaling Innovation Ecosystems for a Borderless Economy: Earth, Orbit & Beyond.”
The focus comes as Sarawak moves into the next phase of its digital economy agenda, with growing capabilities across AI, semiconductor design, smart infrastructure and space technology.
The state is also exploring the development of satellite-grade semiconductor chips and systems alongside its planned satellite programme. These capabilities could open potential downstream applications in areas including earth observation, forestry, disaster management, carbon tracking and maritime monitoring.
For Yang Berhormat Dato Sri Haji Julaihi Haji Narawi, Minister for Utility and Telecommunication, the priority is ensuring the right conditions are in place for these emerging industries to develop and create economic value.
“Sarawak has made deliberate investments over the years to build the foundations of a digital economy, from connectivity and infrastructure to talent and innovation. We are now entering the next phase, where the measure of success is not how much technology we deploy, but the economic value we create from it. Our ambition is to build a RM282 billion economy by 2030. Digitalisation will be critical to that growth because it gives us the ability to raise productivity across industries, compete for higher-value investment and develop new sources of economic growth.”
He added that Sarawak wants its investments to attract private capital, create higher-value industries within the state and give Sarawakian companies and talent a stronger position in regional and global markets.
“IDECS26 is where we bring those ambitions together with the partners who can help us take them to scale,” he said.
