SDEC Chairman Tan Sri Datuk Amar Mohamad Morshidi bin Abdul Ghani said IDECS26 would build on Sarawak’s work in AI, digital talent and future cities while bringing semiconductors and the space economy further into the discussion.
“IDECS must therefore be more than a conference where ideas are presented. It should be a place where international knowledge meets local capability, where relationships are formed, and where conversations can move towards research, investment, deployment and commercial opportunities,” he said.
The five tracks are designed to address different parts of the same economic challenge.
The Future will examine the infrastructure and capabilities required to support emerging industries, while Future Cities will explore how technology can address operational and public-service challenges.
The CoE for Digital Research Conference will connect research with potential users and commercial applications. Startup Village will focus on helping turn ideas into companies, customers and investment.
Meanwhile, the SHE-TECH Asia Forum 2026 will examine whether leadership and the talent pipeline can keep pace with the industries being developed.
Together, the tracks provide industry participants with multiple entry points into the same ecosystem, whether through research collaboration, technology testing, startup partnerships, investment opportunities or public and industry challenges that could lead to deployment.
IDECS26 will also bring international perspectives to the discussion through five highlight speakers whose work spans industries shaping the next phase of the digital economy.
Dr Soichi Noguchi, former astronaut and project professor at the University of Tokyo, will bring insight into the growing commercial space economy.
Architect and urbanist Professor Jason Pomeroy will examine the future of sustainable and technology-enabled cities, while technology entrepreneur and futurist Dr Catherine Ball will explore emerging technologies and new possibilities for industry.
AI pioneer Professor De Kai will address how artificial intelligence is reshaping the way businesses and societies operate, while Dr Nici Sweaney, founder of AI Her Way, will examine the leadership required as AI becomes increasingly embedded in organisations and decision-making.
Dr Noguchi will open IDECS26 with the keynote “Earth, Orbit and Beyond: The Potential of the Space Business”, examining how the space sector is moving beyond government-led programmes into a growing commercial economy.
He will also explore what this shift could mean for regions beginning to develop their own space capabilities.
“A satellite launch is an important milestone, but the economic value comes from the services built around it. For Sarawak, that means developing the talent and partnerships to turn satellite data into solutions for environmental monitoring, disaster response and resource management, and finding the people and businesses who will use them,” Noguchi said.
Across its five tracks, IDECS26 will focus on what it takes for technology to progress beyond research and pilot projects into wider industry use.
This includes putting the right infrastructure in place, connecting research with businesses that can apply it, helping startups find customers and capital, and developing the talent required to support emerging industries as they grow.
For Sarawak, the conference provides a platform to bring these different elements together as the state continues building its digital economy and exploring new opportunities across AI, semiconductors, smart infrastructure and the space economy.

title: IRGCE 2026 Generates Over RM6 Billion in Potential Rubber Glove Business
bodyText:
The 12th International Rubber Glove Conference & Exhibition 2026 (IRGCE 2026) concluded at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre (KLCC), recording strong international participation and encouraging business prospects for Malaysia’s rubber glove industry.
Held from 8 to 10 September 2026, the event was organised by the Malaysian Rubber Glove Manufacturers Association (MARGMA), together with co-host the Malaysian Rubber Council (MRC).
IRGCE 2026 attracted nearly 9,000 visitors from 75 countries, with 215 exhibitors from 17 countries occupying 605 exhibition booths. The conference also drew approximately 600 delegates from 22 countries.
Post-event feedback indicated potential business sales of more than US$1.48 billion, equivalent to over RM6 billion, over the following six months. MARGMA said the figure reflected the commercial opportunities and business connections generated through the event.
MARGMA President Mr Oon Kim Hung said the strong participation reaffirmed IRGCE’s role as an important global platform for the rubber glove industry.
“IRGCE is more than an exhibition and conference. It is where the industry comes together to exchange ideas, understand market developments, explore new technologies and create new business opportunities and partnerships.”
Held under the theme “Synergising Innovation: Redefining the Future of the Rubber Glove Ecosystem,” IRGCE 2026 brought together manufacturers, buyers, suppliers, technology providers, researchers, regulators and other stakeholders from across the global rubber glove ecosystem.
The conference addressed developments shaping the future of the industry, including global trade and market access, automation, artificial intelligence, advanced materials, sustainability, regulatory requirements and talent development.
The exhibition, meanwhile, provided participants with opportunities to explore new technologies and solutions, reconnect with business partners and establish new commercial relationships.
IRGCE 2026 also featured international and Malaysian experts from academia, research and industry.
Speakers included Dr Robert G. Hamilton of Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Dr Zhaomin Hou of RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science, Prof Dato’ Dr Adeeba Kamarulzaman of Monash University Malaysia, Prof Alex Routh of the University of Cambridge and Prof Dr Yeah Kim Leng of the Jeffrey Cheah Institute on Southeast Asia.
Oon said the continued competitiveness of the rubber glove industry would increasingly depend on its ability to innovate, improve productivity and create greater value.
“Our future cannot depend only on scale. It must depend on how well we operate, how quickly we adapt, how effectively we innovate and how much value we can create.”
The event comes as Malaysia’s rubber glove industry continues to contribute significantly to the country’s rubber exports.
In the first half of 2026, rubber gloves generated more than RM7 billion in export revenue, accounting for approximately 66% of Malaysia’s total rubber product exports.
The Malaysian Rubber Council has also projected global glove consumption to reach approximately 405 billion pieces in 2026, compared with around 290 billion pieces in 2019.
The projected growth reflects continued demand for rubber gloves across healthcare, industrial, cleanroom and other applications.
MARGMA said the outlook reinforces the importance of continued investment in innovation, technology, productivity and higher-value manufacturing to strengthen Malaysia’s competitiveness in the global market.
MARGMA expressed its appreciation to the Malaysian Rubber Council as co-host, along with supporting ministries and agencies, sponsors, supporting organisations, exhibitors, speakers, delegates and industry partners for their contribution to IRGCE 2026.
Following the conclusion of this year’s event, MARGMA announced that the 13th International Rubber Glove Conference & Exhibition will return to the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre from 5 to 7 September 2028.
“We look forward to building on the momentum of IRGCE 2026 and welcoming the global rubber glove community back to Kuala Lumpur in 2028,” Oon said.

title: Invest Melaka Brings Halal Businesses Together at MIHAS 2026
bodyText:
Invest Melaka Berhad brought together eight companies under the Melaka Pavilion at the 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) 2026, held from 23 to 26 September at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC) in Kuala Lumpur.
The pavilion presented a broader view of Melaka’s halal-related business capabilities, while highlighting the industrial development and supporting infrastructure needed to support the sector’s next phase of growth.
Datuk Ginie Lim Siew Lin, Chief Executive Officer of Invest Melaka Berhad, said MIHAS provided a clearer perspective on the state’s existing halal industry capabilities and the opportunities to strengthen connections between established businesses and wider industrial development.
“Our companies have built their capabilities and established their businesses, and they are an important part of the state’s halal industry foundation,” she said.
For Invest Melaka, she added, the focus is on making these strengths more visible while creating stronger connections between established businesses and the wider industrial development taking place in the state.
Lim said Invest Melaka wants companies already operating in the state to continue growing, while new industrial spaces and development projects create the conditions for more businesses to establish and expand in Melaka.
“We want to see companies that are already in Melaka continue to grow, while new industrial spaces and development projects create the conditions for more businesses to establish and expand here,” she said.
She added that bringing businesses, industrial developments and supporting initiatives together over time could help build a stronger and more complete halal industry ecosystem in Melaka.
Invest Melaka’s role includes promoting investment opportunities and facilitating business growth in the state, with halal products listed among its key industry sectors.
PDG Property participated as the Melaka Pavilion’s Platinum Partner, bringing attention to the Melaka Halal Hub 2.0 development in Mukim Serkam.
Jojo Gwee, Chief Executive Officer of PDG Property, said the development of the halal industry should be viewed as a long-term process, particularly as growing companies require greater capacity and stronger industrial facilities.
“The companies that are growing today will eventually require greater capacity, better facilities and a stronger industrial environment to support their next stage,” she said.
Gwee added that PDG Property’s participation at MIHAS reflected its interest in understanding this progression, while Melaka Halal Hub 2.0 represents the company’s contribution towards building industrial capacity to support the sector.
The Melaka Pavilion brought together eight participating companies from different areas of the halal-related business landscape.
They were:
The collective presence provided a platform for businesses across different parts of the halal ecosystem to showcase their capabilities and engage with potential partners and industry stakeholders.
The Melaka Pavilion also served as a focal point for engagements with national-level industry stakeholders during MIHAS.
YB Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry, visited the pavilion and engaged with senior representatives from the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), including its Chief Executive Officer, Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof.
The participation marked a broader collective presence for Melaka at MIHAS, reflecting Invest Melaka’s role in bringing businesses, industrial developments and relevant stakeholders together.
Through the Melaka Pavilion and developments such as Melaka Halal Hub 2.0, Invest Melaka is positioning the state’s existing halal businesses alongside the industrial capacity needed to support their continued expansion and strengthen Melaka’s role within the wider halal economy.

title: What Makes a Workplace Worth Growing With?
bodyText:
By Satveer Bhatt, Head of Human Resources, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, Boehringer Ingelheim
Job security remains important, but it does not necessarily determine whether employees can see a future with an organisation.
For business leaders, this is more than a workforce issue. When experienced employees leave, organisations also lose knowledge, relationships and capabilities that can take time to rebuild.
Employees are more likely to see a future within an organisation when they can continue learning, access new opportunities and receive support as their responsibilities change.
People’s needs and ambitions rarely remain unchanged throughout their careers. A graduate seeking guidance may later want regional exposure. An experienced specialist may decide to lead a team. A new parent or caregiver may need greater flexibility without wanting to put their career on hold.
The question for employers is therefore not only how to attract people, but whether the workplace can remain relevant as employees’ capabilities, ambitions and circumstances change.
The first few years of a career shape how people apply their knowledge, work through uncertainty and understand the contribution they can make.
New employees do not all arrive with the same level of exposure. Some may have completed several internships, while others may be entering a corporate workplace for the first time. What they need is clarity about expectations, regular feedback and opportunities to learn through meaningful work.
Managers play an important role in making development tangible. This can involve explaining the reasoning behind a decision, giving an employee responsibility before they feel completely ready and treating mistakes as opportunities to improve. Such day-to-day support can be as important as formal training.
Career development also works best as a shared effort. Employees bring their aspirations and willingness to learn, while organisations provide accessible learning, open conversations and opportunities that help them identify where their strengths could take them.
At Boehringer Ingelheim, employees can access learning through Boehringer Ingelheim University, alongside opportunities to gain experience across functions, countries and regional development programmes. These resources are intended to help employees build relevant skills and explore different career directions as their interests and aspirations develop.
For this to work, employees also need clear visibility of the opportunities available and confidence that they will be considered fairly.
As employees gain experience, career development becomes less straightforward. One person may want to manage a team, another may want to deepen their expertise, while someone else may be ready to move into a different function or market.
Employers therefore need to recognise that a lateral move, cross-functional project or regional assignment can be as valuable as a promotion. Such experiences allow employees to develop a broader understanding of the business beyond the boundaries of one role.
However, internal mobility depends on more than having opportunities available. Managers must be willing to discuss employees’ ambitions, including when the best next move may be into another team.
This can be difficult, particularly when it means losing a strong performer. Yet holding people back can eventually mean losing them altogether.
Employee retention should not be understood as keeping people in the same role for as long as possible. Instead, it means giving employees enough room to develop so that they do not always have to look elsewhere for their next opportunity.
People’s circumstances change throughout their careers. They may become parents or caregivers, face a health challenge or need greater flexibility at a particular stage of life.
Employee support should therefore account for physical, mental, social and financial wellbeing while recognising that people have responsibilities beyond work.
Flexible arrangements, family-care leave and mental-health coverage can help employees navigate these changes while remaining engaged in their careers.
Leadership development is another important consideration. Strong individual performance does not automatically prepare someone to manage others. First-time managers may need guidance on providing feedback, handling difficult conversations and working with different personalities, while experienced leaders may require support as their influence expands.
A strong company culture is also an important factor in whether people choose to stay.
Employees are more likely to see a future with an organisation when its values are reflected consistently in how people are led, supported and encouraged to contribute. Policies may establish the direction, but managers and leaders determine how that culture is experienced in everyday work.
Senior leaders, in turn, shape whether managers have the capacity to develop their people, whether internal movement is encouraged and whether employees are considered for opportunities beyond their current functions.
Development may be supported by human resources, but it must be championed and enabled across the organisation.
Having been present in Malaysia for 40 years, Boehringer Ingelheim has found that organisational longevity depends in part on the ability to evolve with its people.
Its People Promise reflects this commitment by empowering employees to shape their own career paths within a strong and inclusive culture, while connecting their work to a shared purpose of celebrating differences and improving the lives of people and animals.
The company’s recognition as a Top Employer in Malaysia provides external validation, but the everyday experience of employees remains an important measure.
Organisations must keep listening rather than waiting until employees decide to leave. Can people discuss their ambitions openly? Do they see opportunities to develop before looking elsewhere? Does the support available remain relevant as their circumstances change?
No organisation will meet every need perfectly, and people move on for many valid reasons. An employer’s responsibility is to listen, respond where it can and continue investing in people after they have settled into their roles.
Ultimately, employee retention is not about expecting people to remain where they are. It is about giving them room to contribute in new ways as their aspirations and the organisation’s needs evolve, while retaining the knowledge, capabilities and leadership depth the organisation will need for what comes next.

title: Malaysia and Hong Kong Women Entrepreneurs Strengthen Cross-Border Business Ties
bodyText:
Women entrepreneurs and business leaders from Malaysia and Hong Kong gathered in Kuala Lumpur for the Malaysia-Hong Kong Women Entrepreneurs Business Exchange and Showcase, held at Menara EcoWorld on 29 September 2026.
Jointly organised by the Malaysia-China Chamber of Commerce Women Entrepreneurs Committee (MCCC WEC) and the Golden Bauhinia Women Entrepreneurs Association (GB-WEA), the event provided a platform for women entrepreneurs and business representatives from both markets to explore cross-border collaboration, business matching and market expansion opportunities.
Hosted by MCCC WEC and co-organised by GB-WEA, the programme was supported by EcoWorld, which provided venue and catering sponsorship. The programme was coordinated by MCCC WEC Secretary-General and Organising Committee Chairperson Ms Goh Swee Yong.
The event also marked the first business delegation organised by GB-WEA to Malaysia. Led by GB-WEA Chairperson Ms Priscilla Hui and Permanent Honorary President Ms Kelly Tsim, the delegation met with Malaysian women entrepreneurs from a range of industries.
The programme featured business presentations, company showcases, leadership dialogue, networking and business matching sessions.
Discussions covered a diverse range of sectors, including technology, finance, healthcare and wellness, cross-border services, trade, education, e-commerce and professional services.
Goh said the exchange was intended to go beyond networking by creating meaningful, long-term partnerships between women entrepreneurs in Malaysia and Hong Kong.
MCCC WEC Chairperson Ms Jamie Tiew Yen Houng said Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, trade and professional services, together with Malaysia’s access to the wider ASEAN market, provide opportunities for further business collaboration between the two markets.
The exchange therefore provided participants with opportunities to establish connections, explore potential partnerships and identify avenues for expanding their businesses across borders.
A key highlight of the event was the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between MCCC WEC and GB-WEA to strengthen cooperation in women’s empowerment and entrepreneurship development.
Under the MOU, the two organisations will collaborate through dialogue, information exchange and joint activities, while promoting networking and resource sharing among women entrepreneurs in Malaysia and Hong Kong.
The partnership will also support future business exchanges, business matching and cross-border collaboration, alongside initiatives focused on women’s leadership development and youth entrepreneurship.
The event received the support of MCCC leadership and corporate partners, including MCCC Vice Presidents Dato’ See Meng Geok and Dato’ Angie Ng Wai Sam, as well as Dato’ Ho Kwee Hong, Chief Development Officer of EcoWorld.
Representatives from both organisations also attended the event, including MCCC WEC Vice Chairperson Ms Arlene Tan Eng Guat, Deputy Secretary-General Ms Tern Pei Mee and other council members.
GB-WEA was represented by Permanent Honorary Presidents Ms Carol Yau and Ms Mariana Lam, Executive Vice Chairperson Ms Lisa Chang, Vice Chairperson Ms Winnie Fong and other representatives.
The organisers said the successful exchange marked a further step in strengthening business connections between women entrepreneurs in Malaysia and Hong Kong.
With the new MOU providing a framework for continued cooperation, MCCC WEC and GB-WEA aim to build on the exchange through future business opportunities, cross-border collaboration, women’s leadership development and entrepreneurship initiatives.

title: ACCCIM Calls for Gradual Minimum Wage Increase and Regional Approach
bodyText:
The Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Malaysia (ACCCIM) has cautioned against a substantial increase in Malaysia’s minimum wage from the current RM1,700 per month.
The chamber said a steep adjustment could place additional financial pressure on micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), which have already faced multiple cost increases over the past two years amid a challenging business environment and rising competition from foreign businesses.
ACCCIM said it is not opposed to an increase in the minimum wage. However, it cautioned that an overly large adjustment could create a cost shock for businesses operating on thin profit margins.
According to ACCCIM, businesses facing higher labour costs may pass some of those increases on to consumers through higher retail prices, potentially contributing to cost-push inflation.
ACCCIM said industries with a large proportion of low-wage and entry-level workers could be particularly affected by a significant minimum wage increase.
These include retail, restaurants, food services, agriculture and small and medium-sized manufacturing, where higher labour costs could translate into increased operating expenses.
The chamber also highlighted the potential ripple effect on workers earning wages slightly above the minimum wage. When the minimum wage rises, businesses may also face pressure to adjust wages for employees whose pay is already above the new wage floor.
In addition, higher wages would directly increase employers’ statutory contributions, including contributions to the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), Social Security Organisation (SOCSO) and Employment Insurance System (EIS).
ACCCIM president Datuk Ng Yih Pyng said an appropriate minimum wage level would be RM1,900 per month, representing an 11.8% increase from the current RM1,700.
Ng said minimum wage increases should balance improvements in workers’ incomes with the operational survival of MSMEs.
ACCCIM argued that a one-size-fits-all approach to minimum wage increases could place disproportionate pressure on smaller businesses, potentially leading some to reduce their workforce or close down.
Instead, the chamber said future wage increases should take into account productivity and performance, sector-specific financial capacity, as well as broader economic and business conditions.
The proposed RM1,900 figure and ACCCIM’s concerns come as the Government reviews the next minimum wage adjustment. On 30 September, the Cabinet agreed that MSMEs would be temporarily exempted from the new minimum wage increase, with the Government also considering wage subsidies under the Progressive Wage Policy as an alternative way to support wage growth.
ACCCIM also called on the Government to explore a tiered regional minimum wage system rather than applying a uniform national rate.
The chamber said Malaysia’s states and regions differ in terms of cost of living, socio-economic conditions, labour market conditions, and levels of economic and business development.
According to ACCCIM, these differences can create different pressures for both employers and workers. Businesses in lower-wage states, for example, could face difficulties absorbing higher labour costs, while workers in higher-cost areas may find that a uniform minimum wage does not adequately cover basic living expenses.
A tiered approach could calibrate minimum wages according to regional cost-of-living differences, allowing higher wages in areas with higher living costs while reducing the risk of sudden labour cost increases for businesses in economically weaker regions.
ACCCIM said a regional approach could better reflect local economic conditions while supporting workers’ livelihoods and protecting businesses from unsustainable labour cost increases.
The chamber has previously advocated for regional minimum wage considerations, citing differences in cost of living, economic development and labour market conditions across Malaysia.
As Malaysia considers the next stage of minimum wage policy, ACCCIM’s proposal centres on a gradual adjustment that takes into account productivity, business capacity and regional differences rather than applying the same wage increase uniformly across all businesses and locations.

title: SME Malaysia Welcomes Temporary Minimum Wage Exemption for MSMEs
bodyText:
The SME Association of Malaysia (SME Malaysia) has welcomed the Cabinet’s decision to temporarily exempt micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) from further increases in the minimum wage.
The decision follows efforts by Entrepreneur and Cooperatives Development Minister YB Steven Sim to highlight the operating pressures currently faced by the sector. The Cabinet agreed to the temporary exemption on 30 September 2026, citing the ability of MSMEs to manage operating cost pressures and current economic challenges.
SME Malaysia said the decision would provide MSMEs with much-needed breathing space amid rising operating costs and ongoing economic challenges.
According to the association, the temporary exemption would help businesses maintain continuity, protect employment and remain competitive while continuing to contribute to Malaysia’s economic growth.
At the same time, SME Malaysia said it supports the Government’s continued efforts to improve workers’ wages and welcomed the use of the Progressive Wage Policy (Dasar Gaji Progresif) to provide wage subsidy support.
The policy is intended to link wage growth with improvements in productivity and operates as a complement to the national minimum wage.
SME Malaysia said the Government should further strengthen the wage incentives and subsidies available under the Progressive Wage Policy by increasing the level of financial support, expanding its coverage and simplifying the application and approval process.
The association said a simpler and more accessible mechanism would allow more MSMEs to benefit from the programme, progressively raise workers’ wages and better manage the additional cost burden arising from wage adjustments.
SME Malaysia believes that improving workers’ wages and maintaining business competitiveness can be pursued together.
The association said stronger wage subsidies and incentives would give MSMEs greater capacity to improve employee remuneration while investing in productivity enhancement, digitalisation, skills development and training.
This approach is also in line with the Government’s stated emphasis on linking wage improvements with productivity, training and workers’ skills. The Economy Ministry said in September that the effectiveness of the Progressive Wage Policy is scheduled to be assessed towards the end of 2026 or early 2027.
SME Malaysia said it appreciates the Government’s continued engagement with the SME community and looks forward to further constructive dialogue on a wage policy framework that balances workers’ income growth, business competitiveness and sustainable economic growth.
SME Malaysia will also hold a joint press conference with the Malaysia Retail Chain Association (MRCA) to further address the minimum wage issue and release findings from its recently conducted SMEAM Quick Business Survey: Minimum Wage Review 2026.
The survey is expected to provide further insight into the operating cost pressures faced by businesses, their capacity to absorb further minimum wage adjustments, as well as industry views on the Government’s wage policies and supporting measures.
SME Malaysia hopes the survey findings and feedback from businesses will provide useful input to the Government as it continues reviewing and refining wage policies.
The association said it hopes future measures will remain responsive to the realities faced by businesses, particularly MSMEs, while supporting sustainable wage growth and economic development.

title: Mercedes-AMG GT Coupés Bring V8 Power and Electric Performance to Malaysia
bodyText:
Mercedes-Benz Malaysia has unveiled the new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+ Coupé and offered a first look at the all-new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupé as Formula 1 returns to Malaysia.
Showcased at KLCC Plaza, the two high-performance models represent different expressions of Mercedes-AMG’s performance philosophy. The AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+ Coupé combines a 4.0-litre V8 biturbo engine with enhanced cooling and aerodynamics, while the all-new AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupé brings AMG.EA architecture, axial-flux electric motors and an 800-volt electrical system to high-performance electric driving.
Mercedes-Benz Cars Malaysia & Head of Region, Mercedes-Benz Cars Southeast Asia CEO and President Martin Schulz said the two models reflect AMG’s pursuit of performance while offering different approaches to the high-performance driving experience.
With Formula 1 returning to Malaysia, Mercedes-Benz Malaysia is also using the occasion to celebrate the brand’s motorsport heritage and performance technology with customers.
At the heart of the new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+ Coupé is an AMG 4.0-litre V8 biturbo engine producing 450 kW, or 612 hp, and 850 Nm of torque.
The engine produces 20 kW more power than the AMG GT 63, while maximum torque has increased by 50 Nm. Power is transmitted through the AMG SPEEDSHIFT MCT 9G transmission.
The coupé accelerates from zero to 200 km/h in 10.9 seconds and reaches a top speed of 317 km/h. Its 0–100 km/h acceleration time is 3.2 seconds.
The model is also engineered with racetrack performance in mind. Its enhanced cooling system features additional radiators in the front wheel arches, while the drivetrain’s differentials and transfer case are actively cooled. Revised air guides and brake cover plates also direct more airflow towards the brakes to help manage temperatures under heavy loads.
Mercedes-AMG has also reworked the GT 63 PRO’s aerodynamics to improve its handling at speed.
The redesigned front apron incorporates additional air deflectors, while the vehicle features an active aerodynamic profile in the underbody, AIRPANEL active air control and an aerodynamics package with a fixed rear wing.
Together, these measures reduce aerodynamic lift on the front axle by more than 30kg and increase rear-axle downforce by around 15kg. Additional underbody air deflectors, inspired by the Mercedes-AMG ONE, further help manage airflow.
The vehicle is equipped with AMG ACTIVE RIDE CONTROL suspension with active roll stabilisation, rear-axle steering of up to 2.5 degrees and fully variable AMG Performance 4MATIC+ all-wheel drive.
An AMG ceramic high-performance composite braking system with six-piston fixed callipers at the front and 420mm brake discs is designed to deliver strong braking performance and resistance to fading under heavy braking.
The GT 63 PRO’s exterior further emphasises its motorsport character, with 21-inch AMG cross-spoke forged wheels, black-painted brake callipers and the AMG Night Package II.
An AMG Exterior Carbon Fibre package adds carbon-fibre elements to the front splitter, side sills, diffuser and fixed rear wing. Inside, AMG Performance seats in Nappa leather and MICROCUT microfibre are paired with a carbon-fibre steering wheel, AMG carbon-fibre trim and yellow seat belts.
The cabin also features Mercedes-Benz’s MBUX multimedia system, comprising a 12.3-inch driver display and 11.9-inch central display, alongside a head-up display, augmented-reality navigation and AMG TRACK PACE for analysing lap, sector and acceleration times on closed circuits.
For collectors, Mercedes-AMG is also offering a Motorsport Collectors Edition limited to 200 vehicles worldwide. Based on the GT 63 PRO, the edition features an obsidian black finish, PETRONAS-coloured exterior accents and a combination of AMG Carbon Fibre, Night and Aerodynamics packages.
The Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+ Coupé is priced from an estimated RM2,088,888 in Peninsular Malaysia, while the Motorsport Collectors Edition is estimated at RM2,588,888.
Alongside the V8-powered GT 63 PRO, Mercedes-Benz Malaysia has previewed the all-new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupé, which is based on the high-performance AMG.EA architecture.
The electric performance model uses three axial-flux motors and delivers up to 860 kW, equivalent to 1,169 hp, with maximum torque of 2,000 Nm.
It accelerates from zero to 100 km/h in 2.4 seconds and has a top speed of 260 km/h. The vehicle is equipped with a 106 kWh battery, offering an electric range of up to 697km under the WLTP testing cycle.
The AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupé’s AMG High Performance Electric Battery combines newly developed cylindrical cells, direct cooling for each individual cell and an 800-volt architecture.
The system is designed to support high continuous power, rapid energy absorption and stable performance under sustained loads.
With suitable charging infrastructure, the AMG Performance Charging system supports DC charging at up to 350 kW. The vehicle can charge from 10% to 80% in around 16 minutes at 350 kW, according to the manufacturer’s figures.
Mercedes-AMG has also developed AMGFORCE S+, a driving programme designed to provide an immersive V8-inspired experience in the electric vehicle. The system uses more than 1,600 sound files to dynamically recreate elements of a high-performance V8 soundscape according to driving conditions.
The electric GT 63 4-Door Coupé features the AMG RACE ENGINEER system, which coordinates the vehicle’s powertrain and driving-dynamics systems.
Its AMG RACE ENGINEER Core manages functions including the drive system, recuperation, energy, charging and thermal management, while the AMG RACE ENGINEER Control Unit allows drivers to adjust response, agility and traction characteristics.
The vehicle also features AMG ACTIVE RIDE CONTROL air suspension with semi-active roll stabilisation and active rear-axle steering of up to six degrees. At speeds of up to 80 km/h, the rear wheels steer in the opposite direction to the front wheels for greater agility, while above 80 km/h they steer in the same direction to enhance stability.
The electric AMG GT’s exterior combines a low-slung fastback silhouette with a long bonnet, steeply raked windscreen and active aerodynamic elements.
Its AEROKINETICS system includes an active rear diffuser, Venturi Flow elements and an adjustable rear spoiler designed to manage airflow and downforce according to driving conditions. Inside, the four-door coupé combines sports-car design with grand-tourer features. The cabin includes AMG Performance seats, carbon-fibre trim, a SKY CONTROL panoramic roof and a driver-focused display system comprising a 10.2-inch instrument cluster and 14-inch multimedia monitor, alongside a separate 14-inch passenger display.
Malaysian specifications also include MB.DRIVE ASSIST, a 360-degree camera, Blind Spot Assist, Distance Assist DISTRONIC, PARKTRONIC and GUARD 360° vehicle protection.
The Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupé is priced from an estimated RM1.29 million in Peninsular Malaysia.
The two AMG models arrive as Mercedes-Benz Malaysia marks Formula 1’s return to Malaysia for the first time since 2017.
The brand hosted the Mercedes-AMG F1 Party on 30 September at Raintree Plaza, The Exchange TRX, bringing together the performance and racing spirit associated with Mercedes-AMG. Special appearances from the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team were also planned for the invitation-only event.
With the new V8-powered GT 63 PRO and the electric GT 63 4-Door Coupé, Mercedes-AMG is showcasing two distinct approaches to high-performance driving in Malaysia, from track-focused combustion performance to its latest electric performance architecture.

title: Malaysia and Hong Kong Streamline Dual IPO Listings with Single Submission Arrangement
bodyText:
The Securities Commission Malaysia (SC) and the Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong (SFC) have introduced simplified regulatory procedures to facilitate simultaneous IPO listings in Malaysia and Hong Kong.
The Single Submission Arrangement brings into operation the simplified dual IPO listing framework established under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by the two regulators on 23 July 2026.
Under the new arrangement, an applicant seeking a primary listing on either the Main Board of The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK) or the MAIN Market of Bursa Malaysia Securities Berhad, together with a simultaneous secondary listing on the other market, will only need to make a single listing application submission with a single listing document.
The approach is intended to reduce regulatory duplication and compliance costs during the IPO application process.
A key feature of the simplified dual IPO listing framework is the use of a single listing document.
Applicants can rely on one listing document to meet the statutory and listing requirements of both Malaysia and Hong Kong. They can also submit their listing application through a centralised and coordinated process instead of making separate submissions to both markets.
The framework is designed to streamline the process for companies seeking to access both capital markets while maintaining the respective regulatory requirements of the two jurisdictions.
The SC and SFC have also established dedicated dual-listing review teams and communication channels to act as direct contact points for applicants and their advisers.
The arrangement provides for coordinated regulatory oversight and active case management throughout the listing process.
The SC, SFC and SEHK have also established coordinated review processes to align regulatory timelines, minimise duplication and streamline queries raised with applicants. Under the framework, the regulatory review process can be coordinated through the regulator of the primary listing.
SC Chairman Dato’ Mohammad Faiz Azmi said the operationalisation of the framework reflected the regulatory partnership between the SC and SFC, as well as their shared commitment to strengthening capital market connectivity.
“By streamlining regulatory processes and reducing duplicative submissions, this initiative will enhance access to cross-border fundraising opportunities and broaden investor reach,” he said.
He added that connecting Malaysia with Hong Kong, which the SC described as the world’s third largest global financial centre, would further strengthen the attractiveness of both markets as investment destinations.
SFC Chief Executive Officer Ms Julia Leung said the arrangement established a clearer pathway for businesses in both markets to reach more diverse international investors and deeper pools of capital, while maintaining investor protection.
To support implementation of the new arrangement, the SC has published guidance for the listing of Hong Kong companies on the Main Market of Bursa Malaysia Securities Berhad, while the SFC has issued a circular on the Single Submission Arrangement for dual listings in Hong Kong and Malaysia.
Applicants can also refer to the relevant guidance materials issued by the SC and SEHK, including an explanatory note covering Malaysia-incorporated companies’ compliance with core shareholder protection standards and other matters.
Companies and their sponsors or advisers are encouraged to consult the SC, SFC or SEHK before formally submitting a listing application to discuss the proposed transaction structure and indicative timetable.
The Single Submission Arrangement builds on the July 2026 MoU between the SC and SFC, which established a broader framework for cross-listings and strengthened regulatory cooperation between Malaysia and Hong Kong.
For companies considering simultaneous access to both markets, the streamlined framework provides a more coordinated route to dual IPO listings while supporting the regulators’ broader objective of strengthening cross-border capital market connectivity between Malaysia and Hong Kong.

title: Japanese Wagyu’s Growing Malaysian Trade Puts Secondary Cuts in the Spotlight
bodyText:
As Japanese Wagyu continues to gain traction in Malaysia, food and beverage operators are looking beyond familiar premium cuts such as tenderloin and sirloin to explore the culinary and commercial potential of a wider range of beef cuts.
Against this backdrop, the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) Kuala Lumpur partnered with halal Japanese Wagyu supplier Zenrich Allied Sdn Bhd (Zenrich Wagyu) and the Kurohana Wagyu Export Promotion Consortium, under the Flagship Export Production Area Initiative of Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), to host an exclusive B2B trade masterclass on Japanese Wagyu.
The session brought together chefs, restaurant F&B directors and food-service professionals to explore how secondary cuts can be used more effectively across different dining concepts.
The initiative comes as Japanese Wagyu strengthens its position in Japan-Malaysia food trade.
According to JETRO, Japanese Wagyu beef is currently Japan’s largest food and agricultural export category to Malaysia by value, with export volumes continuing to increase year on year. JETRO has also highlighted the importance of expanding the use of Wagyu beyond premium loin cuts to support broader market growth and more effective whole-carcass utilisation.
The growing trade reflects increasing familiarity with Japanese Wagyu among Malaysian consumers and the food-service industry, while creating opportunities for restaurants and chefs to experiment with cuts beyond conventional steak offerings.
Held at La Moon TTDI in Kuala Lumpur, the masterclass focused on cuts including Shoulder Clod-Misuji, also known as top blade, Togarashi or chuck tender, and Katasan, a shoulder clod cut.
The programme combined practical butchery and slicing demonstrations with discussions on yield, menu applications and purchasing considerations.
For chefs, these cuts can be adapted for a range of dishes, from Shabu-Shabu and Sukiyaki to seared and braised preparations. They can also be incorporated into innovative halal Japanese Wagyu creations, including Dim Sum.
For F&B directors and purchasing decision-makers, greater familiarity with secondary cuts can provide additional options for product mix and menu diversification, while supporting more effective use of the whole carcass.
JETRO Kuala Lumpur Managing Director Mr Koichi Takano said the industry has an opportunity to make Japanese Wagyu more accessible by expanding awareness beyond the cuts most commonly seen in restaurants.
“Japanese Wagyu is something that more people in Malaysia are becoming familiar with, and we believe there is an opportunity to make it more accessible by looking beyond the cuts that are most commonly seen,” he said. “By introducing a wider range of cuts to the food-service industry, we hope more people can discover Japanese Wagyu in different ways and at different types of dining establishments.”
JETRO’s Malaysian B2B promotion activities have similarly focused on helping chefs and food-service professionals understand the handling, cutting and menu applications of Japanese ingredients, including Wagyu.
Zenrich Wagyu has supplied halal-certified Japanese Wagyu to Malaysia’s food-service industry for more than a decade.
The company has imported more than 192,000kg of Japanese Wagyu, equivalent to approximately 600 head of cattle, for supply to culinary establishments nationwide.
With halal requirements playing an important role in Malaysia’s Japanese beef market, the development of halal Japanese Wagyu also provides food-service operators with opportunities to incorporate the premium ingredient into a wider range of dining concepts.
The masterclass forms part of JETRO KL and Zenrich Wagyu’s efforts to strengthen connections between Japanese food suppliers and Malaysia’s food-service industry.
By encouraging chefs and purchasing decision-makers to explore secondary cuts, the initiative aims to broaden appreciation and utilisation of Japanese Wagyu across the whole carcass.
For Malaysia’s growing Japanese food and F&B sector, this creates opportunities to move beyond conventional premium Wagyu offerings and explore new dishes, menu formats and culinary applications while making greater use of the product supplied to the market.

title: ACCCIM Welcomes Temporary Minimum Wage Exemption for MSMEs
bodyText:
The Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Malaysia (ACCCIM) has welcomed the Government’s decision to temporarily exempt micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) from the upcoming minimum wage increase.
The Cabinet agreed to the exemption on 30 September, with Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives Minister Steven Sim Chee Keong saying the decision took into account the operating cost pressures and current economic challenges faced by MSMEs. The Government said it would consider other approaches to raising wages in the sector, including wage subsidy support under the Progressive Wage Policy.
ACCCIM President Datuk Ng Yih Pyng said the exemption would provide timely financial relief to about 1.3 million MSMEs, which have faced multiple cost increases over the past two years amid a challenging business environment and growing competition from foreign businesses.
Ng said an appropriate minimum wage should balance improvements in workers’ incomes with the operational viability of MSMEs.
According to ACCCIM, a one-size-fits-all approach to minimum wage increases could place additional pressure on smaller businesses, potentially leading some to reduce their workforce or close down.
The chamber said wage increases should instead take into account productivity and performance, the financial capacity of different sectors, as well as broader economic and business conditions.
ACCCIM therefore supports a productivity-linked wage system, where workers’ pay is more closely tied to output, performance or company profits.
The chamber said such a system could reward productivity-driven performance and allow employees’ incomes to grow alongside company profitability, while encouraging employers to improve competitiveness and align labour costs more closely with actual business revenue.
ACCCIM also welcomed the Government’s consideration of other measures to increase wages for MSME employees, including wage subsidies under the Progressive Wage System (PWS).
The voluntary, incentive-based programme is designed to raise workers’ salaries in line with productivity and skills training. According to ACCCIM, the PWS has benefited 51,363 workers, exceeding its initial target of 50,000.
More than RM73 million has been disbursed under the programme, including about RM10.2 million for entry-level workers and RM62.9 million for non-entry-level workers.
The Government has similarly said wage subsidy support under the Progressive Wage Policy is intended to ensure wage increases move alongside productivity growth.
Beyond productivity-linked wages, ACCCIM has called on the Government to consider a tiered regional minimum wage system instead of a uniform national rate.
Ng said a national minimum wage should take into account differences in regional cost of living, socio-economic conditions and levels of economic and business development between states.
The chamber noted that the cost of living, prices of goods and services and labour market conditions can vary substantially across Malaysia. Some states have stronger economic activity and lower unemployment, while others face weaker business conditions and higher unemployment.
According to ACCCIM, these differences can create challenges for both employers and workers. Businesses in lower-wage states could face difficulties absorbing higher labour costs, while workers in higher-cost areas may find that a uniform minimum wage remains insufficient to cover basic expenses.
ACCCIM said a tiered approach, with minimum wages calibrated to regional cost-of-living differences, could better reflect local economic conditions.
The chamber said higher-cost cities could support higher minimum wages to account for greater living expenses, while regional tiering could help protect low-margin businesses in economically weaker areas from unsustainable increases in labour costs.
The proposal comes as Malaysia reviews its minimum wage framework. The current minimum wage is RM1,700, while the Government has said MSMEs will be temporarily exempted from the upcoming increase as it considers their operating costs and economic conditions.
For ACCCIM, the focus is therefore on finding a balance between improving workers’ incomes and maintaining the competitiveness and sustainability of Malaysia’s MSMEs.

title: Tealive Revs Up F1 Season with ‘High-Octane’ Orange Coffee
bodyText:
Tealive is gearing up to capture a larger share of Malaysia’s coffee market with a limited-time Orange Coffee series launched in conjunction with the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix weekend at the Petronas Sepang International Circuit (SIC).
The Malaysian beverage brand is adding a citrus twist to its “high-octane” coffee with two new drinks, Orange Americano and Orange Latte, combining coffee beans sourced from Ethiopia, Indonesia and China with orange juice.
The new drinks will be available at Tealive outlets nationwide from 1 October to 29 October, coinciding with International Coffee Day.
The Orange Coffee series is built around a blend designed to balance different flavour profiles.
The formulation comprises 60% Yunnan beans for chocolate depth, 20% high-altitude Ethiopian arabica for bright fruit notes and 20% Sumatra-grown Mandheling for a smooth finish.
According to Tealive, the combination creates a complex cup that shifts from fruity to nutty notes, offering a depth typically associated with multiple single-origin coffees.
The Orange Americano combines coffee with sweet orange juice for a refreshing profile featuring natural acidity and fruity notes. Meanwhile, the Orange Latte blends espresso, orange juice and milk for a creamier alternative.
Tealive’s latest launch forms part of its broader effort to offer customers more choices beyond its core tea offering.
Loob Holding Sdn Bhd Founder and Chief Executive Officer Bryan Loo said the Orange Coffee series was designed to give customers a different kind of caffeine experience while attracting more coffee lovers to the brand.
“Coffee has always been part of Malaysians’ daily routines, and we want to give them more choices when they come to Tealive,” he said. “This series allows us to offer our customers another reason to choose Tealive when they want coffee, not just tea.”
Tealive currently operates more than 1,000 outlets worldwide and serves more than five million consumers per month in Malaysia.
The launch will also receive an F1-themed push through a special Tealive pop-up store at the SIC Mall from 2 to 4 October, giving F1 fans an opportunity to try the new Orange Coffee series during the race weekend.
Customers who purchase any two Orange Coffee drinks at the pop-up store during the F1 weekend will receive limited-edition Tealive merchandise, while stocks last.
For Loo, the Orange Coffee series reflects Tealive’s wider approach to menu innovation as the brand continues exploring new ways to remain relevant to consumers.
“For us, innovation is about constantly finding new ways to stay relevant to our consumers,” Loo said. “From FMCG and ready-to-drink products to sparkling drinks and refreshing our menu, we continue to explore what comes next. Orange Coffee is the latest expression in this journey.”
With its latest limited-time launch, Tealive is bringing together coffee, citrus flavours and the excitement surrounding Formula 1 as it continues to expand its beverage offering in Malaysia.

title: MICSEA Calls for Gradual, Productivity-Linked Minimum Wage Revision in Budget 2027
bodyText:
The Malaysian Industrial, Commercial and Service Employers Association (MICSEA) has called on the Government to carefully assess and phase in any new national minimum wage rate under Budget 2027, warning that micro and small businesses could struggle to absorb a sharp increase.
MICSEA, which represents employers with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), said it recognised the need for wages to respond to the rising cost of living and for workers’ purchasing power to improve.
However, the association said the pace and scale of any increase should reflect what businesses can realistically afford and the amount of time employers have had to adjust.
Malaysia’s current minimum wage of RM1,700 became applicable to all employers nationwide from 1 August 2025.
MICSEA President YK Lai said employers were not opposed to higher wages, but cautioned that a significant increase could affect smaller businesses operating on relatively thin margins.
“Employers are not against better wages. We want workers to earn more. What worries us is a rate that looks manageable for a large company but is very hard for a small business running on thin margins,” he said.
MICSEA’s call comes as Malaysia records continued growth in labour productivity.
According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), labour productivity increased 5.5% per hour worked and 4.9% per employed person in the second quarter of 2026. Manufacturing recorded stronger growth, with productivity per hour worked increasing 7.1% and productivity per employed person rising 7.3%.
MICSEA said these figures showed that businesses were becoming more productive, but argued that the gap between productivity growth and potential minimum wage increases remained significant.
An increase in the minimum wage from RM1,700 to RM1,900 would represent a rise of approximately 11.8%, while an increase to RM2,000 would be about 17.6%.
Lai stressed that wages and productivity do not necessarily need to increase at the same rate, but said the relationship remained an important consideration for businesses.
“Nobody is saying pay should rise by exactly the same percentage as productivity,” he said. “But the gap matters. If wages rise much faster than output, the difference has to come from somewhere, and for a small firm that usually means fewer hires, less overtime or higher prices.”
The Government’s Pre-Budget Statement 2027 has also linked sustainable wage growth with productivity gains, while highlighting measures around skills development, apprenticeships, AI literacy, digital capability and lifelong learning.
MICSEA said the impact of any minimum wage revision should be assessed against the broader structure of Malaysia’s business landscape.
Micro, small and medium enterprises account for about 96.1% of business establishments in Malaysia, representing approximately 1.086 million firms in 2024. They also contributed about 39.5% of GDP, equivalent to RM652.4 billion.
For smaller businesses, labour is only one of several operating costs. Raw materials, electricity, rent, logistics, financing and compliance expenses also compete for limited cash flow, while businesses continue to operate in competitive markets.
MICSEA therefore argued that the affordability of a new minimum wage should not be assessed solely based on what larger corporations, multinational companies and government-linked companies can absorb.
The association also pointed to findings from the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) Business Conditions Survey for the first half of 2026.
The survey received 670 responses, with SMEs accounting for 72% of respondents. It found that 69% reported higher production costs, while 63% expected costs to rise further in the second half of the year.
Meanwhile, 53% identified higher raw material and intermediate input costs as a major challenge, while 45% cited the West Asia conflict, Red Sea disruptions and higher war-risk costs.
Another 29% said they were having difficulty passing higher costs on to customers, putting further pressure on margins.
Only 38% of respondents expected profits to increase, while another 38% expected profits to decline.
MICSEA said these figures did not mean Malaysia could not afford higher wages, but highlighted the importance of timing and implementation.
“Businesses need time to adjust pricing, staffing, technology and their business models,” Lai said.
MICSEA also highlighted wage compression, which can occur when increases in the minimum wage narrow the gap between entry-level and more experienced employees.
For example, if an entry-level worker earning RM1,700 is moved to RM2,000, an experienced operator earning RM2,100 would be only RM100 above the new minimum.
Employers could then face pressure to increase wages for technicians, skilled production workers, quality-control staff, team leaders and junior supervisors to maintain appropriate salary differentials and retain experienced employees.
MICSEA also noted that the direct increase in basic wages is only part of the additional cost.
For a company employing 10 workers at RM1,700 per month, increasing the minimum wage to RM1,900 would add RM24,000 a year to basic payroll costs. Increasing it to RM2,000 would add RM36,000.
Employer EPF contributions, overtime, shift allowances and other wage-linked costs would add to the overall increase.
“An extra RM300 in basic salary is not RM300 more in total cost,” Lai said.
Rather than focusing solely on the minimum wage figure, MICSEA proposed that future wage policy be placed within a broader productivity-linked compensation framework.
The association suggested clearer salary progression based on skills, certification and responsibility rather than tenure alone.
It also proposed incentives tied to measurable outcomes, including output, quality, reduced waste and defects, and improved machine utilisation.
Gainsharing schemes, which allow employees to share in financial gains generated by productivity improvements, were also proposed.
“The aim is to move from a minimum-wage economy to one where pay reflects skills and productivity,” Lai said.
If the Government proceeds with a significant minimum wage increase, MICSEA called for measures to help vulnerable businesses adapt.
Among its proposals are expanded SME productivity grants for automation, digitalisation and artificial intelligence, as well as co-funded training, reskilling and apprenticeship programmes.
The association also called for affordable financing for machinery, robotics and productivity-enhancing technology, alongside targeted tax deductions or allowances for productivity investments.
Other measures proposed include a reasonable implementation period for substantial adjustments, an assessment of whether a uniform national rate places disproportionate pressure on labour-intensive sectors and regions, and practical guidance for SMEs on managing wage compression and restructuring salary bands.
MICSEA also called for tripartite consultation through the National Wages Consultative Council before any final decision is made.
It said discussions should involve employer organisations, trade unions, SMEs, industry associations, economists and regional business representatives.
The association said the consultation should consider inflation, cost of living, employment, business survival, investment and regional differences alongside the proposed wage figure.
“This should not be workers against employers,” Lai said. “The question is how we raise incomes while protecting jobs, small businesses and Malaysia’s competitiveness.”
MICSEA said it remained ready to work with the Government, unions and employer groups to develop a wage framework that balances higher worker incomes with business sustainability and productivity growth.

title: EY Reveals 12 Top Nominees for Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 Malaysia
bodyText:
EY has unveiled the 12 Top Nominees for the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year (EOY) 2026 Malaysia awards, marking the 25th anniversary of the programme’s recognition of Malaysian entrepreneurs driving innovation, business growth and economic opportunities.
The Top Nominees were selected by an independent panel of judges based on four judging pillars: entrepreneurial spirit, purpose, growth and impact.
The nominees span four categories: Emerging Entrepreneur, Technology Entrepreneur, Woman Entrepreneur and Master Entrepreneur.
The three nominees in the Emerging Entrepreneur category are:
The Technology Entrepreneur category features:
The Woman Entrepreneur category recognises:
The Master Entrepreneur category comprises:
The winners of the four categories, alongside the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 Malaysia award winner, will be announced at an awards ceremony on 1 December 2026.
The Malaysia country winner will then join award recipients from around the world in May 2027 to compete for the EY World Entrepreneur Of The Year 2027 award in Monte Carlo, Monaco.
The EOY Malaysia programme has been running for 25 years and is part of EY’s global Entrepreneur Of The Year programme, which celebrates and connects entrepreneurs across more than 60 programmes and 94 countries and territories.
The 2026 nominee pool recorded a record number of overall nominations, according to EY, reflecting the programme’s growing reach across Malaysia’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.
The nominees represent businesses spanning technology, consumer products, healthcare and renewable energy. Collectively, they generate more than RM5.7 billion in revenue and support more than 10,000 jobs.
Dato’ Abdul Rauf Rashid, Malaysia Managing Partner at EY Malaysia, said the 25th anniversary was an opportunity to recognise entrepreneurs who had transformed ideas into businesses and contributed to Malaysia’s development.
“The increase in nominations this year across all categories demonstrates that Malaysia’s entrepreneurial spirit remains vibrant and resilient,” he said.
Philip Rao, EOY Malaysia Program Director and Partner at EY Malaysia, said this year’s theme, “The Shapers”, reflects the influence entrepreneurs can have beyond their own organisations.
The programme aims to recognise business leaders who are shaping industries, strengthening communities and contributing to Malaysia’s future through resilience, innovation and vision.
The awards announcement was officiated by Yang Berhormat Encik Steven Sim Chee Keong, Minister of Entrepreneur and Cooperatives Development.
He said entrepreneurship would become increasingly important to Malaysia’s long-term success as businesses navigate a more competitive global environment.
“For 25 years, the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year program has done more than recognize successful business leaders. It has helped elevate entrepreneurship as a vital force in Malaysia’s development while inspiring generations of entrepreneurs to think bigger and aim higher,” he said.
The programme’s 25th anniversary also includes Road to Monaco, a three-part podcast series produced in collaboration with BFM. The series features established entrepreneurs reflecting on the lessons, resilience and purpose behind their journeys from founders to business leaders.
Alongside the Top Nominees announcement, EY hosted a panel discussion titled “Beyond success: What’s next for Malaysian entrepreneurs?”
The discussion brought together entrepreneurs and business leaders to examine the challenges of building enduring businesses, creating meaningful impact and navigating growth and succession.
Panelists included Tan Sri Datuk Dr Rebecca Sta Maria, Director of the Institute for Democracy and Economic Affairs (IDEAS) and Pro-Chancellor of Sunway University; Dato’ Kamarul Redzuan Muhamed; Ganesh Kumar Bangah; and Joel Neoh, Founding Partner of First Move and EY Emerging Entrepreneur Of The Year 2012 Malaysia.
Moderated by Shankar Kanabiran, Malaysia Consulting Leader and Partner at EY Malaysia, the discussion covered founder’s syndrome, business transformation, leadership transitions and the changing role of technology in entrepreneurship.
The panel also examined the shift from generative AI towards agentic AI, including differences in adoption across industries and the need to balance technological innovation with practical business considerations.
The 2026 programme marks 25 years of EY Entrepreneur Of The Year in Malaysia. Since its launch, the programme has recognised entrepreneurs across different stages of business growth while connecting Malaysian entrepreneurs with a wider global network.
The 2026 judging panel comprises business and industry leaders including Dato’ Fad’l Mohamed, Chief Executive Officer of Bursa Malaysia; Ganesh Kumar Bangah; Ooi Lay Pheng; Anuar Fariz Fadzil; Ronnie Lim; Sharala Axryd; and Dato’ Kamarul Redzuan Muhamed.
With the four category winners and Malaysia’s overall EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 winner to be announced in December, the programme will continue its 25th-anniversary celebration by highlighting entrepreneurs shaping Malaysia’s evolving business landscape.

title: Finnfund Provides US$15 Million Loan to Support Women-Led SMEs and Green Finance in Vietnam
bodyText:
Finnfund has signed a US$15 million senior loan agreement with EVF General Finance JSC (EVF), a Vietnamese non-bank financial institution (NBFI) focused on providing financing to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
The financing will strengthen EVF’s long-term funding base and support its continued development as one of Vietnam’s leading NBFIs. EVF provides financing solutions to SMEs and corporate clients across the country, with a growing focus on green lending and financial inclusion.
By expanding access to finance for underserved businesses, EVF aims to contribute to more inclusive economic growth and sustainable economic development in Vietnam.
A key focus of the partnership is improving access to finance for women-led businesses and underserved SMEs.
Antti Partanen, Investment Manager at Finnfund, said the organisation was pleased to support EVF in expanding financing opportunities for SMEs, particularly businesses led by women.
“At Finnfund, advancing gender equality is a key priority, and we are pleased that EVF qualifies as a 2X-compliant gender lens investment,” he said.
The 2X framework is used to identify investments that contribute to women’s economic empowerment. Through the financing, Finnfund aims to support both financial inclusion and inclusive economic growth in Vietnam.
Beyond providing additional capital, the agreement reflects EVF’s progress in strengthening its environmental and social management practices and expanding collaboration with international financial institutions.
Dinh Ngoc Bao, Director of International Markets at EVF, said the partnership would help the company diversify and strengthen its long-term international funding base while embedding international ESG and gender-lens standards into its operations.
He added that these efforts would enhance EVF’s ability to serve women-led and underserved SMEs across Vietnam.
The partnership also supports EVF’s ambition to develop as a development-oriented financial institution capable of attracting international capital while delivering sustainable economic impact.
The financing comes as EVF expands its green lending portfolio and supports businesses investing in renewable energy and energy-efficiency solutions.
Vietnam has set climate targets that require significant investment to support its transition towards a low-carbon economy. According to Finnfund, EVF is positioned to channel more financing towards businesses investing in sustainable technologies and energy solutions.
“We believe the company can play an important role in channelling more financing towards sustainable growth in Vietnam,” Partanen said.
EVF said it plans to continue growing its green lending portfolio while supporting Vietnam’s transition towards a low-carbon and sustainable economy.
The partnership brings together Finnfund’s development financing and impact investment expertise with EVF’s reach among Vietnamese SMEs and corporate clients.
For EVF, the US$15 million senior loan provides a stronger long-term funding base while supporting its expansion of SME financing, green lending and gender-focused financial services.
For Malaysian and regional businesses following developments in sustainable finance, the agreement also highlights the growing role of financial institutions in directing capital towards SMEs, women-led businesses and the green transition.
Finnfund is a Finnish development financier and impact investor that invests in businesses addressing global development challenges, with a focus that includes clean energy, digital infrastructure, agriculture and financing for SMEs through financial institutions.

title: MIHAS 2026 Generates RM6.78 Billion in Sales as Malaysian SMEs Expand Global Opportunities
bodyText:
The 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) 2026 delivered RM6.78 billion in total sales over its four-day run from 23 to 26 September, marking a RM730 million or 12.0% increase from the RM6.05 billion recorded in 2025.
The figure also exceeded MIHAS 2026’s RM5.0 billion sales target by RM1.78 billion, or 35.5%, reinforcing the event’s role as a major halal marketplace connecting Malaysian businesses with international buyers and turning trade engagements into commercial opportunities.
Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof, Chief Executive Officer of the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), said the results demonstrated MIHAS’ growing contribution to Malaysian businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs) seeking access to international markets.
“MIHAS 2026 demonstrates that the platform is not only growing in terms of sales, but is also creating greater opportunities for Malaysian businesses, particularly Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), to access international markets,” he said.
He added that MATRADE remained committed to helping SMEs and Mid-Tier Companies (MTCs) expand into global markets, particularly emerging and non-traditional markets.
The International Sourcing Programme (INSP) was a major contributor to MIHAS 2026’s overall performance, generating RM4.02 billion compared with RM3.63 billion in 2025.
This represented an increase of RM394.5 million, or 10.9%, highlighting the role of structured business matching in connecting Malaysian sellers with international buyers and creating opportunities for sourcing, business development and potential export transactions.
Meanwhile, the MIHAS Exhibition recorded approximately RM1.99 billion in sales, up RM103.9 million or 5.5% from RM1.89 billion in 2025.
Among the leading products driving exhibition sales were processed food and confectionery, food technology and packaging, frozen food, as well as fertilisers and agrochemicals, reflecting the breadth of halal products and solutions showcased at MIHAS.
MIHAS 2026 also recorded its highest visitor turnout since the event began in 2004.
A total of 69,104 visitors from 93 countries attended this year’s showcase, compared with 50,340 visitors in 2025. This represents an increase of 18,764 visitors, or 37.3%.
The event also brought together exhibitors and INSP buyers from 58 countries, further strengthening MIHAS’ international reach as a global halal trade exposition.
The increased participation provided Malaysian companies with greater opportunities to engage international buyers, explore new markets and develop cross-border business relationships.
The growth of MIHAS 2026 was also reflected in its contribution to Malaysian SMEs.
Malaysian SMEs generated RM620 million in sales at the MIHAS Exhibition this year, compared with RM557 million in 2025. This represents an increase of approximately RM63 million, or 11.3%.
SME participation has also expanded significantly over the past six editions. The number of participating Malaysian SMEs rose from 64 companies in 2021 to 339 companies in 2026, representing a 429.7% increase.
The stronger SME performance comes as Malaysia’s halal export sector continues to grow. Malaysia’s halal exports reached RM68.52 billion in 2025, up 10.9% from RM61.79 billion in 2024.
Under the 13th Malaysia Plan (RMK13), Malaysia has set a target of RM80 billion in halal exports, creating further opportunities for Malaysian companies, particularly SMEs, to expand into international markets.
Through international buyer access, business matching, sourcing opportunities and digital tools, MIHAS 2026 continues to support Malaysian SMEs in strengthening their export capabilities and expanding their market reach.
Beyond its sales performance, MIHAS 2026 also marked a significant step in the digital transformation of halal trade through the integration of Agentic AI.
More than 22,000 AI-assisted business appointments were generated during the event, demonstrating how artificial intelligence can support businesses in identifying and connecting with potential trade partners.
Of these AI-assisted appointments, 324 matches reported RM28 million in sales associated with completed AI-assisted appointments.
The AI platform will also remain operational until 2027, allowing participating businesses to continue connecting with potential buyers and pursuing trade opportunities beyond the four-day exhibition.
Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar said the integration of Agentic AI was helping MIHAS evolve into a more connected and digitally enabled trade facilitation ecosystem.
“With the integration of Agentic AI, MIHAS is evolving into a more connected and digitally enabled trade facilitation ecosystem, helping Malaysian companies identify potential buyers, build meaningful business relationships and pursue new export opportunities beyond the exhibition floor,” he said.
Under the MADANI Digital Trade Platform (MDTP), MATRADE also plans to provide Malaysian exporters with continued connectivity to global buyers and support them in securing sustainable export opportunities.
Since its establishment in 2004, the Malaysia International Halal Showcase has grown into a major platform for halal trade, supporting the industry’s development in areas including halal standards, governance and market access.
Hosted by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) and organised by MATRADE, MIHAS now covers 14 sectors, including food and beverages, pharmaceuticals, Islamic finance, modest fashion, personal care, technology, services and Muslim-friendly tourism.
The 22nd edition, themed “Shaping Trust, Driving Resilience”, focused on regulated-by-design governance and technology-enabled trade.
With RM6.78 billion in sales, stronger international participation, growing SME involvement and continued AI-powered business matching, MIHAS 2026 demonstrates how Malaysia’s flagship halal trade platform is expanding beyond a conventional exhibition to create longer-term opportunities for Malaysian businesses and exporters.

title: MATRADE and ICBC Malaysia Partner to Boost Malaysian Exports to China
bodyText:
The Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (Malaysia) Berhad (ICBC Malaysia) have formalised a strategic partnership to accelerate Malaysian exports to China and create new growth opportunities for Malaysian enterprises.
The two organisations exchanged a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) at the Malaysia Pavilion during the 5th Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) in Hangzhou, China, on 29 September 2026.
The partnership establishes a trade promotion and financial support framework aimed at helping Malaysian businesses navigate the China market, while strengthening cross-border commercial connections between Malaysian and Chinese enterprises.
Under the partnership, MATRADE and ICBC Malaysia will combine their institutional networks and financial capabilities to support Malaysian exports across strategic hubs in China.
The collaboration will involve joint trade engagements, cross-border business opportunities and the use of global network platforms to connect Malaysian suppliers and service providers with Chinese business partners.
The partnership will particularly support Malaysian medium and small-sized enterprises seeking to expand their products and services into China, as well as other growing markets including ASEAN.
MATRADE Chief Executive Officer Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof said expanding into major markets such as China requires both commercial access and strong financial infrastructure.
“Expanding into major markets like China requires both commercial access and strong financial infrastructure.”
He said the partnership with ICBC Malaysia aligns with MATRADE’s strategy of helping Malaysian enterprises navigate international growth, establish resilient trade connections and develop a lasting presence across regional markets.
A key component of the partnership is the provision of financial solutions to support MATRADE initiatives aimed at strengthening Malaysia-China trade.
ICBC Malaysia will support trade activities including MATRADE’s Malaysia-China Gateway Initiative (MCGi), providing Malaysian exporters with access to trade finance and market-entry support.
The arrangement is intended to give Malaysian businesses greater support as they enter the China market, combining commercial connections with financial solutions needed to facilitate cross-border trade.
The partnership also reflects MATRADE’s wider efforts to expand Malaysian businesses’ access to China through business matching and trade promotion initiatives. Earlier in September, MATRADE coordinated 67 Malaysian companies at the China-ASEAN Expo 2026 as part of efforts to deepen Malaysia’s market presence in China.
ICBC Malaysia will also promote the use of the Chinese Yuan (RMB) as a settlement currency for trade and investment between Malaysia and China.
