Its financial offering under the partnership will include RMB trade settlement, trade finance and foreign exchange (FX) hedging solutions.
These services are intended to facilitate trade and investment activities while helping Malaysian enterprises manage the financial requirements involved in cross-border business.
ICBC Malaysia Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Geng Hao said the bank was committed to providing financial solutions and access to RMB services while leveraging ICBC’s China and international networks.
“Through this MoU, ICBC Malaysia is committed to providing robust financial solutions, access to RMB financial solutions and leveraging ICBC’s vast China domestic and international network to help Malaysian businesses navigate entry into growth markets.”
The partnership will also focus on connecting Malaysian businesses with credible Chinese business partners.
By combining MATRADE’s trade promotion network with ICBC’s financial and international banking capabilities, the two organisations aim to broaden market access and facilitate new commercial relationships.
This includes opportunities for Malaysian suppliers and service providers to connect with Chinese companies while exploring expansion into China and other regional markets.
The collaboration comes as Malaysia continues to strengthen its trade and digital business links with China. MATRADE reported that Malaysia-China trade rose 35% to RM456.68 billion in the first eight months of 2026, while exports to China increased 23.7% to RM148.56 billion.
The MoU forms part of broader efforts to strengthen bilateral trade and help Malaysian enterprises access one of the country’s key export markets.
At the GDTE, MATRADE has also been working to expand Malaysia’s presence in China’s digital economy, with Malaysian exhibitors showcasing capabilities in digital trade, artificial intelligence, cloud services, smart healthcare and cross-border e-commerce.
Moving forward, MATRADE and ICBC Malaysia will focus on joint initiatives that broaden market access, streamline trade facilitation and support Malaysian enterprises in developing resilient cross-border business opportunities.
For Malaysian SMEs and other businesses looking to expand into China, the partnership brings together two key elements of international expansion: market access and financial support.

title: MDEC CEO Anuar Fariz Fadzil to Conclude Two-Year Tenure After RM180 Billion in Digital Investments
bodyText:
Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC) Chief Executive Officer Anuar Fariz Fadzil will conclude his tenure on 2 October 2026 after completing his two-year contract with the organisation.
MDEC announced on 29 September that Anuar had informed the Board that he would not seek a renewal of his contract as he prepares to pursue new opportunities outside MDEC.
MDEC Chairman Ganesh Kumar Bangah said the Board respected Anuar’s decision and credited his tenure with strengthening the organisation’s focus on execution, accountability and measurable outcomes.
“Having worked closely with Anuar, I have personally valued his judgement, candour as well as his commitment to MDEC and fellow colleagues,” said Ganesh.
He added that Anuar had spearheaded MDEC’s drive towards AI Nation 2030, while placing greater emphasis on investments that create jobs, strengthen Malaysian companies and expand opportunities for local talent.
From 2025 to August 2026, MDEC secured close to RM180 billion in digital investments from more than 1,000 Malaysia Digital (MD) status companies.
According to MDEC, these investments are expected to generate more than 42,000 high-value jobs for Malaysians. Bernama reported the same figures following the announcement of Anuar’s departure.
MDEC said the investment outcomes reflect the continued development of Malaysia’s digital economy towards higher-value, AI-led growth.
The agency has increasingly positioned Malaysia not only as a consumer of technology, but also as a creator of technology and home-grown digital innovation.
Beyond investment figures, MDEC said Anuar strengthened the organisation’s focus on execution, accountability and measurable economic outcomes.
Its performance under his leadership was anchored around areas including jobs, exports, revenue and investment, with MDEC repositioned as a specialist digital implementation agency.
The organisation said this approach was intended to support Malaysia’s transition towards becoming an inclusive, trusted and globally competitive AI Nation by 2030.
MDEC has previously described its role in the AI transition as translating Malaysia’s national digital agenda into execution by bringing together industry, talent, infrastructure and innovation.
During his tenure, Anuar also prepared MDEC for responsibilities under the Malaysia Digital 2030 (MD2030) action plan, which covers the country’s digital development from 2026 to 2030.
Key areas include AI adoption, high-value digital investments, industry transformation, talent development and the growth of “Made by Malaysia” technologies.
MDEC has said the MD2030 agenda represents a shift towards strengthening home-grown digital innovation and moving Malaysia from being primarily a technology consumer towards becoming a producer of digital solutions.
The agency’s current programmes span digital investment, AI adoption, talent development and digital business growth, reflecting its wider role in Malaysia’s digital economy.
Reflecting on his departure, Anuar said leading MDEC had been one of the greatest privileges of his professional life.
“When I accepted the responsibility of leading MDEC, I did so with a simple belief that we could once again lead from the front and play a defining role in Malaysia’s next digital chapter,” he said.
He said he wanted MDEC to be judged not simply by the number of activities it announced, but by the results delivered for the country, industry and Malaysians.
“Everything we have achieved belongs to the extraordinary people of MDEC and to our partners across the technology ecosystem who believed in our mission,” he added.
Anuar said that after considerable reflection, he had concluded that completing his current contract was the right time to pursue opportunities outside MDEC.
“This has not been an easy decision precisely because MDEC, our people and our mission have come to mean so much to me,” he said.
He added that he was leaving with pride in what had been accomplished during his tenure and confidence in MDEC’s future.
“While I may be leaving this role, my belief in MDEC and in Malaysia’s digital future remains as strong as ever,” he said.
Ganesh said the foundations established during Anuar’s tenure would continue to shape MDEC’s work beyond his departure, describing the organisation as stronger, more focused and better prepared for its next chapter.
With Malaysia continuing to develop its digital economy and AI ecosystem, MDEC’s next phase will build on an agenda centred on digital investment, AI adoption, talent development, industry transformation and the growth of Malaysian technology companies.

title: ConverXion KL 2026 to Put AI in Action Across Customer Experience, Sales and Marketing
bodyText:
ConverXion KL 2026 will return to Kuala Lumpur on 15 October, bringing together business and technology leaders to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) is being deployed across customer experience, sales and marketing.
Organised by Mimin and held at Aloft Kuala Lumpur Sentral, the summit will take place under the theme “AI in Action”, shifting the conversation from what AI could potentially do to what businesses are actually implementing.
The programme will focus on practical applications, implementation decisions and lessons from organisations putting AI into real-world use.
According to Mimin CEO and Founder Joseph Simbar, business leaders are increasingly looking beyond AI demonstrations and possibilities towards understanding what works, how solutions are implemented and whether successful approaches can be replicated.
“The AI conversation has moved. Business leaders no longer just want to know what is possible; they want to understand what is working, how it was implemented, and whether it can be replicated,” he said.
ConverXion KL 2026 will examine AI through three practical lenses: execution, application and implication.
The execution aspect will explore how organisations move AI initiatives from concepts into deployment, including implementation timelines and decisions around building AI solutions internally or buying existing technologies.
The application side will look at where AI is already changing customer interactions and commercial processes, including customer experience, sales and marketing.
The programme will also consider the wider implications of AI adoption, including trust, data privacy and the changing role of people within AI-enabled organisations.
Topics will include conversational AI, customer experience, omnichannel engagement, personalisation and customer loyalty, AI-powered sales and marketing, AI ethics and data privacy.
Rather than focusing on a single technology or industry, the summit will bring together perspectives from multiple sectors to examine how AI adoption differs across operating environments.
This includes exploring how businesses are using AI to improve customer interactions, strengthen engagement and support commercial processes.
The approach reflects a wider shift in the AI conversation, as businesses move from experimentation towards implementation and seek to understand where the technology can create measurable value.
ConverXion’s official programme similarly positions the 2026 event around real deployments, implementation timelines, build-versus-buy decisions and live use cases across industries including retail, banking and healthcare.
Confirmed speakers include Chee Mun Foong, CEO of YTL AI Labs; Bernard Yong, CXO of Mah Sing Berhad; Dario Bianchi, CPO of Mindvalley; and Dr Devina Njoo, Patient Experience Director of EMC Healthcare.
Mimin COO and Co-Founder Bayu Eka Putra said the value of ConverXion lies not only in the technology being discussed, but also in the people involved in the conversation.
“What makes ConverXion valuable is not only the technology being discussed, but the people having the conversation,” he said.
He added that the participants are responsible for decisions involving customers, revenue, operations and business transformation, allowing discussions to move beyond what AI can theoretically do towards what businesses are already doing with it.
The 2026 edition builds on last year’s ConverXion KL, which attracted more than 150 delegates from over 40 Malaysian and regional organisations.
The 2025 event featured more than 20 speakers, representatives from 15 industries and 10 roundtable discussions. The 2026 programme will continue this format through a combination of keynotes, fireside conversations, panel discussions and facilitated roundtables.
The event is designed to give delegates opportunities to hear from industry leaders while exchanging experiences directly with other business decision-makers.
The official ConverXion programme reports that more than 70% of its 2025 attendees held C-level, director or head-of-department roles, reflecting the event’s focus on senior decision-makers involved in customer experience, digital transformation, marketing, operations and technology.
ConverXion KL 2026 will take place on Thursday, 15 October 2026, at Aloft Kuala Lumpur Sentral.
With AI increasingly moving into everyday business processes, the summit will provide a platform for leaders to examine the practical realities of implementation, from customer experience and sales to marketing, data privacy and organisational change.
Rather than focusing solely on the possibilities of AI, this year’s event aims to examine the lessons emerging from organisations already putting the technology into practice.
Registration is available through the official ConverXion website .

title: Pos Malaysia Launches SME Jumpstart Workshop to Help Businesses Scale Beyond Marketplaces
bodyText:
Pos Malaysia Berhad is launching the SME Jumpstart Workshop 2026, a one-day programme designed to help Malaysian small and medium enterprises (SMEs) move beyond online marketplaces and build stronger direct-to-consumer (D2C) business models.
Set for 7 October 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, the workshop will focus on helping SMEs strengthen their owned sales channels, improve customer retention and profitability, and develop more resilient business models through digital commerce, logistics and fulfilment.
While online marketplaces have helped many SMEs gain visibility and generate sales, Pos Malaysia said the next stage of growth increasingly depends on businesses being able to own customer relationships, encourage repeat purchases and protect their margins.
The workshop is aimed at SMEs, entrepreneurs and aspiring founders looking to scale beyond marketplace platforms and build more sustainable, customer-led businesses.
According to Pos Malaysia Group Chief Sales Officer Charles William, businesses need to look beyond sales volume when building a profitable online operation.
“Growing a profitable online business means understanding your customer economics. Too many SMEs chase volume without looking at acquisition costs or repeat purchase rates.”
He said selling directly to customers through a business website, social media channels or repeat-purchase programmes can give SMEs greater control over customer data and relationships, while helping them improve margins and build greater resilience.
The workshop will therefore focus on the shift from simply generating orders to developing businesses around customer lifetime value, repeat purchases and brand loyalty.
“The SME Jumpstart Workshop 2026 is designed to give entrepreneurs the tools they need to make that shift from volume-chasing to profit-building.”
Organised by Pos Malaysia and supported by title partner ZUS Coffee, the workshop will bring together founders, business leaders, industry experts, ecosystem partners and supporting agencies.
The programme will cover areas including D2C growth, customer acquisition, brand building, digital readiness, SME funding, logistics enablement and sustainable business expansion.
Speakers will include Charles William, Datuk Wira Dr Azizan Osman of RichWorks and Edwin Wang, Co-Founder of Signature Market.
Through keynote presentations, founder stories, expert-led discussions and an interactive panel featuring live audience polling, participants will gain practical insights and real-world perspectives on scaling an SME.
The initiative also reflects Pos Malaysia’s broader transformation from a traditional postal operator into a logistics, fulfilment and commerce partner for Malaysian businesses.
Its nationwide delivery network, retail presence and parcel logistics capabilities can support SMEs in areas such as direct online sales, fulfilment and delivery.
Pos Malaysia currently offers business customers end-to-end fulfilment covering storage, order processing, packing and shipment coordination, alongside real-time inventory and order visibility.
For SMEs building D2C operations, reliable fulfilment and delivery can form an important part of the customer experience, particularly as businesses seek to encourage repeat purchases and strengthen brand trust.
The workshop will also examine how SMEs can improve their online discoverability as search behaviour continues to evolve.
Participants will be introduced to SEO (Search Engine Optimisation), AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation) and GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation), helping businesses understand how to increase visibility across traditional search engines, answer engines and AI-powered discovery platforms.
Beyond the learning sessions, attendees will have opportunities to connect with business leaders, ecosystem partners and supporting agencies covering digital transformation, compliance, SME financing, marketing, customer engagement, logistics, fulfilment and regional expansion.
The workshop is organised in collaboration with ecosystem partners across company registration, digital transformation, SME financing, customer engagement, marketing, export readiness and business advisory.
Partners include Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM), FundedHere, Infobip, Luxana Technologies, Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC), Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), NP Digital, RichWorks Consulting Group and SME Corp. Malaysia.
Participants will also receive a Brew Passport, allowing them to connect with exhibiting partners, explore business solutions and obtain expert guidance at each booth. Completed passports can be redeemed for an exclusive goodie bag containing complimentary products, special offers and partner giveaways.
The inaugural SME Jumpstart Workshop marks the beginning of a broader SME engagement platform by Pos Malaysia, with future themed editions expected to be announced.
The initiative is intended to give Malaysian SMEs greater access to relevant expertise, business networks and practical solutions as they navigate digital commerce and seek sustainable growth.
For businesses looking to strengthen their direct-to-consumer strategies, the programme provides a platform to explore how customer relationships, digital readiness, logistics and fulfilment can work together to support long-term growth.
The Pos Malaysia SME Jumpstart Workshop 2026, themed “Scale Beyond Marketplaces to D2C”, will take place on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, from 8.30am to 4.30pm at Courtyard by Marriott Kuala Lumpur South.
Tickets are priced at RM90, with registration closing on 30 September 2026. Places are limited.
Interested participants can register through the official event registration platform. Pos Malaysia’s business services also include scalable domestic and international delivery solutions for businesses, with international shipping available to more than 230 countries and territories.

title: MCCC WEC’s HER POWER Day Highlights Employment and Women’s Rights
bodyText:
The Women Entrepreneurs Committee of the Malaysia-China Chamber of Commerce (MCCC WEC) organised HER POWER · Employment & Women’s Rights Empowerment Day 2026 on 27 September under the theme “Empower Women, Change the Future.”
The programme brought together business representatives, women leaders, professionals, women’s rights advocates and members of the community to highlight employment opportunities, career development and awareness of women’s rights.
MCCC WEC President Jamie Tiew Yen Houng said women’s empowerment should not only focus on women who have already achieved success, but also on creating opportunities for those facing challenges to rebuild their lives and shape their futures.
She noted that women continue to face challenges involving employment, family responsibilities, marriage, workplace issues and personal safety. In response, the programme focused on two practical areas: creating employment and entrepreneurship opportunities, and strengthening women’s awareness of their rights.
“When a woman has economic independence, she has more choices. When a mother has a stable income, she is better positioned to create a better future for her children.”
The first part of HER POWER Day focused on employment and career opportunities.
Participating companies shared employment information, career opportunities and potential pathways for women seeking to enter or re-enter the workforce.
The participating companies included Agency Perkerjaan Kainan Sdn Bhd, Benten Global Sdn Bhd, Melife Global (M) Sdn Bhd and IQI Holdings Sdn Bhd.
By bringing businesses and women seeking employment together, the initiative aimed to connect women with practical opportunities to strengthen their financial independence and develop their careers.
Employment and entrepreneurship were positioned as important aspects of empowerment, particularly for women who may have experienced interruptions or challenges in their working lives.
The second part of the programme featured a Women’s Rights Awareness Forum, providing practical knowledge on issues affecting women in their daily lives.
Topics included marriage, workplace rights, harassment, domestic violence, and the protection of women and their children.
The forum featured Dato’ Sri Chong Eng, Miss Ho Yock Lin, President of All Women’s Action Society (AWAM), lawyer Victoria Tey Zi Xin, and Ps. Pauline Leong, Founder and Chairman of Pertubuhan Kebajikan Wanita Dan Keluarga Abundant ARK Selangor. Dato’ Sri Jess served as moderator.
The focus on rights awareness complemented the programme’s employment component by highlighting that economic independence and knowledge of legal rights can both contribute to women’s ability to make informed decisions about their lives.
MCCC WEC Organising Chairperson Grace Lum said women’s advancement should go beyond simply discussing gender equality and should focus on whether women have the genuine ability to make choices about their own lives.
“Whether a woman can work is a matter of choice. Whether she can have her own income is a matter of choice. And when she faces unfair treatment, knowing her legal rights is also a form of choice.”
She identified two fundamental elements of women’s empowerment: having the ability to support oneself and having the knowledge to protect oneself.
“When a woman has both choices and confidence, she can take greater ownership of her own life.”
Lum also expressed her appreciation to MCCC WEC President Jamie Tiew, committee members and the organising team for bringing the programme from planning to implementation.
She thanked Ps. Pauline Leong and the ARK team for providing the venue and support, as well as the participating corporate representatives, moderator, panellists, partners, media and attendees.
MCCC WEC said it will continue developing initiatives focused on entrepreneurship, leadership, employment, education, family support and women’s personal development.
The committee aims to connect business resources with community needs while creating practical opportunities for more women.
The organisation framed these efforts as part of a broader approach to women’s empowerment, where employment opportunities, economic independence, rights awareness and personal development can work together.
“An empowered woman can influence a family. A stronger family can strengthen a community. And when women come together, their collective strength can contribute to positive change.”
The initiative concluded with a simple message that reflects its focus on practical, community-level empowerment:
“We may not be able to help the whole world, but we can start by helping those around us.”

title: AI in Accounting: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping the Future of Finance
bodyText:
By Saritha Subramaniam, Director of Southeast Asia and Australasia at AICPA & CIMA
Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer simply a collection of time-saving tools or a major technological advance. It is an exponential force reshaping the accountancy and finance profession, with professionals already using AI across a growing range of operational and strategic functions.
From data entry and bank account reconciliation to fraud detection, tax research and advanced financial analysis, AI is increasingly becoming part of everyday finance work.
Yet while concerns about AI replacing jobs continue, the technology could instead create opportunities for finance professionals to apply their human expertise in new ways.
A Deloitte survey found that finance departments globally are facing a shortage of skilled staff, with 40% investing in AI and automation to address productivity gaps. The research also found that 64% of finance leaders planned to add more technical skills and capabilities to their functions.
Rather than simply replacing professionals, AI can act as a force multiplier, improving efficiency and productivity while allowing finance teams to focus on higher-value work.
Across Southeast Asia, this transition is reaching an important stage as organisations move from exploring AI to deploying it more widely.
Research by McKinsey and Singapore’s Economic Development Board has described a region moving rapidly from AI exploration to deployment, with leading organisations embedding the technology into workflows and establishing formal governance rather than relying on isolated pilot projects.
Finance is firmly part of this transformation. Wolters Kluwer’s 2026 Future Ready CFO research found that 83% of Asia-Pacific CFOs identified AI adoption as a key force reshaping the finance function, compared with 85% globally.
The research also points to a broader transformation of the CFO role, with AI increasingly influencing financial modelling, reporting, capital allocation, budgeting, forecasting and scenario planning.
What stands out in Southeast Asia, however, is the emphasis on implementing AI responsibly and effectively.
Finance leaders are weighing governance, data quality and return on investment rather than pursuing adoption simply for its own sake. In diverse markets where regulations and levels of technological maturity vary considerably, this measured approach plays directly to the strengths of finance professionals.
Those who can bring judgement, ethical oversight and clear thinking to the use of AI will be better positioned to turn the technology into lasting organisational value.
AI can generate new insights and improve organisational performance, but finance professionals must avoid becoming overly dependent on automated systems.
One concern is “cognitive offloading”, where people outsource their thinking and decision-making to AI tools. Instead, intelligent systems should be viewed as collaborative partners that free professionals to apply critical thinking, solve problems and create greater value.
Human judgement therefore remains central.
AI can process information at a scale that would be difficult for an individual or team to replicate, but professionals still need to understand the context behind the information, question outputs and determine how insights should influence business decisions.
This balance between technology and human judgement is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes embedded in finance functions.
Another opportunity lies in using AI to look beyond what has already happened.
Finance professionals have traditionally played an important role in analysing historical performance and helping organisations plan ahead. AI can extend this capability by identifying market trends, analysing scenarios and helping organisations anticipate potential opportunities and risks.
No technology can perfectly predict the future. However, AI tools can help finance teams examine different scenarios and identify connections between issues.
This can support a more systems-based approach to decision-making, allowing professionals to assess the ripple effects of decisions across different parts of an organisation.
Instead of simply responding to problems after they emerge, finance professionals can increasingly help organisations identify and address potential challenges before they become crises.
As AI becomes more deeply integrated into business operations, finance professionals can also play a role in ensuring that these technologies are adopted responsibly.
Their professional ethics and judgement can help organisations assess whether AI systems are being used competently and appropriately. Finance professionals can also provide assurance that systems are operating reliably and as intended.
This responsibility extends beyond day-to-day operations.
AI and automation can raise complex questions about accountability, decision-making and trust. Finance professionals can therefore help their organisations navigate these issues while maintaining confidence among employees, customers and other stakeholders.
The ability to combine AI capabilities with ethical oversight could become an increasingly important part of the future finance profession.
AI could also accelerate the profession’s evolution from business partner to strategic adviser.
By automating repetitive processes, AI can give finance professionals more time to focus on analysis, strategy and decision-making. This creates an opportunity to move further upstream, from recording what has happened to helping determine what should happen next.
In this sense, the role of the finance professional could become less about being a scorekeeper and more about acting as a strategic adviser and futurist.
The shift is already reflected in broader research on the changing finance function. Deloitte’s 2026 research found that finance leaders are increasingly combining traditional finance expertise with technical capabilities, while AI adoption continues to change how finance teams operate.
The potential of AI to reshape accountancy and finance is also reflected in Rise2040 , a profession-wide research initiative launched by AICPA and CIMA.
The initiative brought together more than 6,000 insights from accounting and finance professionals across more than 25 countries to explore how the profession could evolve amid technological advancement, expanding data and increasing complexity.
Its research highlights AI as an enabler for the public accounting and finance profession, particularly through its ability to automate repetitive work and free professionals to focus on higher-order advisory work, judgement and strategy.
However, capturing these benefits will also require the profession to address the risks associated with AI.
These include training gaps among early-career professionals, overreliance on automation and the potential erosion of experiential learning.
AI is likely to transform the accountancy and finance profession, creating new opportunities for professionals to deliver value while changing the skills required to succeed.
The challenge is therefore not simply whether finance professionals will use AI, but how effectively they can combine the technology with human judgement, ethical responsibility and strategic thinking.
For Southeast Asia, where organisations are moving increasingly from AI experimentation towards deployment, this distinction could become particularly important.
The future finance professional will need to understand both the technology and the business context in which it operates. Continuous learning and adaptability will be essential as AI capabilities continue to evolve.
AI may be the entry point to the future of the profession, but it is not the endpoint.

title: REHDA Institute Survey Highlights Graduate Readiness Gap as AI Reshapes Future Jobs
bodyText:
A gap between students’ expectations and employers’ assessments of graduate workplace readiness has emerged from the REHDA Institute Youth Initiative (RIYI) 2026 survey, highlighting the need for closer collaboration between universities and industry as artificial intelligence (AI) changes the skills required of fresh graduates.
The survey found that 41.6% of student respondents considered one to three months a realistic timeframe for fresh graduates to begin adding commercial value at work. Among employer respondents, only 2.9% shared that view.
There was also a difference in perceptions of university preparation. While 62.0% of students felt well prepared by their universities, only 32.3% of employers agreed that local universities adequately prepare graduates for workplace realities.
The findings form part of RIYI 2026’s closing summary report, which draws on responses from students and recent graduates across 21 Malaysian universities, alongside employers. The targeted surveys provide insights into graduate expectations and employer perspectives but are not nationally representative.
The findings come against the backdrop of the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK13), covering 2026 to 2030, which calls for higher education programmes to align more closely with industry needs and for greater industry involvement in talent development.
RMK13 also targets average labour productivity growth of 3.6% a year between 2026 and 2030. The plan proposes measures including a mandatory paid internship scheme and more demand-driven learning through collaboration between public universities and the private sector.
RIYI’s mentorship programme provides another form of early industry exposure, allowing students to engage with senior professionals, receive feedback on their career plans and gain a clearer understanding of workplace expectations.
The RIYI 2026 closing report was presented to Economy Minister YB Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir at the programme’s closing event at Monash University Malaysia. The event also featured a town hall titled “Advancing Malaysia’s ESG-Ready Built Environment: Connecting Government, Youth, Universities and Industry under RMK13.”
RIYI 2026 brought together 50 students from 15 collaborating universities, alongside students from six other universities, with senior industry leaders for practical exposure to workplace expectations, career development, leadership and the skills required in a technology-driven economy.
REHDA Institute Chairman Dato’ Jeffrey Ng Tiong Lip said closer university-industry collaboration was needed to give students earlier exposure to workplace realities.
“A university qualification provides an important foundation, but young people also need to understand how workplaces operate, how decisions are made and what employers expect from them. “This is where RIYI plays an important role in bringing students closer to industry through direct engagement and mentorship, while helping them develop the judgement, resilience, communication and adaptability needed to build sustainable careers,” he said.
REHDA Institute describes RIYI as a year-long programme designed to bridge academia and industry through corporate mentorship, practical exposure and future-ready skills development.
Ng added that engagement with industry leaders can give students access to workplace lessons that cannot be gained purely from textbooks, helping them understand what it takes to progress from fresh graduates to future leaders.
Artificial intelligence emerged as another major theme in the RIYI survey, particularly in relation to entry-level employment.
While 76.4% of student respondents said they regularly use AI tools, 50.0% of employers surveyed expected AI to reduce the number of entry-level roles they hire for over the next three years.
The findings point to the importance of developing practical judgement, problem-solving and adaptability alongside digital skills.
RMK13 places AI and digitalisation at the centre of Malaysia’s economic transition and calls for collaboration between the public sector, industry and academia to equip talent with advanced technology skills.
For students entering an increasingly AI-enabled workplace, the issue is therefore not limited to familiarity with digital tools. The ability to apply judgement, solve problems, communicate effectively and adapt to changing work requirements is also becoming increasingly important.
The RIYI surveys also identified areas of common ground between students and employers around career development.
Some 79.4% of employers said they were willing to provide structured, quality training and a clear career path in exchange for a retention commitment, while 67.6% of students said they would accept such an arrangement outright.
Pay transparency and talent retention also emerged as areas of concern. Among respondents, 82.4% of students and 58.3% of employers supported compulsory salary-range disclosure in job advertisements.
Meanwhile, 57.1% of student respondents said they were likely or very likely to work outside Malaysia within five years.
The findings add student and employer perspectives to RMK13’s wider labour market agenda, which includes raising the share of employee compensation in GDP to 40% by 2030 and measures relating to graduate starting salaries and the Progressive Wage Policy.
RIYI’s focus comes as young Malaysians continue to face a different labour market experience from the overall workforce.
According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia, Malaysia’s unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 24 stood at 10.2% in June 2026, compared with a national unemployment rate of 3.0%.
Against this backdrop, earlier exposure to employers and practical workplace expectations is one area RIYI seeks to address. The programme brings together students, universities and industry leaders to develop workplace readiness and strengthen the connection between academic learning and employment.
The university-industry skills gap also has particular relevance to Malaysia’s property and built-environment workforce.
Under RMK13, the wider use of technologies such as the Industrialised Building System (IBS) and Building Information Modelling (BIM) is envisaged, particularly in affordable housing. The plan also encourages developers to seek Green Building Index certification.
These priorities point towards demand for professionals who can apply technology and sustainability principles to real-world property and construction projects.
RIYI therefore provides an avenue for young people to engage directly with an industry that will be responsible for implementing many of these priorities.
The final RIYI session, themed “Climbing the Career Ladder in the AI Era”, examined AI’s impact on junior roles, productivity, decision-making and the capabilities expected of future leaders.
Participants took part in clinics on AI-augmented judgement, strategic value, leadership influence and stakeholder management before presenting their Three-Year Career Mastery Blueprints for feedback from industry mentors.
The programme concluded with a negotiation and influence masterclass covering workplace communication, deadlines, career progression, salary discussions and managing professional expectations.
Students involved in RIYI 2026 came from more than 21 universities across Malaysia, including Universiti Malaya, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Universiti Teknologi MARA, Monash University Malaysia, Taylor’s University, Sunway University, UCSI University, Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman and Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia.
REHDA Institute aims to develop RIYI into a longer-term platform connecting universities, employers and young talent, while contributing industry perspectives to Malaysia’s graduate employability and future workforce development.
The initiative reflects a broader effort to bring academic preparation and workplace expectations closer together as Malaysia’s labour market evolves alongside AI, digitalisation and new technology-driven industries.

title: JurisTech deploys technology platform for Proton Capital in 3.5 months
bodyText:
Juris Technologies Sdn. Bhd. (JurisTech) has deployed the end-to-end lending technology platform underpinning Proton Capital Sdn Bhd, PROTON’s newly launched automotive financing business — completing the implementation in just 3.5 months.
The platform enables Proton Capital to manage the financing lifecycle from originating customer financing through to the management of loan contracts, providing the technology foundation required to operate and scale its new financing business.
Proton Capital was launched on 21 September with conventional hire-purchase financing for new PROTON vehicles through 12 participating PROTON outlets in the Klang Valley to provide complete and straightforward applications that can receive an initial financing decision within one working day.

The technology deployed for Proton Capital is part of JurisTech’s wider lending platform, which supports financial institutions across digital onboarding, origination, credit decisioning, loan management, collections and recovery.
JurisTech was recently named Asia’s Best Lending Solution at the Euromoney Awards for Excellence 2026, recognising its technology across the credit lifecycle.
“Proton Capital wasn’t simply implementing a new lending system, it was launching a new financing business. That requires a technology foundation capable of supporting the financing lifecycle from origination through contract management, with the controls and flexibility needed to grow. We are very proud that our teams were able to deliver that foundation in just 3.5 months,” said See Wai Hun, CEO and Co-Founder of JurisTech.
“As automotive financing becomes more closely integrated with the vehicle-purchase journey, technology needs to support both customer experience and the underlying financing operation. The same platform can support Proton Capital as it introduces new products and serves different customer segments over time.”


JurisTech’s enterprise solutions support financing models including automotive finance marketplaces in Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand. Its international work also includes credit assessment and digital onboarding capabilities for global automotive companies.
JurisTech was also named a Representative Provider in the 2024 Gartner® Innovation Insight: How Ecosystems Drive Lending Transformation and Asset Growth. The report examined the role of technology and partnerships in emerging lending models that enable economic ecosystems.
Proton Capital brings financing into the vehicle-purchase process, closer to the point at which customers need it. For many Malaysians, access to a vehicle is closely linked to employment, business and everyday economic activity.
At launch, Proton Capital offers conventional hire-purchase financing for new Proton vehicles and plans to roll out more products progressively.
“By bringing financing closer to the ownership process, we can progressively develop solutions for different customer groups and make the experience more integrated, efficient and responsive to their needs.”

title: ScaleX: Taking AgriFoodTech to the People
bodyText:
By Aileen Anthony, Executive Editor, MALAYSIA SME
That conviction sits behind ScaleX, Malaysia’s first National AgriFoodTech Scale-Up Programme, developed by agrifoodtech ecosystem enabler Impact Circle. Its founding cohort spans crop science, aquaculture, livestock, farm robotics, biotechnology, circularity, food innovation, and digitalisation—capabilities that, when connected, can help transform the food system from seed and soil to market and consumer. (Featured Pic: ScaleX founding cohort was launched on 2 July 2026 by YBhg. Datuk Seri Isham Ishak, Secretary-General of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (KPKM), at Wisma Tani, Putrajaya.)
MALAYSIA SME spoke with Ong at a ScaleX founders’ gathering , where some cohort members came together to understand one another’s businesses, sharpen how they position their technologies and identify opportunities to collaborate. Food security, she stressed, is not achieved by isolated technologies. It is built when innovators, farmers, government, financiers, and markets work as one system. As Ong categorically explained to each cohort member, ScaleX’s intention became clear to me: ScaleX wants to build an AgriFoodTech ecosystem that can move forward together.

ScaleX grew partly out of Ong’s work through Impact Circle, with selected companies coming through Securities Commission Malaysia’s GrowMatch initiative. She noticed that participating companies were at various stages of maturity. Some were proven businesses with products and customers, while others were still developing prototypes or validating their ideas. That difference mattered because companies at different stages require different forms of support.
“We need to understand where they are before deciding what support they need,” she explained. She then proposed segmenting them according to maturity. Early-stage businesses could pursue grants and prototype development. Companies gaining traction needed further commercial development. Those already operating successfully in the market required a different pathway. “They are ready for the next stage, and we can help them attract capital locally or internationally,” said Ong. That thinking eventually became ScaleX.
The “X” stands for multiplication: not simply scaling one company but multiplying impact by deploying complementary technologies in real production systems and then replicating what works. “These solutions are urgently needed to raise food productivity, strengthen resilience and protect smallholder incomes,” Ong said. ScaleX helps founders clarify what differentiates their businesses, understand where their capabilities intersect and build partnerships across the value chain.



A significant part of the cohort demonstrates how science is changing what can happen before and during food production. Nomatech applies crop-science R&D and breeding to rice commercialisation, including Primera low-GI red rice. Qarbotech uses carbon quantum-dot nanotechnology designed to improve plants’ light absorption and photosynthetic performance, showing how advanced science can translate into higher farm productivity.
Ong emphasised a principle that applies across the cohort: “Every company has a different story. You need to understand what the real innovation is and build the story around that.” Grusonn Wellness cultivates functional mushrooms, including Tiger Milk Mushroom, and develops wellness and functional-food products from locally grown resources such as mushrooms and cacao. Afiat develops wellness products based on Malaysian botanicals and traditional herbs. BeNature BioLab , from South Korea, applies proprietary formulation technology to improve the solubility, stability, and bioavailability of plant-derived bioactives, while Hong Kong-based Meat the Next develops protein-focused food innovations -Tiga Milk plant milk from tiger nuts.
Aquaculture has its own scientific layer. Johor-based YHL Aquatic has established Malaysia’s first shrimp Nucleus Centre and genetic Broodstock Multiplication Centre, developing selected Pacific white shrimp lines for stronger growth, resilience, and local supply security. These businesses show how food production increasingly begins with genetics, biotechnology, plant science, and R&D.

Technology then moves into the farm itself. HAVVA provides controlled-environment and digital farming systems, including IoT-enabled farms and greenhouses, while Braintree Technologies combines drones, robotics and AI for precision agriculture and automated field operations. The test is practical: technology must reduce labour bottlenecks, improve consistency, and give farmers better information without adding unnecessary complexity.
In AI-enabled aquaculture, Pacton Technologies uses AI and computer vision through FishSpeak to give farmers better visibility into fish condition and water quality. IPINFRA integrates AI and IoT for cattle identification, weight estimation, traceability, and farm monitoring. In both cases, data helps producers spot risks earlier and manage operations with greater confidence.
Flow Studios extends IoT and digitalisation across farm operations. Farmy combines integrated farming with direct retail access, connecting food production more closely with consumers while shortening the supply chain, while AIREI works across the oil-palm value chain, developing solutions for both smallholder and milling applications to improve productivity, operational efficiency, and sustainability from cultivation through to processing.
Borneo Eco Fish produces red tilapia at scale through cage farming in Batang Ai, Sarawak, harnessing the reservoir’s distinctive water environment to support high-quality aquaculture. It raises its fish without antibiotics, strengthening the company’s commitment to responsible production, food safety, and healthier seafood.
Livestock health provides another connection. Vetomin-M develops Virgin Coconut Oil (VCO) -based natural multivitamin products for livestock, while Maypreen develops plant-based, eco-friendly detergent and bio-hygiene formulations and is extending its expertise into agricultural bio-solutions that strengthen post-harvest protection and supply-chain resilience. What happens on the farm ultimately affects the safety, quality, and resilience of the wider food chain.

The food system also must deal with what it leaves behind. Entomal provides an end-to-end black soldier fly solution, spanning breeding and rearing through to production. Its technology upcycles organic waste into insect protein for pet food, poultry feed, and aquaculture feed, while also producing biofertiliser as a valuable agricultural input. MAEKO provides advanced, technology-enabled composting systems for industrial, retail, and household applications, transforming food waste into fertiliser and helping users close the loop at the point of waste generation. Its proprietary technology supports remote monitoring and maintenance, while an integrated app enables impact and ESG performance to be measured, tracked and reported.
Reclimate develops biochar carbon-removal projects that create value from agricultural residues and help restore soil fertility. Tan Lan Agri Venture focuses on soil reconditioning and healthier soil conditions for long-term agricultural production.  Thailand-based LOCOL develops a cocoa-extract cattle-feed supplement to reduce enteric methane while supporting animal performance. Across the cohort, the circular proposition is clear: food waste can become feed or fertiliser, agricultural residues can become biochar, soil can be restored and lower-carbon production can create value rather than cost alone.

Producing more creates lasting value only when producers can reach markets. Haroct Technologies integrates inputs, crop trading, logistics and financing to connect farmers with buyers and services. Kapitani connects directly with farmers and digitises in farm records in line with myGAP requirements, while Good Growers works with Orang Asli communities through sustainable agriculture and market access. Together, they strengthen the commercial infrastructure that converts better production into better income.
Gaia Eats brings plant-based food brands and ready-to-heat Malaysian meals, including Pinxin and Mirra, to health-conscious consumers. Meet Mee manufactures halal, non-fried Malaysian instant Pan Mee noodles, and pantry products. These companies extend food security beyond volume to nutrition, affordability, consumer choice, and local value creation.
Seen individually, these businesses are vastly different. Together, they cover much of the journey from science and farm operations to circularity and market access. That breadth is ScaleX’s strength: it treats food security as a connected system rather than a collection of stand-alone projects.

Technology alone does not transform a food system. Adoption happens when a solution is useful, affordable, and trusted by the people who must operate it. For Ong, farmers cannot be treated as the final recipients of technology. They must be partners in defining the problem, shaping the pilot, and judging whether a solution delivers practical value in real operating conditions.
“A successful deployment is not a machine installed or an app downloaded. It is a farmer seeing better yield, lower losses, reduced risk, safer production, or higher income,” she said. “That means listening first, designing with farmers, providing training and after-sales support, and measuring what changes on the ground.”

“For food and agriculture, government involvement is important because deployment ultimately happens on the ground,” said Ong. ScaleX positions high-potential companies within the broader national food-security agenda, with the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (KPKM) as programme endorser and national policy anchor, and the Securities Commission Malaysia as a strategic pipeline partner through GrowMatch. The purpose is to connect policy priorities with technologies that can be adopted and scaled in Malaysia’s production systems.

“My vision for Impact Circle has always been to make innovation useful to the people who produce our food. I am doing this because food security is not solved by technology, capital or policy working in separate silos; it is strengthened when we connect them so that proven solutions reach farms, fisheries and food businesses, raise productivity and resilience, and create better livelihoods.”
ScaleX is now advancing into State and Corporate Living Labs, where partnerships can be deployed with state authorities, agencies, corporates, and farming communities. “Different companies solve different parts of the problem, and that is where the ecosystem becomes valuable,” Ong said. Investment remains an enabler, not the finishing line: the measure of success is whether companies secure the right opportunities, deploy their technologies and show meaningful outcomes.
ScaleX began with companies ready to scale. Its greater purpose is to turn innovation into stronger farms, more resilient supply chains and a food system that can nourish Malaysia—by scaling what works with farmers, not around them.

title: MRCA Marks 34 Years of Retail Growth as Dato’ Liew Bin Takes the Helm
bodyText:
The Malaysia Retail Chain Association (MRCA) marked 34 years of supporting Malaysia’s retail industry with its Installation & 34th Anniversary Night on 25 September 2026 at Sunway Resort Hotel.
The biennial event marked the formal transition to MRCA’s new 2026–2028 council while bringing together around 1,000 attendees, including MRCA council members, retailers, business leaders, corporate partners and other distinguished guests.
The event was attended by YB Hannah Yeoh, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories), as Guest of Honour.
Founded in 1992, MRCA represents retailers through networking, education, training and the pooling of resources and expertise.
A key highlight of the evening was the formal transition of leadership from Immediate Past President Datuk Dr Ken Phua to newly installed MRCA President Dato’ Liew Bin for the 2026–2028 term.
A symbolic Key Handover Ceremony took place in the presence of YB Hannah Yeoh to mark the leadership transition.
In his inaugural address, Dato’ Liew Bin outlined his vision of positioning MRCA as “The Home of Retailers”, with the association seeking to provide an inclusive platform where retail businesses of different sizes can find value, build connections and grow together.
MRCA’s official 2026–2028 council lists Dato’ Liew Bin as President, with Datuk Dr Ken Phua serving as Immediate Past President.
The association currently represents 600 members and more than 40,000 outlets locally and internationally, with its wider network supporting more than 400,000 job opportunities.
During her keynote address, YB Hannah Yeoh commended MRCA’s 34-year legacy and highlighted its “Member Get Member” initiative, which aims to grow the association’s membership to 1,000 members and represent more than 10,000 businesses through strategic affiliations.
The initiative forms part of MRCA’s efforts to broaden its retail network and strengthen its role as a platform for businesses across Malaysia’s retail sector.
YB Hannah Yeoh also highlighted the importance of collaboration between the government and the retail sector in supporting urban economic growth.
She said the government, together with Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) and Putrajaya Corporation, is working to streamline licensing and regulatory processes for retail businesses.
The aim is to reduce unnecessary administrative procedures and make it easier for businesses to open and operate. Bernama separately reported that the government is reviewing processes to move business applications further online and reduce administrative burdens on entrepreneurs.
“The MADANI government is deeply committed to ensuring dynamic and sustainable economic development,” said YB Hannah Yeoh.
She added that pro-business policies should help create a more liveable city while allowing businesses, retailers and communities to develop alongside one another.
The anniversary celebration also featured a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) exchange between MRCA and Lark Technologies Pte. Ltd.
The strategic collaboration will focus on advancing AI-powered digital transformation across Malaysia’s retail industry.
The partnership comes as retailers increasingly explore digital tools and artificial intelligence to improve business operations, customer engagement and competitiveness.
For MRCA, the collaboration also aligns with its broader focus on helping retailers strengthen their businesses through innovation, education, training and knowledge-sharing. The association’s Retail Division specifically identifies business development and innovation, as well as engagement with technology and other partners, among its objectives.
With a new council in place and a stated ambition to become “The Home of Retailers”, MRCA is positioning its next term around a stronger network for businesses operating in Malaysia’s changing retail landscape.
The association’s 2026–2028 leadership, together with its growing membership base and new collaboration with Lark Technologies, reflects a continued focus on retail networking, digital transformation and industry development.
The evening concluded with recognition of the corporate patrons and sponsors whose support contributed to the event, including RHB Bank, U Mobile, Lark Technologies, Berjaya Sompo Insurance, Adyen Malaysia and Illuminext, alongside the event’s Diamond, Platinum, Gold and Silver sponsors.

title: BMW Motorrad Malaysia Introduces BMW R 1300 GS with Automated Shift Assistant
bodyText:
BMW Motorrad Malaysia has introduced the latest variant of the BMW R 1300 GS, adding the new Automated Shift Assistant (ASA) to the adventure motorcycle’s extensive range of technology, touring and comfort features.
Introduced to the Malaysian market at the Malaysia Autoshow in 2024, the BMW R 1300 GS has established itself in the adventure touring segment. The latest variant builds on its combination of performance, control and long-distance capability with ASA as part of an enhanced Dynamic Package.
The package also includes Dynamic Suspension Adjustment (DSA), Gear Shift Assistant Pro, Riding Modes Pro and Sports Brake.
The new Automated Shift Assistant represents the latest development in BMW Motorrad’s gearshift technology, automating clutch control and gear shifting while retaining the dynamic riding experience associated with the BMW R 1300 GS.
With no need for manual clutch operation, ASA is designed to make starting, stopping and manoeuvring easier while allowing riders to focus more closely on the road and riding conditions.
Riders can choose between manual and fully automated shifting depending on their preferred riding style and conditions.
In “M” shift mode, riders select gears using the foot shift lever while the Automated Shift Assistant manages clutch operation automatically. In “D” shift mode, gear changes are fully automated according to engine speed and load, providing smoother and more comfortable shifting.
Whether riding on everyday roads, tackling inclines or venturing off-road, ASA is designed to complement the BMW R 1300 GS’s boxer engine while making the motorcycle more accessible and relaxed to ride.
Beyond the Automated Shift Assistant and Dynamic Package, the BMW R 1300 GS comes with a range of equipment designed for everyday riding and longer adventures.
The Touring Package includes preparation for a GPS device, a Central Locking System, Hand Protector Extension and left and right case holders.
The Comfort Package adds a Passenger Kit, electrically adjustable windscreen and main stand, while Adaptive Height Adjustment, a Deluxe headlight and M lightweight battery come as standard.
The BMW R 1300 GS with Automated Shift Assistant is available in White Aluminium Metallic, a new colour option, as well as Black Storm Metallic.
At the heart of the BMW R 1300 GS with Automated Shift Assistant is BMW Motorrad’s two-cylinder boxer engine.
With a displacement of 1,300 cc, the engine develops 107 kW (145 hp) at 7,750 rpm and maximum torque of 149 Nm at 6,500 rpm. BMW Motorrad describes it as the most powerful series-produced BMW boxer engine to date. The current BMW Motorrad Malaysia specification also lists the R 1300 GS with a 1,300 cc engine and 145 hp output.
The motorcycle’s compact configuration places the gearbox beneath the engine, contributing to a total weight of 237 kg according to BMW Motorrad Malaysia.
The combination of the boxer engine, compact construction and updated shift technology is designed to maintain the R 1300 GS’s performance and adventure capabilities while making the riding experience more effortless.
BMW Motorrad Malaysia is also offering financing options through BMW Group Financial Services Malaysia.
Under the stated financing plan, ownership of the BMW R 1300 GS with Automated Shift Assistant starts from RM2,048 per month. The estimate is based on Straight Line Financing at a 4.50% flat rate, with a 90% loan over seven years.
Owners can also access BMW Motorrad Malaysia’s Premium Engine Oil Inclusive, Service Inclusive and Warranty Extension programmes.
The BMW R 1300 GS with Automated Shift Assistant is priced at RM145,000 on the road, excluding insurance, and comes with BMW Motorrad Malaysia’s three-year warranty and three-year roadside assistance programmes. The launch price has also been reported locally at RM145,000.
The latest BMW R 1300 GS variant combines BMW Motorrad’s established adventure touring platform with automated shifting technology, expanded touring equipment and comfort-focused features, offering Malaysian riders another configuration of the R 1300 GS for both everyday journeys and longer adventures.

title: Lenovo Modernises Virtualisation Infrastructure for an AI-Ready Future
bodyText:
Lenovo has announced a new portfolio of infrastructure solutions and services designed to help enterprises modernise the technology foundations behind their virtualised environments while preparing for the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI).
The expanded portfolio includes the Lenovo ThinkAgile VX850 V4, designed for highly virtualised environments and demanding in-memory workloads; Lenovo Premier Deploy for Infrastructure, which offers three pre-defined service levels to support the transition from deployment to production-ready operations; and expanded Lenovo Express Solutions, which provide validated modernisation paths across leading virtualisation and hybrid cloud platforms.
“Organisations are focused on modernising virtualised infrastructure to improve efficiency and resilience while maintaining flexibility in an increasingly complex IT landscape,” said Scott Patti, Vice President, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Lenovo. “Lenovo is helping customers modernise the infrastructure they rely on today with greater choice and control, while building an AI-ready foundation that can evolve as their requirements change.”
The Lenovo ThinkAgile VX850 V4 expands Lenovo’s virtualisation portfolio with infrastructure designed for highly virtualised enterprise environments and demanding workloads.
Supporting both structured and unstructured data, the VX850 V4 provides a foundation for consolidating and modernising critical workloads. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into enterprise applications and workflows, the infrastructure is designed to support existing business-critical applications while creating additional capacity for emerging workloads.
Lenovo’s wider ThinkAgile portfolio is positioned to support enterprise workloads including virtualisation, analytics, in-memory databases and AI, giving organisations options for modernising their infrastructure without having to replace their entire technology environment.
Alongside new hardware, Lenovo is expanding its Infrastructure Deployment Services with three clearly defined deployment options: Standard Deploy, Premier Deploy and Premier Deploy Plus.
The structure is intended to make it easier for customers to select a deployment approach based on project complexity, business criticality, internal IT capabilities and the level of support required after go-live.
All three options provide a structured readiness foundation and expert hardware installation. Premier Deploy and Premier Deploy Plus add implementation and operational hand-off support for projects requiring additional assistance in moving from infrastructure delivery to production-ready operations.
Premier Deploy Plus further includes extended post-deployment assistance and a one-year infrastructure health assessment, excluding DE Storage Array. This is designed to help customers identify issues early and determine their next steps.
Lenovo is also expanding its Lenovo Express Solutions portfolio through the Lenovo Top Choice Express programme.
The pre-validated infrastructure configurations combine Lenovo technology with leading software platforms to simplify deployment, reduce integration complexity and accelerate time to value.
The expanded portfolio provides modernisation options across several virtualisation and hybrid cloud platforms while maintaining flexibility and customer choice. These include:
By combining Lenovo infrastructure with tested configurations from technology partners, the solutions are intended to reduce the integration burden on IT teams and provide a more predictable path from evaluation to deployment. Lenovo describes these validated modernisation paths as a way for organisations to evolve existing virtual environments rather than start again from scratch.
As enterprises modernise their virtualisation strategies, Lenovo is also placing emphasis on infrastructure resilience and data protection.
Lenovo ThinkSystem Storage and ThinkAgile HCI solutions support modernised virtualised environments, disaggregated infrastructure, integrated data protection and scalable AI workloads.
Integrated cyber-resilience capabilities are designed to strengthen ransomware recovery, recovery planning and operational continuity, helping organisations keep the data supporting business-critical and AI workloads protected and recoverable.
Lenovo is also highlighting the importance of open standards as organisations modernise their infrastructure. XClarity Controller 3 and XClarity One use standards-based management to help customers integrate, automate and operate infrastructure more consistently.
The latest portfolio reflects a broader shift in enterprise IT infrastructure as businesses seek to introduce AI while continuing to support existing applications and virtualised workloads.
Rather than requiring organisations to replace their current infrastructure wholesale, Lenovo is positioning its solutions around incremental modernisation across virtualisation, hybrid cloud, storage, infrastructure management and deployment services.
“Modernisation is an in-place initiative; it does not require starting over,” said Matt Eastwood, Senior Vice President, IDC’s Enterprise Infrastructure and Datacenter Group.
He said Lenovo’s combination of virtualisation, hybrid cloud, storage, infrastructure management, deployment services and technology partners provides a flexible foundation for traditional enterprise, cloud-native and AI-native workloads.
The approach is intended to allow organisations to modernise incrementally while maintaining control over how and where workloads and data are deployed, as enterprises continue building the infrastructure needed for an increasingly AI-enabled technology environment.

title: Java Kapital Group, SME Association of Malaysia and SEAMEO VOCTECH Forge ASEAN Skills Partnership
bodyText:
Java Kapital Group, the SME Association of Malaysia and the SEAMEO Regional Centre for Vocational and Technical Education and Training (SEAMEO VOCTECH) have formalised a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening vocational-technical education, workforce development and digital transformation for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across ASEAN.
The three parties signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on Malaysia Day, 16 September 2026, marking a new phase of cooperation between industry, the SME community and regional technical and vocational education and training (TVET) expertise.
The signing ceremony was represented by Dato’ Dr. Danny Mah, Executive Director of Java Kapital Group and National Deputy Secretary-General of the SME Association of Malaysia, together with Haji Norjemee Bin Jenek, Director of SEAMEO VOCTECH.
Under the MoU, the partners will deepen cooperation in ASEAN vocational-technical education, workforce development and digital transformation for SMEs.
Java Kapital Group will contribute its technological expertise in areas including computing data centres, robotics, the low-altitude economy and artificial intelligence (AI). These technologies are expected to form part of broader efforts to equip workers and businesses with skills relevant to emerging industries.
Meanwhile, the SME Association of Malaysia will leverage its industry network to support SMEs and strengthen their access to relevant knowledge, skills and opportunities.
SEAMEO VOCTECH, which is headquartered in Brunei, will provide a professional platform drawing on its regional experience in TVET. Its council comprises senior education officials and representatives from SEAMEO member states, giving the organisation a regional perspective on vocational and technical education.
The partnership will place a strong emphasis on developing skills that can support Southeast Asia’s evolving industrial and technological landscape.
Moving forward, the three parties will jointly develop skills-training curricula, industry seminars, e-learning programmes and industrial practical projects. These initiatives are intended to facilitate the exchange of technology and knowledge between education providers, industry and SMEs.
The partners will also identify viable project proposals and explore different financing mechanisms to support potential areas of cooperation.
The scope of the collaboration may subsequently be expanded to other areas mutually agreed upon by the three parties.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Dato’ Dr. Danny Mah said computing infrastructure, robotics, the low-altitude economy and artificial intelligence represent core growth sectors for Southeast Asia’s economy and human capital.
He highlighted the importance of developing skilled talent for emerging industries while strengthening the digital capabilities of SMEs.
As businesses increasingly adopt new technologies, access to appropriate skills and technical expertise will be important in helping SMEs participate in emerging areas of the digital economy. The partnership therefore brings together technology capabilities, industry networks and regional TVET expertise to address both workforce development and business needs.
The MoU represents a collaboration between three complementary areas: corporate technology, SME industry networks and regional vocational education.
By connecting these capabilities, the partnership aims to bridge TVET systems with industry across ASEAN and create opportunities for greater technology and knowledge exchange.
Through skills training, practical industrial projects, e-learning and industry seminars, the partners will work towards developing talent equipped for emerging industries while supporting SMEs in their digital transformation journey.
The collaboration ultimately seeks to contribute to regional talent development and higher-quality digital transformation for small and medium-sized enterprises across Southeast Asia.

title: Malaysian Women More Confident About Equal Pay, but Less So About Career Opportunities
bodyText:
Malaysian women are more likely than men to believe that men and women earn about the same for the same job, but are less likely to believe that women have equal job and career opportunities, according to findings from the 2026 WIN Worldviews Survey highlighted by Central Force Insights.
The survey found that 67% of Malaysian women believe men and women receive equal pay for the same job, compared with 60% of Malaysian men.
The Malaysian results differ from the global findings. Worldwide, 51% of men surveyed believe men and women earn about the same for the same job, compared with 38% of women.
However, the picture changes when respondents were asked about career opportunities.
Only 54% of Malaysian women surveyed believe women have the same job and career opportunities as men, compared with 62% of male respondents.
Meanwhile, nearly one in three Malaysian women, or 31%, believe women have fewer job and career opportunities than men. This compares with 17% of male respondents.
For Central Force Insights, the contrast raises questions about whether positive perceptions of equal pay also extend to the career opportunities that influence people’s earning potential over time.
See Toh Wai Yu, Chief Executive Officer of Central Force Insights and President of The Market Research Society Malaysia, said equal pay within the same role does not necessarily indicate that a workplace provides equal opportunities for career progression.
“You can pay men and women equally in the same role and still have an unequal workplace.”
She said employers should examine who receives training, who gets promoted and how employees’ careers are affected following career breaks.
“A fair payslip does not automatically mean a fair career. Employers need to be able to demonstrate both.”
Across Malaysian respondents overall, 64% believe men and women earn about the same for the same job. This compares with a global average of 45%.
However, Central Force Insights stressed that the survey measures perceptions rather than verified workplace pay practices.
As a result, positive perceptions of workplace fairness do not necessarily establish whether individual employers have equal pay practices or whether men and women in equivalent roles receive the same remuneration.
Separate data from the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) provides a broader picture of wages in Malaysia’s formal sector.
In March 2026, male formal-sector employees recorded a median monthly wage of RM3,064, compared with RM3,000 for female employees.
These figures cover formal employees across the workforce and describe overall median earnings. They do not establish whether men and women performing equivalent jobs are paid differently.
Central Force Insights therefore cautioned against using either survey perceptions or headline wage statistics alone to determine whether workplaces are fair.
Understanding differences in pay and career outcomes requires closer examination of how employers make decisions around remuneration, promotion, training and career progression.
Central Force Insights, which is a signatory to the Women’s Empowerment Principles (WEPs), a joint initiative of UN Women and the UN Global Compact, is calling on employers to examine workplace practices beyond remuneration.
It recommends that organisations review pay, promotion, access to training and outcomes following career breaks.
Such reviews should compare employees in equivalent roles and circumstances, while also considering whether employees have equitable access to opportunities to gain skills, experience and greater responsibilities.
The emphasis, according to Central Force Insights, should therefore be on measuring who progresses, rather than looking only at what employees earn at a particular point in time.
The organisation also said employers should not be the only judges of their own workplace fairness.
Employees should have a voice in reviews and a clear understanding of how decisions around pay and promotion are made. Where differences emerge, Central Force Insights said they should be investigated rather than dismissed or automatically attributed to discrimination.
Wai Yu said organisations should be able to explain how they assess merit when making decisions about career progression.
“A company cannot claim to reward merit without showing how merit is measured.”
She added that equal opportunity does not mean every employee will have the same career or salary, but that gender should not determine whose skills are recognised or who receives opportunities to progress.
For Malaysian employers, the survey findings highlight a distinction between equal pay and equal opportunity, with both potentially requiring separate measures and closer examination of workplace practices.

title: Malaysia Showcases Digital Capabilities at Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou
bodyText:
Malaysia is showcasing its technology and digital trade capabilities at the 5th Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) in Hangzhou, China, marking the country’s first participation in the international expo as Guest Country of Honour.
Coordinated by the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), the Malaysia Pavilion brings together 15 exhibitors, including four government agencies, to showcase Malaysian capabilities across digital trade, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud services, smart healthcare and cross-border e-commerce.
The expo is taking place from 23 to 27 September 2026 at the Hangzhou Grand Convention and Exhibition Centre.
Malaysia’s participation was officially marked by the presence of Prime Minister Dato’ Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who officiated the Malaysia Pavilion in person.
His presence at the Pavilion highlights Malaysia’s efforts to deepen its engagement with China’s rapidly growing digital economy and create greater opportunities for Malaysian technology companies in the market.
For MATRADE, the participation also supports Malaysia’s wider strategy of expanding its presence in China by diversifying both its geographical reach and export offerings.
Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof, Chief Executive Officer of MATRADE, said Malaysian digital and technology companies have the capabilities to compete in international markets, with GDTE providing an opportunity to access China’s expanding digital economy.
He said Malaysia’s participation also aligns with MATRADE’s export strategy of expanding into second-, third- and fourth-tier cities in China while diversifying the country’s product mix to include more high-technology goods and solutions.
The strategy reflects the growing importance of digital trade and technology-driven exports in strengthening Malaysia’s position within regional and global markets.
Alongside Malaysia’s participation at GDTE, MATRADE exchanged a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), one of the world’s largest banks.
The partnership aims to strengthen the export capacity of Malaysian micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and facilitate their access to the Chinese market.
The collaboration will also explore opportunities to support Malaysian businesses through cross-border digital trade platforms, potentially making it easier for MSMEs to connect with customers and business partners in China.
The agreement adds a financial and digital trade dimension to Malaysia’s participation at GDTE, complementing the technology solutions being showcased at the Malaysia Pavilion.
Held under the theme “Meeting the AI Future”, the 5th GDTE brings together exhibitors and participants from around the world.
International exhibitors account for more than 20% of the expo’s 170,000-square-metre exhibition area. Malaysia and Hungary are serving as joint Countries of Honour, while representatives from 121 countries and regions and 29 international organisations are participating in the event.
