The scale of the expo provides Malaysian companies with an opportunity to engage international businesses and explore new partnerships within the digital economy.
Malaysia’s participation in the 5th GDTE reflects its ambition to strengthen its position as a digital trade hub within ASEAN and serve as a bridge between Southeast Asia and China.
The country is positioning its growing technology ecosystem, supportive government policies and expanding pipeline of technology-driven businesses as foundations for deeper international collaboration.
Through platforms such as GDTE, Malaysia aims to create opportunities for technology companies and MSMEs to expand their exports, establish partnerships and access new markets.
The Malaysia Pavilion therefore serves not only as a showcase of Malaysian digital capabilities, but also as a platform for strengthening commercial links between Malaysian businesses, Chinese partners and the wider global digital economy.

title: The MECA Gold Standard: When Good Industrial Relations Prevents the Dispute
bodyText:
MECA Employers Consulting Agency (MECA) CEO Dharmen Sivalingam shares what has gone into creating a Convention experience that could mark a first in the way Industrial Relations is taught and understood—bringing MECA’s accumulated experience to the industry through an approach designed not simply to explain IR principles, but to show how they unfold in real workplace situations.
The MECA IR Convention 2026 deliberately centres its discussion around three areas. “Misconduct, performance management, and retrenchment or restructuring,” said Dharmen. “These are areas where the law matters greatly, but they are also areas where the legal framework alone does not tell the full story.”

Each presents employers with a different challenge. In performance management, Dharmen shared that employers can become preoccupied with whether the Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) has been correctly structured and documented. Yet he reminded that “The quality of the conversations leading up to and during a PIP may ultimately matter as much as the document itself.”
The same consideration applies to misconduct. “In misconduct, the employer may have strong evidence, but the way the investigation is conducted, the way questions are asked and whether the employee genuinely feels heard can have a major impact on whether the matter escalates,” said Dharmen.
Retrenchment and restructuring introduce another set of sensitivities because a sound commercial rationale does not necessarily prevent employees from questioning how decisions are reached. “Problems can arise from unclear selection criteria, poor communication, inconsistent treatment or the perception that a particular person is targeted,” emphasised Dharmen.

One of the most consequential changes, Dharmen shared, has taken place among employees themselves.“The law itself has not changed dramatically,” he said. While procedural developments have occurred, the far more significant change is employees’ sophistication.
“In the past, there was a greater likelihood that employees would accept a decision to terminate their employment, sometimes without seriously questioning whether they had any right to challenge it,” said Dharmen. Today, employers operate in an environment where decisions are more likely to be questioned, and employees are increasingly prepared to exercise the avenues available to them when they believe their rights have been compromised.
“Compliance with the law remains non-negotiable. But compliance alone does not keep an employer out of trouble,” said Dharmen. He explained that the reason lies in what actually triggers a dispute. “An employee does not need first to prove that the dismissal was legally unfair before filing a complaint. The real trigger is much simpler. The employee feels, considers or perceives that the dismissal was unfair. That is enough to start the dispute.”
Employee perception therefore sits much closer to the centre of Industrial Relations than employers recognise. “An employee does not experience a retrenchment as a statutory principle,” said Dharmen. “They experience somebody telling them: ‘Your role no longer exists.’Performance management is equally personal. “An employee does not experience a PIP as a legal framework. They experience their manager telling them that their performance is not good enough.” A misconduct investigation carries its own human weight because the employee experiences being questioned and investigated while potentially facing the loss of a livelihood.
“These are deeply human situations,” said Dharmen. “And human beings react emotionally before they react legally.”That reaction may be shaped by questions that sit outside the technical process but are central to how fairness is perceived: “ Why me? Was I treated fairly? Did they listen to me? Was the decision already made? Why was somebody else treated differently? Are they trying to get rid of me?”

“These perceptions matter because they often determine whether the employee accepts the outcome or challenges it,” said Dharmen. “So psychology, communication, unconscious bias, fairness, dignity and Industrial Relations are not separate subjects. They are deeply intertwined in every difficult workplace decision.”Communication, Dharmen stressed, becomes especially important because employees process difficult news differently. “One employee may want a very direct conversation. Another may need more explanation. One may want to ask many questions. Another may say very little but react strongly afterwards,” he added.
This means employers need to exercise judgment over who delivers the message, how it is framed, how much explanation is provided and whether the employee genuinely feels heard. “If the objective is merely to comply with the law, the employer can focus on process. If the objective is the gold medal of avoiding the dispute altogether, the communication methodology has to become much sharper.”

The challenge for MECA is in translating these ideas into a Convention where delegates could see and understand how these dynamics play out in practice. “We have spent a great deal of time asking ourselves, ‘How do we make sure the message lands?’” said Dharmen. That question has shaped the MECA IR Convention 2026 into an immersive learning experience. “We have chosen three mini movies dealing with misconduct, performance management and retrenchment or restructuring.” The Convention will complement the mini-movies with a live dramatisation exploring unconscious bias by professional actors.
The intention is for delegates to encounter the complexities of Industrial Relations as situations rather than simply as principles. “We hope this approach will allow participants to absorb the practical lessons in a way that stays with them long after the Convention is over,” said Dharmen. To our knowledge, this is not an approach that has previously been adopted in an Industrial Relations Convention in this way.”
The three specially produced mini movies provide the common experience for the subsequent discussion. “The movies create the experience. The discussion afterwards extracts the learning,” said Dharmen.

“We believe that is a much more powerful way of helping people understand difficult Industrial Relations issues.” Delegates can then examine what happened, what was handled correctly, what could have been done differently and when the problem actually began. The discussion can move from whether the process was legally sound to what should have been documented, how the employee may have perceived the conversation and what could happen if the situation were eventually tested in court.
“The new frame is that Industrial Relations should begin before the dispute ,” said Dharmen. “It should begin at the point where the workplace decision is being considered.” An employer faced with a difficult employment decision will naturally ask, “Can we do this?” Dharmen believes good Industrial Relations requires another question: “What happens if we do?”

That changes the scope of the decision. The employer considers the legal risk and commercial consequences alongside how the employee might react, how the wider workforce may perceive the decision, what evidence exists, whether that evidence will remain available and how the decision will be communicated. The final question is equally important: “Is there a better outcome available?”
MECA’s advisory perspective extends beyond asking whether an employer is legally entitled to take a particular course of action. “A purely legal adviser may ask: ‘Can the employer do this?’ That is obviously important. But experience teaches you to ask more,” said Dharmen. Those questions include whether the employer should act in that way, what happens next, how the employee may react, what evidence exists, whether that evidence and the witnesses will still be available months later, and how the decision might look when examined.
“Going beyond compliance does not mean moving away from compliance,” said Dharmen. “Compliance is non-negotiable. “The proposition is that compliance provides the foundation for a more complete Industrial Relations decision. “Reframing IR means recognising that compliance is the foundation rather than the destination,” said Dharmen.
After three decades of dealing with the consequences of workplace decisions, Dharmen distils the thinking behind the Convention into one simple comparison. Winning in the Industrial Court is the silver medal. The gold medal is never having to go there.”
Themed “Reframing IR: When Compliance Is Not Enough. Why Legally Sound Decisions Still Lead To Conflict,” the convention takes place on 7 –8 October 2026 at the Connexion Conference & Event Centre (CCEC) in Bangsar South, Kuala Lumpur . For more information and to register: https://convention.meca.com.my/meca . For group registrations & corporate rates, please contact MECA at 03 2779 4227 or [email protected] .

title: Elizabeth Sandra: Beyond the Comfort Zone — How TalentCorp’s Women-Industry Network (WIN) Helped Her Discover the Leader Within
bodyText:
By Harriet Santhana
For many professionals, the greatest obstacle to career progression is not a lack of opportunity, it is the quiet voice of self-doubt that questions whether they are truly ready for the next step.
For Sandra, that voice was familiar.
Although she had built a stable career at Lenovo after joining the company in 2019 as an Inside Sales Support Representative, she often found herself wondering whether she was capable of pursuing bigger ambitions. Behind every aspiration was an invisible barrier she had unknowingly built herself.
“The biggest challenge for me was always the glass ceiling that I put on myself,”  Sandra recalled. “I always had aspirations–I wanted to do this, I wanted to do that–but there was always self-doubt. I kept asking myself, ‘Can I do this? Am I good enough?'”
Today, Sandra serves as a senior Inside Sales Representative at Lenovo, is a licensed Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) Practitioner, and continues to invest in empowering other women through professional communities. Looking back, she credits much of that transformation to a willingness to step outside her comfort zone, and to the guidance she received through TalentCorp’s Elevate Your Career Mentee Programme.
Her story is one of more than career progression. It is a reminder that women’s empowerment often begins long before a promotion or leadership title. It begins with believing that growth is possible.

When Sandra transitioned from a non-sales role into sales in 2022, the move represented one of the biggest career decisions she had ever made.
Having spent more than three years supporting Lenovo’s sales team through pre-sales and post-sales operations, she was suddenly entering a customer-facing role despite having no previous sales experience.
The opportunity was exciting, but it was also intimidating.
“I had mixed feelings,” she said. “There was excitement, but also fear and uncertainty because I didn’t have any sales experience before. I wasn’t sure whether I could really do it.”
It was during this period of transition that she discovered TalentCorp’s Elevate Your Career Mentee Programme.
Rather than viewing the programme as a shortcut to success, Sandra saw it as an opportunity to gain clarity. She hoped that guidance from an experienced mentor would help her better understand her new career path while giving her the confidence to navigate unfamiliar territory.
What she found was far more transformative than she had anticipated.

From the outset, she and her mentor established that the relationship would be a collaborative one. Rather than simply receiving advice, Sandra understood that meaningful growth required her own commitment and willingness to participate actively throughout the programme.
“It was a two-way interaction,” she explained. “My mentor didn’t just tell me what to do. She guided me and provided valuable advice on my career path. She also asked a lot of questions.”
Instead of prescribing solutions, her mentor challenged her with thought-provoking questions.
What was truly holding her back?
What did she believe her greatest challenge was?
Where did she see herself in the years ahead?
Those questions became turning points.
“The answers were already there,” Sandra said. “I just never thought about them until someone asked me those questions.”
The reflective approach encouraged her to look inward rather than constantly searching for external validation. Instead of focusing on limitations, she began recognising her own strengths, ambitions, and ability to overcome challenges.
For Sandra, that shift in mindset became one of the programme’s greatest gifts.

Among the many lessons she gained from the programme, one exercise has remained with her long after the mentoring sessions ended: creating a vision board.
Her mentor encouraged her to map out both her current situation and the future she wanted to build over the next three to five years.
Using images, keywords and personal aspirations, she created a visual reminder of the goals she wanted to achieve and displayed it somewhere she would see every day.
“It serves as a daily reminder of what my end goal is,” she said.
While simple in concept, the exercise fundamentally changed how she approached personal and professional development.
Rather than becoming consumed by day-to-day challenges, Sandra learned to keep her long-term aspirations in sight. Every decision became part of a larger journey rather than an isolated task.
It reinforced an important lesson: meaningful career growth is rarely accidental. It begins with intentional planning, followed by consistent action.

Each session built upon the previous one.
Together, they identified specific challenges, developed practical action plans, reviewed progress and refined strategies as new situations emerged.
The personalised nature of the mentoring experience made every conversation directly relevant to her career journey.
Equally valuable was the opportunity to receive guidance from someone completely outside her existing professional network.
“Hearing advice from an experienced leader who was essentially a stranger gave me a completely fresh perspective,” she said.
Without preconceived notions or organisational biases, her mentor was able to challenge assumptions she had unknowingly accepted about herself and her career.
The experience strengthened not only her resilience, but also her confidence in making important career decisions.
Instead of allowing uncertainty to dictate her choices, Elizabeth learned to approach new opportunities with greater curiosity and self-belief.

The impact of that mindset shift became evident sooner than Sandra expected.
When she first accepted her sales role, she told herself she would spend two years testing whether the position was the right fit.
Instead, something remarkable happened.
Within just one year, she was promoted into a senior position.
The achievement surprised even her.
“I didn’t expect to be promoted to a senior role in my second year,” she admitted.
Looking back, Elizabeth believes the mentoring programme played an important role in preparing her for increased responsibilities.
It wasn’t simply because she had acquired new skills.
Instead, she developed something even more valuable: confidence.
“I think with the right mindset and determination, I’ll be able to take on greater responsibilities.”
Today, she approaches career progression differently from when she first entered sales.
She constantly pushes herself beyond perceived limits, embraces continuous learning and remains adaptable in an environment where change is inevitable.
“Changes happen everywhere—in every organisation,” she said. “Being adaptable and resilient helps position yourself for continuous learning and new opportunities.”
Her perspective has also expanded beyond completing individual tasks.
Earlier in her career, success meant meeting deadlines and finishing assigned work.
Today, every project begins with a broader question.
How does this contribute to the organisation?
How does it affect stakeholders?
How can different teams be aligned to achieve a common objective?
“I think more from the bigger perspective now,” Sandra explained. “It’s not just about completing the task anymore. It’s about understanding how it impacts the business and contributes towards achieving the company’s goals.”
That shift, from task execution to strategic thinking, marks the evolution of a professional who is no longer simply performing a role, but actively contributing to organisational success.

Curious about the connection between human mind and behaviour, she pursued another milestone in her personal development by becoming a licensed Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) Practitioner.
For Sandra, the decision was driven by more than professional advancement.
“I’ve always been curious about how the human mind and behaviour are connected,” she said. “On top of that, as an introvert, I wanted to understand how to interact with people better, especially in the workplace.”
The training introduced her to a deeper understanding of how people think, communicate and respond differently depending on their personalities and experiences. More importantly, it reinforced the importance of empathy as a leadership skill.
Rather than approaching every conversation the same way, Sandra learned to adapt her communication style according to the individual and the situation.
“I learned how to converse with people with empathy by putting myself in another person’s shoes while still maintaining professionalism,” she explained. “It also helped me understand different perspectives, not just from my own point of view, but from what the other person may be thinking.”
Those lessons have become invaluable in her day-to-day work.
Whether collaborating across departments, working with customers, or engaging stakeholders, Sandra believes effective communication begins with understanding people before seeking to be understood.
“Everyone is wired differently,” she said. “So I have different approaches for different stakeholders and different situations.”
The result has been smoother collaboration, stronger professional relationships, and greater influence across teams.

For Sandra, growth does not stop with a new role or achievement. She continues to actively invest in expanding her skills, knowledge and network.
Outside of Lenovo, she contributes as an exco member of Women in Tech Malaysia , which is a dynamic and inclusive community dedicated to fostering empowerment, diversity, and innovation within the technology sector. She also regularly participates in seminars, workshops, exhibitions and online learning opportunities to gain new insights and strengthen her professional capabilities.
Looking ahead, Sandra  hopes to continue growing into a role where she can become a trusted advisor, subject matter expert and contributor to larger, more complex projects that create meaningful business value.

Before joining the programme, she felt she had remained in her comfort zone for too long and that her career progression had become stagnant. The mentorship experience helped her gain clarity, confidence, and a new perspective on how she could navigate her career journey.
She encourages professionals, especially those considering their next career step, to approach mentorship with an open mind and a willingness to take ownership of their growth.
“The programme provides valuable guidance and opportunities for self-reflection,” she said. “However, meaningful growth comes from adopting a growth mindset.”
For Sandra, the greatest lesson has been that opportunities rarely arrive when people feel completely ready. Sometimes, growth requires taking the leap first and learning along the way.
Her own transition from a non-sales role into sales is proof of that belief.
What began as an uncertain career move became the foundation for a new chapter, one where she continues to grow as a professional, leader and advocate for women’s empowerment.
Through TalentCorp’s Elevate Your Career Mentee Programme, Sandra discovered that breaking barriers is not always about overcoming external challenges. Sometimes, it begins by challenging the limitations we place on ourselves.

title: No Finish Line— Patricia Tan on Building SCORE for the Long Run
bodyText:
By Natasha Isabel Saravanan
Tan’s understanding of SCORE’s potential changed when the company joined the FitMalaysia movement, travelling across the country to organise events that encouraged people to become more active. “We weren’t just organising races,” Tan said. “We were helping people change their lifestyles.” Seeing participants progress from struggling with 5km runs to completing half and full marathons showed her that a race could have an impact beyond the finish line. “At the end of the day, it’s not just about the event,” she said. “It’s about what happens to people after they take that first step.”
That belief has since shaped SCORE’s approach, with the company expanding beyond race-day logistics to provide education, training clinics and community activities that help runners stay active. For Tan, running is ultimately about creating a sense of belonging. “People want to belong to something,” she said. “Running gives them a reason to come together, but the community is what keeps them coming back.” SCORE therefore aims to build an experience that extends beyond the race itself, helping runners form connections that keep them engaged long after race day.

Tan quickly discovered that organising races involved far more than creating a route and welcoming runners. Cash flow was an early challenge, with expenses such as permits, equipment, manpower, medals, T-shirts and logistics accumulating before an event generated revenue. “So our focus was simple,” she said. “Get more runners. Get more sponsors. Deliver a good event. Repeat. Understanding participants was equally important to SCORE’s growth. “If you listen carefully to your customers, they will tell you where the business needs to go,” Tan said. By listening to runners, observing developments in the industry as well as working with sponsors and government agencies, she has continued to adapt the company’s approach.
“I’m always looking at what can be done better,” Tan said. “The industry keeps changing, and we have to keep learning.”
That willingness to adapt eventually took SCORE beyond Malaysia through a partnership with a Singapore-based organisation to organise the BYD Singapore International Marathon. For Tan, the expansion demonstrated the potential of Malaysian companies to compete in the regional market. “It shows that Malaysian companies can compete regionally,” she said. “We don’t have to think of ourselves as being limited to Malaysia.”

As SCORE grew, Tan found that building the right team was just as important as building the business itself. “As founders, we often spend too much time working in the business and not enough time building the people and systems that allow the business to grow,” she said. Her role has since shifted from solving every problem herself to developing people who can take responsibility. “My job is no longer to solve every problem,” she said. “My job is to build a team that can solve problems well.”
Tan also believes in acting rather than waiting for the perfect answer. “I would rather make a decision, learn from it and improve than wait forever for the perfect answer,” she said. This approach is reflected in SCORE’s emphasis on speed, curiosity, teamwork, customer focus and excellence.
For Tan, however, attitude matters more than technical ability.
“Skills can be taught,” she said. “Attitude is much harder to teach.”
She believes putting the right person in the right role is essential, as even a capable employee can struggle when their strengths do not match the position they occupy.

Tan’s experience has taught her that no business remains unchanged for long. “Every year there is a new challenge,” she said, pointing to COVID-19, inflation, rising costs and changing consumer behaviour. When the pandemic halted physical events, SCORE moved into virtual runs to stay connected with participants. “You keep moving forward,” Tan said. “You may have to change direction, but you cannot stop.”
Technology has also reshaped SCORE operations, from registration and participant tracking to marketing and content creation. Tan sees these developments as opportunities for smaller companies to compete more effectively. “Technology gives smaller companies a chance to move faster,” she said. “If you use it well, you can compete with businesses that have much bigger resources.” She is similarly optimistic about health, wellness, experiences and community-focussed businesses, while SCORE is trying to improve its sustainability efforts through initiatives such as recycled medals and waste reduction programmes.
For Tan, sustainability extends beyond environmental practices to the long-term value a business creates.
“It’s also about building events, communities and businesses that can continue creating value for many years,” she said.

Tan wants SCORE to become the leading mass participation sports platform in ASEAN, creating a regional platform that encourages healthier lives through shared experiences. “We want to create something that is bigger than a single event,” she said. “We want to build a platform that helps people live healthier lives.”
That ambition informs her advice to other Malaysian SMEs. Rather than allowing their current size to limit their vision, she encourages founders to think beyond the present. “Don’t let your current size define your future,” she said. “You have to ask yourself what the business can become five or ten years from now.” She sees opportunities across technology, AI, health, wellness and experience-driven businesses, particularly for companies willing to look beyond Malaysia.
For Tan, however, growth is ultimately a means to a more personal end.
“I hope we’re remembered because we changed lives,” she said.

Her approach is rooted in the same persistence required to complete a difficult race. “Business is never a straight line,” she said. “There will be setbacks, mistakes and difficult periods. The important thing is not to quit.” She believes success belongs to those who keep learning and stay committed for the long term. “Most successful entrepreneurs are not necessarily the smartest,” Tan said. “They simply stayed in the game longer than everyone else.”
As SCORE looks towards its next chapter across ASEAN, Tan’s vision extends beyond growing the number of races it organises. She wants to build something that lasts: a platform that brings people together, changes everyday habits and leaves a meaningful impact on the communities it reaches.
In the end, the finish line is not the measure of success. It is how many people SCORE can inspire to keep moving forward.

title: MIHAS 2026 Connects 450 Global Buyers with 600 Malaysian Exporters
bodyText:
The 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) has opened at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC), Kuala Lumpur, bringing together Malaysian exporters and international buyers through its signature International Sourcing Programme (INSP).
The 2026 edition of INSP features more than 4,000 pre-arranged business-to-business (B2B) meetings connecting around 450 international buyers with 600 Malaysian exporters. The buyers represent 58 economies, with 50 participating as premium buyers.
The programme is designed to facilitate targeted business matching between Malaysian businesses and international buyers, creating opportunities for exporters to develop new commercial relationships and expand into global markets.
The strong participation from international buyers reflects the global demand for Malaysian halal products and services.
This year’s buyer delegation includes representatives from both established and emerging markets. First-time participating economies such as Comoros and Rwanda are engaging directly with Malaysia’s established halal ecosystem to source products and services.
Northeast Asia and ASEAN form the largest regional buyer contingents, while participation from Africa continues to expand as the region emerges as a potential growth market for Malaysian exporters.
The broad geographical representation gives Malaysian businesses opportunities to connect with buyers beyond their traditional export markets and strengthen their international trade networks.
According to MATRADE Chairman Dato’ Seri Reezal Merican Naina Merican, the International Sourcing Programme remains a key driver of MIHAS by directly connecting Malaysian businesses with international buyers seeking halal products and services.
“The INSP represents the core engine and ‘soul’ of MIHAS. With international buyers actively seeking high-quality Malaysian Halal products and services, our local SMEs must take full advantage of this platform.”
He said the programme has served as a direct catalyst for Malaysian businesses by providing access to high-value global trade networks and supporting longer-term export growth.
The participation of premium buyers also extends opportunities beyond conventional food and beverage products.
According to MATRADE, these buyers have a combined annual revenue of nearly RM700 billion, with procurement interests spanning specialised ingredients, biotechnology, Islamic finance, logistics and education.
This broader demand reflects Malaysia’s efforts to expand its halal exports beyond physical products and towards services-led exports and deeper integration into global supply chains.
The physical International Sourcing Programme takes place on 23 September at MITEC, alongside MIHAS 2026.
A virtual component of INSP is also running from 1 April to 30 November 2026, allowing international buyers to engage Malaysian exporters remotely. Up to 150 international virtual buyers are expected to participate in the virtual programme.
The combination of physical and virtual business matching gives Malaysian exporters additional opportunities to reach international markets and establish connections with buyers who may not be attending MIHAS in person.
Businesses and visitors interested in participating in MIHAS 2026 can register through the official MIHAS registration portal . Trade visitor admission is free, with online pre-registration providing priority entry.
MATRADE has previously positioned INSP as a demand-driven initiative designed to connect international buyers with Malaysian exporters through pre-arranged one-to-one business meetings.
Since its launch in 2004, the Malaysia International Halal Showcase has developed into a major platform for international halal trade, bringing together exporters, buyers, investors and industry players.
Hosted by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) and organised by the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), MIHAS now covers 14 sectors across the halal value chain.
These include food and beverages, pharmaceuticals, Islamic finance, modest fashion, personal care, technology, services and Muslim-friendly tourism.
MATRADE describes MIHAS as a major platform for facilitating the sourcing and selling of halal products and services globally, with the showcase attracting participants across sectors including pharmaceuticals, Islamic investment and banking.
Themed “Shaping Trust, Driving Resilience”, MIHAS 2026 is focused on strengthening trust and resilience across the global halal economy.
The showcase will place emphasis on regulated-by-design governance and technology-enabled trade, reflecting the growing importance of digital tools and stronger governance in facilitating international business.
The 22nd edition continues MIHAS’s role as a platform for Malaysian companies seeking to expand their international presence, while giving overseas buyers access to Malaysia’s established halal ecosystem.
With hundreds of international buyers and thousands of scheduled B2B meetings, the International Sourcing Programme remains central to MIHAS 2026’s role in connecting Malaysian exporters with new global trade opportunities.

title: SME Malaysia Welcomes Removal of 30% Bumiputera Equity Requirement for Private Education Operators
bodyText:
The SME Association of Malaysia has welcomed the Government’s decision to remove the requirement for private limited companies operating private educational institutions under the Ministry of Education to maintain at least 30% Bumiputera equity ownership.
The Education Ministry announced the decision on 21 September following discussions with the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI), stating that the adjustment was made to meet the current needs of the education sector and ensure participation remained open to all parties seeking to contribute to Malaysia’s educational development.
For the SME Association of Malaysia, the decision takes into account the practical realities faced by businesses, particularly SMEs and smaller education operators.
The association said mandatory equity requirements can create challenges for existing businesses, particularly tuition centres and private education operators that have been built by their founders over many years.
Many of these businesses are small enterprises established through their owners’ investment, experience, hard work and personal commitment.
According to the association, requiring existing business owners to restructure their company ownership simply to comply with an equity requirement could create unnecessary uncertainty and disruption. It could also discourage entrepreneurship and future investment in Malaysia’s private education sector.
The SME Association of Malaysia said increasing Bumiputera participation in business should focus on creating opportunities for entrepreneurs to establish and grow their own businesses.
Rather than relying primarily on mandatory equity requirements, the association called for practical support such as access to financing, training, mentoring, suitable premises and digitalisation assistance.
It said SME Malaysia supports policies that create opportunities for entrepreneurs from all communities while strengthening Bumiputera entrepreneurship through meaningful and sustainable programmes.
At the same time, the association urged the Government and policymakers to consider whether appropriate local participation requirements or other safeguards should apply to foreign investors entering certain sectors traditionally dominated by Malaysian SMEs, particularly retail and food and beverage.
The association stressed that it was not calling for Malaysia to restrict foreign investment.
Foreign investment remains important to the Malaysian economy, particularly where it brings capital, technology, expertise, employment and access to new markets. However, SME Malaysia said there should be a distinction between investments that introduce new capabilities to Malaysia and businesses entering sectors where thousands of local SMEs are already operating and competing.
For SME-dominated sectors, the association said some form of meaningful Malaysian participation, local partnership or another appropriate policy mechanism could be studied.
SME Malaysia said its concern centres on maintaining a level playing field for local businesses.
Malaysian SMEs are required to manage local wages, EPF and SOCSO contributions, taxation, licensing, rental, utilities and other regulatory and operating costs while facing increasing competitive pressure.
The association therefore said policymakers should ensure that foreign participation in SME-dominated sectors does not unintentionally create unfair competition or gradually displace local entrepreneurs.
“Malaysia needs foreign investment, but at the same time we must continue to develop and protect the ability of Malaysian entrepreneurs to participate meaningfully in our own domestic economy,” the association said.
It added that the objectives of attracting foreign investment and strengthening Malaysian entrepreneurship should complement rather than conflict with each other.
The association said Malaysia needs policies that encourage entrepreneurship, investment and business growth, particularly as SMEs continue to face rising operating costs, manpower challenges and a more competitive business environment.
Against this backdrop, it said policymakers should avoid introducing additional requirements that create uncertainty or make it more difficult for businesses to operate.
The Education Ministry has said the removal of the 30% Bumiputera equity condition is intended to align ownership requirements with the current needs of the education sector, while keeping participation open to all parties contributing to education.
SME Malaysia also highlighted the role of private education operators, including tuition centres, within Malaysia’s wider education ecosystem.
The association said education policy should ultimately focus on quality, accessibility, affordability and the interests of Malaysian children, with private education providers continuing to play an important complementary role.
It also expressed appreciation for political leaders across different parties who, in its view, had approached the matter responsibly and had not sought to politicise or racialise the issue.
According to the association, matters affecting education, entrepreneurship and the business community should be considered based on their practicality, impact and broader interests.
Looking ahead, SME Malaysia called for continued constructive discussion across political and community lines.
It said policies that strengthen SMEs, encourage entrepreneurship and improve Malaysia’s education ecosystem can benefit Malaysians across communities.
The association welcomed the Government’s decision to reconsider the practical implications of the equity requirement and remove it, while urging policymakers to consult affected industries and business associations before implementing future policies concerning business ownership, foreign participation and SMEs.
The association said such consultation would help ensure that policies support entrepreneurship, investment and business growth while taking into account the realities faced by Malaysian businesses.

title: Baker Tilly Appoints Capital Markets Veteran Lee Kuan Teck as Director of IPO Development
bodyText:
Baker Tilly has appointed Lee Kuan Teck as Director, IPO & Capital Markets Development, bringing more than 30 years of experience across financial services, investment banking, regulation and capital market development to the firm.
The appointment comes as Baker Tilly marks two decades of its Transaction Reporting practice, which it describes as the largest dedicated IPO reporting team of its kind in Malaysia. The move further strengthens the firm’s capabilities as it continues to support businesses preparing for public listings and the wider development of Malaysia’s capital markets.
Lee’s career includes almost a decade in investment banking and approximately 17 years at Bursa Malaysia, where he held several senior leadership positions covering listing regulation, IPO approvals and capital market development.
Before joining Baker Tilly, Lee served as Executive Vice President, Listing Development, Securities Market at Bursa Malaysia. In that role, he led the IPO marketing function and spearheaded strategies to attract quality listings to the Malaysian capital market.
He worked closely with regulators, intermediaries, advisers and corporates, contributing to efforts to promote Bursa Malaysia as a preferred listing destination while supporting the development of a vibrant and sustainable capital market ecosystem.
Earlier in his career at Bursa Malaysia Regulation, Lee served as Head of Restructuring, where he oversaw the regularisation of financially distressed listed companies, including PN17 companies.
He also supervised IPO applications from companies seeking admission to the ACE and LEAP Markets. This experience has given him insight into both the regulatory requirements and commercial realities companies face when pursuing a public listing.
In his new role at Baker Tilly, Lee will focus on capital markets development and thought leadership, while broadening the firm’s market engagement and profile across Malaysia’s capital markets.
His responsibilities will include supporting Baker Tilly’s IPO thought leadership initiatives and speaking at IPO seminars, roadshows and client events. He will share practical insights on IPO readiness, listing requirements, regulatory expectations and market trends.
Lee will also work alongside the firm’s Transaction Reporting and corporate advisory teams on client engagements. His responsibilities will include contributing market intelligence on listing developments and investor sentiment, providing strategic input on pre-IPO readiness and restructuring matters, and sharing his capital markets perspective with internal teams.
The appointment builds on Baker Tilly’s longstanding involvement in Malaysia’s IPO ecosystem.
The firm said its Transaction Reporting practice is led by two dedicated IPO reporting partners and a team of around 100 professionals, making it the largest IPO reporting team of its kind in Malaysia. The team has acted as Reporting Accountants on 39 IPOs since 2020.
Baker Tilly has also continued to invest in IPO education and market engagement. Its Roadmap to IPO initiative, launched a decade ago, has helped Malaysian businesses better understand the IPO process, listing requirements and the preparations needed to enter the public market.
Andrew Heng, Group Managing Partner of Baker Tilly (Malaysia), said the firm continues to invest in its people and capabilities as Malaysia’s capital markets evolve.
“As Malaysia’s capital markets continue to mature, businesses require advisers who combine deep technical expertise with practical market experience.”
He added that Lee’s experience across investment banking, market regulation and listing development would help Baker Tilly broaden its capital markets capabilities and support the continued development of Malaysia’s capital markets.
Dato’ Lock Peng Kuan, Managing Partner, Audit & Assurance of Baker Tilly (Malaysia), said the firm had spent the past two decades building its foundations in Malaysia’s capital markets.
He highlighted the firm’s IPO education roadshows and its dedicated Transaction Reporting team, noting that the quality and integrity of financial reporting remain central to investor confidence.
According to Dato’ Lock, Lee’s appointment represents a natural extension of the firm’s existing capabilities, combining Baker Tilly’s IPO reporting expertise with Lee’s experience in investment banking, regulation and capital market development.
Lee said his career had allowed him to view the capital markets from different perspectives, including as an investment banker, regulator and market developer.
He said he looked forward to working with Baker Tilly’s Transaction Reporting team and bringing a market development perspective to the firm’s work with businesses preparing for their IPO journey.
With Lee joining its capital markets team, Baker Tilly aims to deepen its engagement with businesses, strengthen its IPO thought leadership and contribute to the continued development of Malaysia’s capital market ecosystem.

title: Rolls-Royce Begins Global Testing of 100-Unit Project Nightingale
bodyText:
Rolls-Royce Motor Cars has begun its global testing programme for Project Nightingale, an exclusive Coachbuild Collection limited to just 100 client motor cars.
Announced in April 2026, Project Nightingale combines the design freedom of Rolls-Royce Coachbuild with an all-electric powertrain and an open-top driving experience. The project is designed as an expression of the marque’s current capabilities while offering a glimpse into its future direction.
Preparing the vehicles for clients who intend to drive them around the world has led Rolls-Royce to develop one of the most extensive testing programmes in its history.
Engineers will devote 350 collective weeks to testing Project Nightingale across a range of driving conditions, from Mediterranean coastal roads and the Arctic Circle to the deserts of the Arabian Peninsula.
The prototypes will also be tested at altitudes of up to 2,750 metres and in extreme temperatures, with the programme beginning in Southern Europe.
The decision to begin testing in Southern Europe carries particular significance for Rolls-Royce.
The region is where the marque established its approach to rigorous motor car development more than a century ago. In Southern France, Project Nightingale’s name also has a historical connection to Sir Henry Royce.
The name comes from Le Rossignol, French for “the nightingale”, which was the name of the house Royce built for his designers and engineers near his winter home on the French Riviera.
In the early 20th century, Rolls-Royce engineers used the area, alongside the marque’s test facility in Châteauroux, for speed and durability testing. They also conducted trials on roads between Monte Carlo and London.
More than 100 years later, Project Nightingale returns to these roads as it begins its own extensive development and validation programme.
The on-road programme is the latest stage of a development process that began almost three years ago.
Static prototypes have already completed more than 1,430 hours of aerodynamic modelling, including advanced digital simulations and wind tunnel testing.
The results will now be validated at a private high-speed testing facility, where Project Nightingale will reach speeds of up to 155 mph, or approximately 249 km/h.
Engineers will also analyse the vehicle’s aerodynamic performance and work to reduce wind noise to barely perceptible levels, maintaining the combination of refinement, serenity and performance expected of a Rolls-Royce.
Project Nightingale features several engineering solutions developed specifically for its open-top configuration.
Among them is a fully electric wind deflector developed and patented by Rolls-Royce specifically for the motor car. The system is designed to prevent high-pressure air from circulating back into the cabin from behind.
During testing, the wind deflector will be assessed at different speeds to minimise interior turbulence while helping retain warmth when the vehicle is driven with its roof lowered in colder climates.
The roof itself will also undergo extensive testing. Lined with a sound-deadening material combining cashmere, fabric and high-performance composites, it will undergo 10 separate tests covering its fabric, closing mechanism and overall performance.
Testing will take place in temperatures of up to 80°C, reflecting the expectation that Project Nightingale’s commissioning clients may drive their vehicles throughout the year and across different parts of the world.
One of Project Nightingale’s most distinctive engineering details is the Piano Boot, a feature that has never previously appeared on a Rolls-Royce.
The boot opens sideways using a cantilever mechanism and will be subjected to up to 15,000 opening and closing cycles.
The testing is intended to ensure that repeated use does not compromise the smoothness, precision or effortless operation of the feature, preserving the experience for generations of use.
For Rolls-Royce Chief Executive Chris Brownridge, Project Nightingale reflects the same spirit of experimentation that influenced Sir Henry Royce’s development of experimental “EX” motor cars in the 1920s.
“Project Nightingale captures the same audacious spirit that drove Sir Henry Royce to build his experimental ‘EX’ motor cars in the 1920s: a desire to discover what Rolls-Royce is truly capable of, unconstrained by convention,” he said.
Brownridge said the testing programme would take the prototypes through the environments in which clients may eventually drive them, while refining the vehicle to an extraordinary degree.
“Nothing less would be worthy of the brand, or this truly exceptional motor car,” he said.
Project Nightingale brings together Rolls-Royce’s Coachbuild tradition with an all-electric powertrain and open-top design, making its development a significant exercise in combining bespoke luxury with new technology.
Limited to just 100 client motor cars, the collection is being subjected to extensive real-world testing before reaching its final form.
From aerodynamic simulations and high-speed testing to extreme temperatures, open-top airflow and thousands of boot cycles, the programme is designed to ensure that every element of Project Nightingale meets Rolls-Royce’s exacting standards.
The global testing programme will now continue across the climates and environments in which its future clients intend to experience the car.

title: Lion Parcel Opens First International Office in Malaysia to Expand Cross-Border Logistics
bodyText:
Indonesia-based logistics service provider Lion Parcel has officially opened its first international office in Subang Jaya, Malaysia, marking the company’s first step into an international market and strengthening logistics connectivity between Malaysia, Indonesia and other international destinations.
Malaysia was selected as Lion Parcel’s first overseas market due to its strategic position as a regional logistics hub. Through its Malaysian operations, the company aims to create more opportunities for businesses and communities to meet their cross-border delivery needs while connecting Malaysia with Indonesia and other international markets.
The move also positions Malaysia as part of Lion Parcel’s broader international expansion strategy, with the company looking to use the country as a base for wider regional connectivity.
Lion Parcel Chief Executive Officer Farian Kirana said Malaysia represents an important first step in the company’s international journey, particularly because of the connectivity available through the wider Lion Group ecosystem.
“Malaysia is an important first step in Lion Parcel’s international journey. We see significant opportunities to optimise the Lion Group ecosystem, particularly Batik Air Malaysia’s air connectivity,” he said.
According to Farian, Batik Air Malaysia’s international network gives Lion Parcel’s business partners access to a wider range of destinations, while the cargo infrastructure supported by Batik Air Malaysia’s Cargo Terminal Operator (CTO) provides additional operational capabilities.
The integration of air connectivity and cargo infrastructure is intended to support more efficient delivery processes and help packages move between markets faster and more securely.
Farian added that Lion Parcel aims to serve not only as a logistics provider, but also as an enabler within the wider business ecosystem by helping companies access markets and growth opportunities.
Alvin Williams, Country Head of Lion Parcel Malaysia, said the company sees Malaysia as both an important market and a strategic location within the region’s evolving logistics landscape.
“Malaysia has an important role to play in the development of regional logistics connectivity, particularly with Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) continuing to develop its position as a regional air cargo and transshipment hub,” he said.
For Lion Parcel, Malaysia’s air cargo infrastructure creates opportunities to connect delivery services with wider regional networks and support the movement of goods between Malaysia, Indonesia and other international markets.
Lion Parcel Malaysia currently provides delivery services for both business-to-business (B2B) and retail customers, including international shipments to destinations served through the Lion Group’s flight network.
Lion Parcel’s Malaysian operations are supported by Batik Air Malaysia’s air connectivity, which currently serves more than 60 destinations across 20 countries, covering markets across Southeast Asia, China, India, Australia and other regional destinations.
The logistics provider plans to leverage this network as part of its operational development while expanding delivery connectivity between Malaysia, Indonesia and international markets.
Lion Parcel is also supported by a Cargo Terminal Operator operated by Batik Air Malaysia at KLIA Cargo Village in Selangor.
The integrated cargo infrastructure serves as an important part of Lion Parcel’s Malaysian operations, helping support air freight, transshipment and international delivery processes.
By connecting its delivery services with the existing air cargo network, Lion Parcel aims to improve the efficiency and connectivity of cross-border logistics.
The company’s Malaysian expansion comes as businesses increasingly require logistics networks that can support cross-border trade and access to regional markets.
Lion Parcel said its Malaysian presence will help businesses and communities move goods more efficiently across markets and reach wider opportunities.
The company is also looking to leverage partnerships and existing infrastructure as it develops its Malaysian operations, rather than building an entirely separate logistics ecosystem. Recent reporting indicates that Lion Parcel intends to work with local partners across areas including first-mile, last-mile delivery and customs clearance while focusing its own capabilities on mid-mile services and air cargo capacity.
As its first international market, Malaysia marks the beginning of Lion Parcel’s broader international expansion journey.
The company said it will continue exploring opportunities to expand its connectivity and collaborate with partners across different markets, with Malaysia expected to play a role in connecting future regional operations.
With its first international office now established in Subang Jaya, Lion Parcel is positioning Malaysia as a key link between its Indonesian operations, the Lion Group’s international air network and businesses seeking cross-border logistics solutions.
The company’s Malaysian operations are available to both B2B and retail customers, with international shipments supported through destinations served by the Lion Group’s flight network.

title: SEAM Cohort 2 Backs Nine Malaysian Social Enterprises for Sustainable Growth
bodyText:
The Social Enterprise Accelerator Malaysia (SEAM) has announced nine Malaysian impact-driven enterprises selected for its second cohort, as social entrepreneurship continues to gain momentum across the country.
The 12-month programme, run by Biji-biji Initiative in partnership with IKEA Social Entrepreneurship and supported by IKEA Malaysia, aims to help social enterprises strengthen their business models, organisational capabilities and long-term sustainability while expanding their social and environmental impact.
The new cohort spans Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Penang, Kelantan and Sabah, with participating organisations working across inclusive employment, the circular economy, sustainable food and agriculture, and aquaculture and marine livelihoods.
Collectively, the nine enterprises create economic opportunities for communities including B40 youth, single mothers, women from the Asnaf community, persons with disabilities (PwD), refugees, marginalised artisans and coastal fishing families.
SEAM is designed to help impact-driven organisations scale sustainably through tailored capacity building, mentorship, strategic support, funding and access to wider networks.
Cohort 2 builds on the progress recorded by SEAM’s inaugural cohort of 10 social enterprises.
The first cohort received tailored business development and mentoring, alongside access to funding, networks and market opportunities. The programme was established to help Malaysian social enterprises address social and environmental challenges while strengthening their ability to grow.
Among the reported achievements from the first cohort, seven of 10 participating enterprises recorded top-line revenue growth, while nine reported improved financial stability and cost discipline. Eight also expanded their active reach among the communities they serve.
Individual enterprises recorded further commercial and operational gains. Earth Heir added RM429,293 in B2B orders for Earth Heir Collective, Batik Boutique doubled its weekly fabric output, while Upcycled more than doubled its baseline income and generated more than RM101,200 in direct community wages.
For SEAM Programme Director and Biji-biji Initiative Chief Executive Officer Juliana Adam, the first cohort demonstrated that social enterprises can take different routes towards growth.
“Cohort 1 reinforced that there is no single pathway to scale. For one enterprise, growth may mean entering a new market; for another, it could mean strengthening production, building a team or becoming ready for corporate procurement,” she said.
She added that the challenge is to bridge proven community impact with the capabilities required to grow sustainably, from winning customers and building partnerships to strengthening internal systems without losing sight of the communities and purpose behind each enterprise.
The nine organisations selected for SEAM Cohort 2 represent a range of approaches to social entrepreneurship in Malaysia.
Brutti is a sustainable furniture social enterprise based in Kota Kinabalu that creates dignified livelihoods for B40 youth communities in Sabah. Using reclaimed pallet wood, it produces bespoke furniture for homeowners and B2B clients while diverting more than 57 tonnes of waste and preserving an estimated 600 trees.
Dodo Vegan Hut is a halal-certified plant-based food enterprise providing sustainable food products alongside employment opportunities for B40 communities. Its portfolio includes frozen vegan meals and SAKRAE coconut ice cream, with products reaching hotels, restaurants and cafés across Malaysia.
Enable OKU Solutions (ENOKU) focuses on employment opportunities and workplace inclusion for persons with disabilities. Through diversity, equity and inclusion training, tailored employment placement and long-term inclusion frameworks, ENOKU works with multinational corporations to create more inclusive workplaces.
Green Shoots transforms corporate spending on gifts and packaging into social and environmental impact through circular product design and responsible production. The enterprise creates income opportunities for underserved women while reducing waste and reinvesting revenue into therapy support and wellbeing initiatives.
Heartworks Solution provides flexible employment opportunities for persons with disabilities, single mothers, caregivers and women who face barriers to traditional employment. Its virtual assistant model combines paid work with training, guidance and ongoing support, with a growing community of 30 virtual assistants serving corporate clients including Naluri, SEEK Asia and Malaysia Food & Travel.
Ibupreneur supports Asnaf women and single mothers from B40 communities through its Maker Hub marketplace and Academy. The enterprise reports that 659 mothers across 11 states have increased their incomes by an average of 86% within 12 months, with corporate clients including Mandarin Oriental and Banyan Tree.
Koperasi Penternak Akuakultur (KoAKUA) supports coastal fishing communities in Kelantan by pooling resources and strengthening distribution for its 50 members. By reducing dependence on intermediaries, the cooperative aims to improve returns for traditional fishermen and farmers while developing additional products, including salted duck eggs and smoked duck, to create income beyond the fishing season.
PichaEats creates livelihood opportunities for refugee communities in Malaysia by supporting Syrian, Afghan, Myanmar and Palestinian individuals as chefs, caterers and culinary apprentices. Its services include catering, meal box deliveries, cultural dining experiences and skills development, connecting the culinary heritage of displaced communities with customers.
Sagemaker Asia is a community-powered production enterprise connecting marginalised artisans with skills development, employment and commercial opportunities. Through its Rumah Sage production house in Ampang, more than 70 Sagemakers produce sensory materials, upcycled products and bespoke corporate merchandise for clients including PETRONAS and Pos Malaysia.
Rather than applying a standardised curriculum, SEAM takes a tailored approach based on each organisation’s growth priorities, challenges and operating context.
Participants are paired with IKEA senior leaders and co-workers who serve as Thought Partners, while also gaining access to industry mentors, experts, strategic advisory support and wider ecosystem connections.
The approach is designed to give each enterprise space to test assumptions, strengthen internal systems and refine the decisions needed for its next stage of growth.
Participants will also have access to a programme funding pool of up to RM750,000, with financial support linked to the business growth roadmaps developed and refined throughout the programme.
Åsa Skogström Feldt, Managing Director of IKEA Social Entrepreneurship, said scaling a social enterprise should not simply mean becoming bigger, but becoming stronger through better capabilities, partnerships and business foundations.
“What makes SEAM important is that the journey is shaped around the realities of each enterprise. By bringing together social entrepreneurs, IKEA co-workers as Thought Partners, specialist mentors and funding, we can create the space for entrepreneurs to test decisions, learn and build a more resilient pathway for their business and their impact,” she said.
The nine enterprises will begin the programme with a Strategy & Scoping phase, working with their Thought Partners and the Biji-biji Initiative team to refine their growth priorities and develop a Growth Experimentation Plan (GEP).
From January to August 2027, the programme will move into its Experimentation & Learning phase. Participants will put their strategies into practice through continued Thought Partner engagement, mentorship, field visits and learning opportunities, allowing them to test and adapt their approaches based on real-world results.
The programme will conclude with a Closing Summit and final reports documenting the outcomes, pivots and lessons generated throughout the year.
SEAM Cohort 2 comes as Malaysia continues to build a stronger ecosystem for social enterprises and impact-driven businesses. The programme itself is part of a wider effort to address gaps in funding, capacity building and collaboration that can limit the ability of social enterprises to scale.
Biji-biji Initiative has described SEAM as an accelerator designed to strengthen organisations addressing social and environmental challenges while supporting sustainable growth and community impact.
For the new cohort, the longer-term ambition is to build stronger, more resilient social enterprises that can continue supporting marginalised communities across Malaysia.
By strengthening business capacity and creating pathways for sustainable growth, SEAM aims to help these enterprises deepen their impact while developing a more resilient Malaysian social entrepreneurship ecosystem.

title: Malaysia’s Exports to 40 Countries Surpass 2025 Records as Market Diversification Gains Momentum
bodyText:
Malaysia’s exports continued to record strong growth in the first eight months of 2026, rising 31.2% to RM1.356 trillion from RM1.033 trillion in the same period last year.
According to the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), exports to 40 countries, including the United States, France and Ireland, had already surpassed their full-year export values recorded in 2025. The performance highlights the increasingly broad-based nature of Malaysia’s export growth across both established and emerging markets.
The expansion comes as Malaysia continues to diversify its export markets and products amid an increasingly uncertain global trading environment. MATRADE has highlighted market diversification as part of efforts to strengthen Malaysia’s export resilience and expand access to new sources of demand.
Emerging markets recorded significant export growth during the period, contributing to Malaysia’s wider market diversification efforts.
Exports to Namibia surged 430.6%, while shipments to Angola increased 215.4%. Exports to Ethiopia, Tanzania and Bangladesh also rose by 51.2%, 50.2% and 20.2%, respectively.
The strong performance in these markets points to growing opportunities beyond Malaysia’s traditional export destinations, with non-traditional markets playing an increasingly important role in broadening the country’s export base.
Among BRICS member countries, Malaysia’s exports expanded 19.1% to RM251.47 billion. Double-digit growth was recorded across several major markets, including China, India, Brazil and South Africa.
Exports to China increased 23.7%, while those to India rose 23.4%. Exports to Brazil grew 27.5% and South Africa recorded a 43.4% increase.
Notably, Malaysia’s exports to Ethiopia had already surpassed the full-year export value recorded in 2025, further highlighting the potential of non-traditional markets.
Malaysia’s export expansion is also becoming more diversified across industries and products.
While electrical and electronic (E&E) products remain an important contributor to Malaysia’s export performance, other manufactured goods also recorded significant growth. Exports of optical and scientific equipment increased 37.6%, followed by petroleum products at 26.6%, manufactures of metal at 21.6%, machinery, appliances and parts at 18.4%, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) at 17.2%.
The broader performance complements Malaysia’s strong E&E export growth. MATRADE reported that E&E exports reached RM656.14 billion between January and August 2026, putting the sector on track to surpass its full-year export value recorded in 2025.
Palm oil-based manufactured products also recorded strong growth, driven particularly by oleochemicals, which increased 12.6%.
Malaysian SMEs contributed significantly to the expansion of this export segment, highlighting the role of local businesses in strengthening Malaysia’s value-added and downstream exports.
The growth of palm oil-based manufactured products demonstrates how Malaysian SMEs can contribute to expanding the country’s export base beyond major sectors such as E&E.
By moving further into value-added and downstream activities, businesses can develop more diversified products for international markets while strengthening Malaysia’s position across global supply chains.
MATRADE Chief Executive Officer Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof said the latest export performance showed that the strategic shift towards market and product diversification in recent years was beginning to deliver results despite uncertainties in global supply chains.
“Our historic export numbers demonstrate that the strategic shift to market and product diversification over the past recent years has started to bear fruits amid the uncertainties in the global supply chain that have opened up demand opportunities for Malaysia’s exports,” he said.
He added that the changing global landscape also highlighted the agility and resilience of Malaysian exporters, including micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), in responding to global uncertainties.
MATRADE will continue to strengthen market access through integrated and customised capacity-building programmes, while expanding its whole-of-government approach and strategic partnerships with private-sector stakeholders.
“MATRADE continues to deepen market access initiatives through exporters’ integrated and customised capacity-building programmes by enhancing the whole-of-government approach and strategic partnership with the private stakeholders,” said Dato’ Indera.
The agency will also continue intensifying export promotion activities both locally and internationally to showcase the capabilities of Malaysian companies.
One of its upcoming programmes is the Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS), which will take place from 23 to 26 September 2026 at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC) in Kuala Lumpur.
The event is expected to bring together 1,700 local and international exhibitors, 300 international buyers and 27 international media outlets, providing another platform for Malaysian companies to strengthen international market access and develop new export opportunities.
With export growth increasingly spread across markets, industries and products, Malaysia’s latest performance points to a continued emphasis on diversification as businesses seek new opportunities in the global economy.

title: Managing Gen Z: The Real Question Is Not “How Do We Manage Them?”But “Why Should They Care?”
bodyText:
by Marcus Tioh | Sales Trainer | Coach | HRD Corp Accredited Trainer

I recently had the opportunity to speak to entrepreneurs and business leaders about managing Gen Z sales teams. One question kept coming back in different forms: “Why are Gen Z employees so difficult to manage?” They are sometimes described as fragile, difficult to retain, too dependent on recognition, unwilling to work overtime, or too quick to question instructions. My perspective is slightly different.
“Perhaps Gen Z is not necessarily more difficult to manage. Perhaps we are still trying to manage them using the same methods we were managed with.”
Every generation enters the workplace with different experiences, expectations and references. Gen Z has grown up in an environment shaped by smartphones, instant information, social media, AI, online learning and global exposure. In my view, that does not automatically make them better or worse employees. It means managers need to understand what may influence how they approach work. One of the key messages is simple: different environment, different expectations. Not wrong. Just different.
One of the biggest things I emphasise when talking about Gen Z is purpose. Managers often tell employees what they need to do. But Gen Z employees may ask: “Why do I need to do this?” I do not think managers should automatically interpret that question as attitude or disrespect. Instead, we should ask whether we have explained the purpose behind the task. If an employee understands why something matters, and that purpose connects with something they personally believe in, the level of commitment can be very different.
I experienced this myself when I founded Jobworks. Our purpose was to create job opportunities for part-time workers without discriminating based on race, gender, age, including retirees, or circumstances such as pregnancy. That purpose resonated strongly with our team. They were not simply working to complete another company KPI. They believed in what we were trying to achieve.
I remember one particular situation very clearly. A client had delayed payment to us because of documentation issues. However, we had made a promise to our part-time workers that they would receive their payment within seven days. The team could have simply told the workers, “Sorry, the client has not paid us yet.” Instead, some of my team members took money from their own salaries, which they had already received, and used it to pay our part-time workers first.
That was not something I instructed them to do. It happened because they believed in the purpose of the organisation. “When people believe in what they are working towards, commitment can go far beyond the job description.” That experience taught me that purpose is not just a nice statement on a company website. When people genuinely connect with it, it can influence how they behave when nobody is telling them what to do.
I am also careful not to say that every Gen Z employee needs purpose and will suddenly become highly motivated. That would simply create another stereotype. There will always be employees who are not motivated, regardless of how good the manager, company or purpose is.
Managers still need to manage performance. If someone is willing to learn, improve and contribute, the manager has a responsibility to coach and develop that person. But if someone consistently shows no willingness to change or contribute, sometimes the right decision is to let that person go.
“The goal is not to keep everyone. The goal is to build a team where the individual and organisational expectations are aligned.”
This is why I believe the interview process is extremely important. Before hiring someone, managers should understand what the candidate wants from their career and whether the company can realistically help them move towards those goals.
One of the biggest mistakes I see managers make is comparing today’s employees with how they themselves were managed. I often hear: “Last time my manager also trained me like this.”
“Yes. But you are not managing yourself 20 years ago. You are managing someone today.”
Managers need to recognise that the workplace has changed. That does not mean standards should disappear. Sales targets still matter. KPIs still matter. Accountability still matters. But the way we get people to achieve those outcomes may need to change. Instead of only asking, “Why did you not hit your target?”, perhaps ask, “What obstacles are stopping you?” Instead of saying, “You should know,” try, “Let’s figure it out.” Instead of saying, “Do what I say,” ask, “What do you think?”
I call this the Conversation Shift. It moves the manager from simply giving instructions towards creating a conversation that helps the employee think, solve problems and take ownership.
My approach is captured in my M.A.R.C.U.S. Leadership Framework:
M Mentor, not Micromanage
A Appreciate Small Wins
R Respect Their Voice
C Coach Through Questions
U Understand Their Purpose
S Stretch Their Potential
These principles are not exclusively for Gen Z. They are good leadership practices generally. However, they become particularly relevant when managers are leading employees who expect more dialogue, feedback and involvement in their work.
Another thing managers need to reconsider is the fear of allowing younger employees to make mistakes. Of course, there are mistakes that can seriously damage a business. But if every small mistake is immediately punished, corrected or micromanaged, how will young employees learn to make decisions?
“Allow them to make mistakes, so long as it does not cost the company a limb.”

A mistake can become a very expensive lesson. Or it can become a very valuable learning experience. The manager’s role is to create boundaries around the risk, allow the employee to learn, and then coach them through what happened. That is very different from simply saying, “I told you so.”
There is another issue that sometimes enters the workplace which managers may not be prepared for: parental involvement in their children’s careers. I once coached a junior sales professional whom I personally considered very promising. She was not leaving because she was lazy or unmotivated. She was leaving because her parents were extremely protective and did not want her working overtime or on weekends.
That experience reminded me that younger employees can sometimes be influenced by the expectations and protection of the environment around them. Parents can provide guidance, but young adults also need space to make their own career decisions, experience challenges and learn from consequences.
For me, one of the most important lessons for SME owners is this: do not wait until the employee joins your company to discover whether you are aligned. It should start during the interview. Most interviews focus heavily on whether the candidate can do the job, whether they have the experience, their strengths and their salary expectations. Those questions are important.
But I would also ask:
• What do you want to achieve in your career?
• What is important to you at this stage of your life?
• What motivates you?
• What kind of environment allows you to perform at your best?
Then the company needs to ask itself: “Can we actually provide that?”
If the answer is no, we should not be surprised when that employee eventually leaves.
Money and job titles still matter. But for many younger employees, they are not necessarily the only factors influencing whether they stay and perform. Purpose, growth, learning, recognition, trust, autonomy and the relationship with their manager can also shape their experience at work.
My answer is: sometimes yes. But so is every generation. Every generation has employees who are difficult. Every generation has high performers. Every generation has people who need coaching. And every generation has people who simply are not the right fit for a particular organisation. The mistake is turning an entire generation into a management problem.
Instead, managers should ask themselves:
• Have I clearly explained the purpose?
• Does their purpose align with our organisation?
• Have I given them enough opportunity to learn?
• Am I coaching them or simply controlling them?
• Am I trying to make them work the way I used to work, or am I learning how to lead the person in front of me?
“Every generation changes the workplace. Great leaders change themselves first. Lead the person. Not the generation.”

1. Introduce short, regular micro-feedback conversations rather than waiting for formal reviews.
2. Ask more questions before giving answers. Help employees develop their own problem-solving ability.
3. Explain the “why” behind routine tasks so employees can connect their work with the bigger purpose.
About the Author: Marcus Tioh, also known as Uncle Marcus, is a Sales Trainer, Coach and HRD Corp Accredited Trainer with experience across sales, hospitality, human resources, business development and leadership. He is the founder of Marcus Skills Builder and has worked with organisations across multiple industries on sales, leadership, communication and people development.

title: How Print Innovation Is Opening New Opportunities for Malaysia’s Creative Entrepreneurs
bodyText:
By Sandy Lee, Head of Personal System Devices Division at Canon Marketing Malaysia
Creativity has evolved beyond a form of expression and identity to become an economic opportunity for many Malaysians. From design, arts and crafts to personalised creations and merchandise, a new generation of creators is finding ways to turn their skills and ideas into commercial ventures.
