The growing economic significance of the sector is reflected in Malaysia’s cultural and creative industry, which contributed 6.8% to the nation’s GDP in 2024, generating RM130.7 billion in gross value added and recording 7.1% growth from the previous year, according to the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM).
Within the industry’s core domain, books and press accounted for 9.5% while visual arts and crafts contributed 6.6% of gross value added, highlighting the economic value generated by creative activities.
As more Malaysians explore creative entrepreneurship, accessible tools and production solutions could play an increasingly important role in helping them bring their ideas to market.
For emerging creators looking to commercialise original designs, personalised gifts, merchandise or craft products, turning an idea into a finished product is not always straightforward.
Customisation gives creators greater freedom to experiment and develop distinctive offerings, but production can present practical challenges. Outsourcing, for example, may be less suitable for small businesses that need limited quantities to test new ideas, experiment with designs or fulfil customised orders.
Managing production costs and turnaround times while maintaining quality, consistency and creative freedom can therefore become a barrier to growth.
For small-scale creative businesses, the ability to produce efficiently at a scale that matches demand can provide greater flexibility. It also allows entrepreneurs to respond more quickly to changing customer requirements while continuing to experiment with new products and designs.
Print and Cut solutions offer one way of addressing these challenges by making small-scale production more accessible, flexible and commercially viable.
The process allows creators to develop their own designs, print them according to their intended application and cut them into the desired shapes. This creates greater opportunities for customisation without requiring large production runs.
Recognising this potential, Canon Malaysia has partnered with Siser Asia to combine their respective expertise in printing and cutting technology.
The partnership brings together Canon’s GX business printer, which features a full pigment ink system designed to produce vibrant, water-resistant prints, with the Siser Juliet Cutter’s high-definition cutting capabilities.
Together, the technologies are designed to provide durability, accuracy and consistency across small-scale projects, giving creative entrepreneurs greater control over the production process.
The applications of Print and Cut technology extend across a range of creative businesses and projects.
Entrepreneurs can use the solution for personalised merchandise, customised stickers and labels, apparel, craft projects and other small-batch creations. The flexibility of producing in smaller quantities also gives creators more room to test concepts and develop distinctive product offerings.
For businesses built around personalisation, this can help reduce the constraints associated with traditional production methods while allowing entrepreneurs to respond to individual customer requirements.
More importantly, greater control over printing and cutting can give creators the freedom to experiment with different designs and product ideas before committing to larger production volumes.
As Malaysia continues to strengthen its cultural and creative economy, the growth of creative entrepreneurship presents an opportunity to broaden participation in the sector and develop a stronger pipeline of homegrown creative businesses.
DOSM’s latest data shows that the cultural and creative industry employed 763,100 people in 2024, accounting for 4.7% of Malaysia’s total employment.
Sustaining this momentum will require an ecosystem that encourages innovation, capability building and collaboration as new commercial opportunities emerge.
For Canon Malaysia, supporting this development reflects its corporate philosophy of “Kyosei”, which centres on living and working together for the common good and highlights the role businesses can play in supporting the communities and industries they serve.
Through continued print innovation and industry partnerships, Canon Malaysia aims to empower more creative entrepreneurs to pursue their passions and turn creativity into commercial opportunities, contributing to the continued growth of Malaysia’s creative sector.

title: From a Toddler’s Question to an Ipoh Custard Business with Bigger Dreams
bodyText:
By Natasha Isabel Saravanan
Uncle Law remembers the beginning almost casually. He had never known how to make custard, nor did he have a background in baking. Then, one day, his toddler asked him a simple question: why not try making custard? With some ideas and ingredients to work with, he decided to give it a go.
The first attempts were unsuccessful. Yet instead of abandoning the idea, he kept trying until he finally got the recipe right. His family tasted it and encouraged him to make it for others. That small experiment eventually became the foundation of Uncle Law Caramel Custard.
When the business began in 2022, however, there was little indication that it would become what it is today. Uncle Law started by operating from his son’s stall at the Perak Stadium Hawkers Centre. “It was not easy. When I first started operating the business at my son’s stall, I could hardly sell more than two pieces a day,” he said.
The turning point came through customers themselves. Those who tried the custard began recommending it to others, gradually creating demand beyond the stall. Eventually, Uncle Law was given a place in a coffee shop, giving him the opportunity to develop the business further.
For him, those early days reinforced one lesson: patience matters. “Initially, it was really tough. If you do not have patience, you will give up,” he reflected. That patience remains central to the way he approaches the business today. Rather than expecting immediate success, Uncle Law watched demand grow piece by piece, allowing the product to establish itself through the response of the people who tasted it.

One of the most important elements of Uncle Law’s custard is also one of the easiest to underestimate. The caramel may appear to be a simple layer at the bottom of a cup, but perfecting it took considerable effort, precision and even physical pain.
Uncle Law recalled being badly burned while learning how to handle the caramel. The injury was serious enough for him to require bandaging for more than a month. At the time, he had underestimated how dangerous the hot caramel could be. “The most difficult part was the caramel initially. I got hurt and burned. I even had to be bandaged for more than a month because of it,” he recalled.
The experience taught him that caramel could not simply be left to chance. It had to reach the right temperature and be prepared at precisely the right moment. Boil it for too long and the flavour changes; stop too early and it does not develop the character he wants. “It has to be timed at the boiling point. Not one minute more, not one minute less. Then the caramel comes out strongly, with that little bitterness that people enjoy,” he described.
The custard itself requires the same attention. Eggs and milk have to be mixed carefully, as excessive stirring can make the mixture too watery. Once filtered and poured into cups, it is steamed until it reaches the desired texture. To someone eating the finished product, these details may be invisible. To Uncle Law, they are what separate a satisfactory custard from the one he wants to serve.
“It looks simple, but when it comes to making it, it is not that simple,” he observed.
His son, Gary, has experienced that difficulty himself. Despite being the second generation and having watched his father make the custard, he has failed numerous times when attempting the process. “When the timing is wrong, it is either burnt or undercooked, and I have to start all over again,” Gary mused with a laugh.
For the father and son, the demanding process is part of the product’s identity. The recipe is not something to be rushed simply to increase output. Its consistency depends on maintaining the same care that went into the original method.

For Uncle Law, authenticity begins with refusing to compromise the foundation of the custard. The ingredients and preparation methods are deliberately kept simple, relying on fresh eggs, milk and sugar rather than powders or shortcuts. That commitment is closely tied to the flavour he associates with traditional custard. Even when experimenting with variations, he believes the original custard must remain untouched.
“I have tried adding things such as green tea, but it does not come out the same. If you want to add something, it should be an extra. The original base has to remain authentic first,” he explained.
Gary acknowledges that there is room for the business to explore new flavours, but he believes experimentation needs to serve a purpose. A new flavour cannot exist simply because it is fashionable. It has to complement the custard and meet what customers actually want. “There are thoughts to expand the varieties, but it has to be a perfect match. It is not enough to put in matcha or chocolate and expect it to work,” he acknowledged.
For now, the nostalgic character of the original product remains important. That nostalgia can be seen most clearly in customers’ reactions. Uncle Law remembers a young boy who returns almost every week after school to eat his custard. Older customers, too, often return after their first taste. For him, those repeat visits mean more than simply making another sale.
“We want to make something that people really enjoy, not just sell for the sake of selling a product. To sell something that is genuinely satisfying to them is the most important thing,” he emphasised.
Gary has noticed the same reactions. Some customers barely speak after their first bite. Instead, they simply nod before beginning to describe what they like about it.
“For those who are genuinely enjoying it, they put it in their mouths and just nod. Then they start describing it. That is when you know the preference is already there,” he said. That response is particularly meaningful for a product rooted in memory. A familiar taste can connect customers not only to the food itself, but also to the experiences and places associated with it.

One of Uncle Law Caramel Custard’s biggest milestones came during Chinese New Year in 2024, when people returning to Ipoh from Kuala Lumpur began placing larger orders. Uncle Law vividly remembers one customer asking for a box of 50 custards. He had never sold that many at once and initially needed two days to fulfil the order. The customer was willing to wait.
“I had never tried selling 50 in one go, but suddenly somebody gave me an order for 50. Those days really encouraged me because it showed that the product was doing well, even with people from out of state,” he reminisced with a fond smile.
The business has since begun looking beyond its home city. Gary is now focused on expanding distribution, with Ipoh remaining the central kitchen while the business reaches customers in the north and south of Malaysia. The Kuala Lumpur market is one of the areas being developed, with the family exploring partnerships with resellers and distributors who can bring the custard into kopitiams and cafés.
The longer-term ambition is even bigger. Customers who have travelled overseas have asked whether Uncle Law Caramel Custard can be exported to places such as Europe and London. Gary sees the demand as encouraging, but he also understands that getting a fresh custard product across borders presents practical and technical challenges.
“We have people coming back from overseas asking whether we can export our caramel custards to Europe or London. We have to think about the science of the product and how we can export it,” he said.
For now, expansion remains a gradual process. Rather than rushing towards a national or international presence, Gary believes each stage has to be properly established before moving to the next.
“You cannot skip one step and leap to another. Even if you try to take shortcuts, you may eventually find yourself back at square one,” he cautioned.

The division between father and son has become an important part of Uncle Law Caramel Custard’s growth. Uncle Law remains closely involved in production, personally making the custard and protecting the standards that shaped the product from the beginning. Gary, meanwhile, focuses on the business side, including expansion and scaling.
It is a partnership that reflects two different approaches to the same business. Uncle Law remains firmly rooted in the old-school method, while Gary looks at how that heritage can be carried into new markets.
When asked where the business would be in five years, Uncle Law jokingly turned to his son. “That is his problem, not my problem,” he said with a laugh. Behind the joke is a clear understanding of their respective roles. Gary may be thinking about distribution, technology and overseas possibilities, but the foundation remains his father’s craft.
For both of them, however, the lessons of the business are remarkably simple. Uncle Law believes entrepreneurs need to focus on what they are doing, believe in their product and accept failure as part of learning.
“Everyone fails. If you do not fail, you will not succeed. Failure teaches you, and then you try to improve ,” he opined.

For Gary, perseverance means taking each challenge as it comes, without shortcuts. It is a philosophy that has guided the family as the business continues to grow. Uncle Law, who started making custard in his sixties, has a simple message for anyone thinking of starting something new: “Age is not a problem.”
From one or two cups a day to orders of dozens at a time, the journey of Uncle Law Caramel Custard remains a reminder that growth does not always happen in leaps. Sometimes, it happens one scoop, one customer and one step at a time.

title: CGC100 Concludes with 100 Graduates, 58 Businesses and 86 New Jobs
bodyText:
Credit Guarantee Corporation Malaysia Berhad (CGC) has concluded its CGC100 Youth Entrepreneurship Programme with 100 young Malaysians graduating from the initiative and 58 graduates registering businesses that have collectively created 86 new jobs.
The milestone was marked at CGC’s headquarters as the corporation celebrated the 30 graduates of CGC100’s third and final cohort.
Launched in 2022 in collaboration with PINTAR Foundation and with support from the Ministry of Education, CGC100 was designed for young Malaysians aged 18 to 23 from unserved and underserved communities, particularly those from Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) backgrounds.
The programme combined structured entrepreneurship training, mentoring, financial literacy education and hands-on business experience to help participants develop the knowledge and confidence needed to start and grow businesses.
The final cohort, conducted between August 2025 and February 2026, brought together 30 participants from across Malaysia.
Over six months, participants were exposed to business fundamentals, branding, digital skills, financial literacy and sustainability. They also had the opportunity to develop and pitch their own business ideas.
Graduates have since established businesses across sectors including agriculture, food and beverage, fashion and services.
According to PINTAR Foundation’s post-programme impact assessment, 58 per cent of graduates generated income from their businesses after completing the programme.
The assessment also found that an increasing number of graduates have moved into the RM10,000 to RM50,000 monthly revenue bracket, pointing to progress in business resilience, growth potential and commercial sustainability.
A key objective of CGC100 was to equip aspiring entrepreneurs not only with business knowledge, but also with the financial literacy and financing readiness required to navigate the business landscape.
CGC Chairman Dato’ Mohammed Hussein encouraged the graduates to view setbacks as part of the entrepreneurial journey and to be willing to take calculated risks.
“One of the greatest advantages of being young is that you can afford to fail. No successful entrepreneur reaches the top without experiencing setbacks along the way,” he said.
He added that young entrepreneurs should be prepared to take calculated risks, describing risk-taking as an important element of entrepreneurship.
For some participants, CGC100 marked the beginning of their first serious steps into entrepreneurship.
Kaliswaran A/L Seran, 23, from Pulau Pinang, joined the programme without an existing business but said he gained the knowledge, skills and confidence to pursue his entrepreneurial ambitions.
“I started the programme with only an interest in entrepreneurship. Today, I have not only gained valuable entrepreneurial knowledge and skills, but also the confidence, direction and mindset needed to pursue my business aspirations,” he said.
Nur’zuriatina binti Zamri, 23, from Pahang, said the programme helped participants build confidence while developing practical business skills.
“CGC100 is not just about building businesses. It serves as a catalyst for change by providing practical business knowledge and skills, building confidence, and giving entrepreneurs the courage to grow their businesses and pursue greater opportunities,” she said.
For Alexander Conrad Johnny, 19, from Sarawak, the programme also changed how he viewed entrepreneurship and the role of ideas in creating wider impact.
“Entrepreneurship is not merely about building a business, but about having the courage to view challenges from a different perspective,” he said.
With CGC100 now completed, CGC is continuing its youth entrepreneurship efforts through the CGC Youth Entrepreneurship Programme (CGC YEP), which will become its flagship youth entrepreneurship initiative.
While CGC100 primarily focused on young Malaysians from TVET backgrounds, CGC YEP is open to aspiring entrepreneurs aged 18 to 35 from all backgrounds.
The broader eligibility is intended to allow the programme to reach a larger and more diverse group of aspiring entrepreneurs.
CGC YEP will build on the foundation established by CGC100 by equipping participants with business knowledge, practical skills and financing readiness, while supporting them in developing sustainable businesses and creating employment opportunities.
CGC President and Chief Executive Officer Mohamed Nazri Omar said the corporation recognises that financing alone is not sufficient to help entrepreneurs succeed, highlighting the importance of capacity building, experiential learning and guidance.
The programme is also expected to expand its reach, with CGC looking at collaborations with corporates, government-linked companies and the private sector.
CGC100’s conclusion marks the end of one programme, but its impact will continue through the businesses established by its graduates and the employment opportunities they have created.
With 100 young Malaysians completing the programme, 58 registered businesses and 86 new jobs created, CGC is now broadening its youth entrepreneurship efforts through CGC YEP.
The next phase will extend entrepreneurship opportunities beyond a specific educational background, with the aim of helping more young Malaysians build sustainable businesses and contribute to the country’s economic development.

title: Ant International Unveils Full-Stack AI-Native Financial Solutions for Global Businesses
bodyText:
Ant International has launched a full stack of AI-native solutions covering payment, account, foreign exchange (FX), treasury and growth operations for global businesses, in what the company describes as an industry first.
The latest product upgrade brings close to 100 key products across Ant International’s four business pillars, Alipay+, Antom, WorldFirst and Bettr. The solutions are designed to help businesses improve existing operations with AI while preparing for the wider adoption of agentic capabilities.
The AI-native financial stack is built on a two-layered security architecture and two proprietary foundation models: the Antom 3-in-1 Transformer for payments and FalconTST, a time-series transformer designed for FX and liquidity forecasting.
It is also supported by the Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) for payment interoperability and WhaleRTP, a blockchain-based wholesale settlement platform.
Peng Yang, CEO of Ant International, introduced the new financial stack to more than 1,100 executives at the company’s annual VOYAGE merchant event in Shanghai.
“The future fintech leader delivers two things: a future-ready trust infrastructure and foundational FinAI models that combine complex types of deep data and rich domain expertise, and a full stack of connected AI-native solutions across payment, account, FX, treasury and growth operations that prepare them for today and the fully agentised future,” he said.
Ant International said 89.5 per cent of merchants using its main merchant payment service had already deployed its FinAI solutions over the past 12 months, while 81.4 per cent of payment tasks were completed with AI assistance.
The company said demand is increasingly extending beyond payments, as businesses seek connected fintech solutions to manage the complexity of global operations.
Through its four business pillars, Ant International provides cross-border digital payment, account, treasury management and credit technology solutions. Its network connects 150 million global merchants with more than two billion consumer accounts across 210 markets, with average daily transactions exceeding 25 million.
At the centre of the payment technology stack is the Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, which Ant International describes as an industry-first payment foundation model capable of processing sequential, tabular and graph data within a unified architecture.
Built with more than 10 billion parameters, the model processes 90 trillion data points annually and combines fraud detection, scam prevention, abuse prevention and payment success optimisation.
Ant International said that among leading large language model clients using its newly launched subscription service, chargeback rates fell by as much as 87 per cent.
The company’s payment portfolio also includes Antom Autopilot, which brings merchant payment operations into a single conversational interface covering onboarding, integration, payment orchestration, risk protection, revenue recovery, troubleshooting, financial analysis, reconciliation and new market expansion.
Ant International said Antom Autopilot has reduced the time required to reach a merchant’s first transaction from days to minutes, while the number of merchants using AI for integration quadrupled over the past year.
Other AI-powered payment products include Antom Revenue Booster, Antom EasySafePay, Antom Shield, Antom AgentSafePay, Antom Connect and Antom Agentic Payments.
Ant International has also introduced FalconTST, an AI model designed to forecast foreign exchange exposure and cash flows.
The model uses data spanning finance, retail, energy, travel and other economic sectors. With more than 8.5 billion parameters, the company said FalconTST has achieved more than 93 per cent accuracy in FX and cash-flow forecasting in its reported cases, while reducing corporate FX hedging and allocation costs by between 30 and 60 per cent.
FalconTST forms part of the company’s broader AI-native treasury offering, helping businesses monitor cash positions, forecast liquidity, manage FX risks and make global payout decisions.
As businesses increasingly allow AI agents to perform financial tasks, Ant International is also placing greater emphasis on security and control.
Its two-layered security architecture includes a Know Your Agent (KYA) framework, supported by the Alipay+ Agentic Mobile Protocol, and AgentSafePay, which the company describes as an industry-first security product offering a fund-back guarantee against losses arising from agent-specific risks.
Launched in April 2026, AMP is an open payment protocol designed for digital wallets, super apps, smart devices and other mobile interfaces to enable payments initiated by AI agents.
Ant International said 10 Alipay+ wallet partners and seven acquirers currently support AMP in its first phase. The protocol is designed to reduce the steps required to connect payment agents with wallets by 50 per cent while giving users greater visibility and control over agent permissions.
The framework also supports agent-to-agent settlement for transactions as small as US$0.000001 and includes collaboration with Mastercard and Visa on interoperable KYA security standards.
Another component of the AI-native financial stack is WhaleRTP, a blockchain-based wholesale settlement platform designed to improve liquidity management and interoperability across blockchain assets from 23 financial institutions.
Ant International said WhaleRTP processed 45 per cent of its cross-border transaction volume in 2025, reducing working capital requirements by 60 per cent and increasing interest income by 23 per cent.
The platform also supports Whale Pooling, which uses real-time connectivity, AI forecasting and embedded governance to determine when, where and how much funds should be moved within a customer’s defined policies and controls.
WorldFirst, Ant International’s global account brand, has also been upgraded with AI-native onboarding, payment, account management and treasury capabilities for enterprises and SMEs.
WorldFirst for Enterprise uses AI autopilots to support compliance and eKYC/KYB processes, payment management, fraud defence and chargeback control, as well as AI-powered FX and treasury management.
For SMEs, Wyn is a natural-language AI agent that can manage account workflows, including opening accounts and applying for World Card services supporting 17 currencies.
WorldFirst also offers A2A Supplier Connections, allowing businesses to connect with agents operated by other service providers for functions such as advertising, logistics, tax, marketing and compliance.
The company has also introduced smart liquidity management tools that use real-time data, trends and market signals to provide business analytics and liquidity advice.
WorldFirst for Enterprise Treasury Autopilot brings together tools for cash visibility, liquidity management and FX risk control.
Its World Map dashboard provides unified visibility of cash positions across markets, banks, currencies and accounts, with data refreshed every 30 minutes.
Falcon Forecast, powered by FalconTST, predicts cash flow, liquidity and FX positions from minutes ahead to several months. Falcon FX provides AI-powered solutions for FX risk management, including dynamic pricing and smart hedging recommendations.
Meanwhile, Whale Pooling supports instant funds operations and same-day settlement, with the company reporting a same-day settlement rate of more than 98 per cent.
World Payout uses intelligent decision-making to assess factors including cost, success rate, speed and risk to identify suitable payout routes.
Ant International has also introduced WorldFirst for Enterprise Account for Agent (AFA), which it describes as the world’s first agentic account for businesses. The account combines KYA-enabled smart contracts, full-chain security controls, dynamic monitoring and intervention, and feedback mechanisms for continuous agent tuning.
The new AI-native stack also extends into customer acquisition, market expansion, billing, taxation and credit.
Antom Billing and Antom Tax support functions including subscription management, metering, automated invoice generation, tax monitoring, filing support and reporting across multiple jurisdictions.
Antom Agentic Commerce Hub allows merchants to integrate and distribute product catalogues across third-party agentic platforms, while Antom Shopping Agent supports direct-to-consumer agentic shopping experiences.
A+Rewards has also been upgraded as an AI-powered growth engine connected to the Alipay+ network, linking merchants to more than 30 AI and e-commerce platforms for campaign distribution and customer acquisition. Ant International said recent e-commerce cases using cross-channel AI marketing recorded 41 per cent annual user growth.
For SMEs, Bettr AI Credit Engine provides AI-enhanced credit services, including dynamic risk assessment and automated lending decisions. The platform currently supports 49 institutions across 28 markets, providing access to more than 100 million users.
Bettr Global Credit offers flexible funding for SMEs, with credit decisions available in as little as one minute and real-time risk management powered by the Bettr AI Credit Engine.
Ant International said its new products will be rolled out across global markets during autumn and winter 2026.
The company’s latest upgrade reflects a broader shift towards AI-native financial services, where AI agents are increasingly integrated into payments, treasury, account management, FX and business operations.
By bringing these functions together within a single financial technology stack, Ant International aims to help businesses improve the efficiency of existing operations while preparing for an increasingly agent-driven global financial ecosystem.

title: Huawei Cloud Launches CodeArts Agent in Malaysia to Accelerate Enterprise AI Development
bodyText:
Huawei Cloud has commercially launched CodeArts Agent in Malaysia, introducing an enterprise-grade artificial intelligence (AI) coding solution designed to help developers handle complex software engineering tasks and accelerate AI-powered software development.
The launch took place during Huawei Cloud AI Boost Day Malaysia, held as part of the inaugural WAIC CONNECT Malaysia 2026. The event also saw Huawei Cloud outline its five-layer structure for Agentic Cloud as it continues to strengthen its enterprise AI capabilities.
CodeArts Agent is designed to support developers throughout the software development process, combining AI-powered coding capabilities with tools for complex enterprise software projects.
Nicolas Yuan Yu, Executive Vice President of Huawei Technologies (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd and Head of Huawei Cloud in Malaysia, said Malaysia is developing into a major data centre and AI hub in Southeast Asia.
“Driven by major cloud and AI players, Malaysia has become Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing data centre and AI hub. Johor and the Klang Valley now account for over 1.5 gigawatts of new AI-ready capacity, surpassing conventional regional hubs and laying the physical foundation for enterprise AI at scale across ASEAN,” he said.
Yuan added that Huawei has invested in Malaysia for more than 25 years and remains committed to supporting the country’s development through its latest cloud and AI capabilities.
Huawei Cloud has developed an end-to-end technology stack covering AI data centre infrastructure (AIDC), Agentic Infrastructure, Model as a Service (MaaS) and agent development platforms.
Together with partners and developers worldwide, Huawei Cloud is also building an Industrial AI Foundry to support the development and deployment of AI across different industries.
A key highlight of Huawei Cloud’s AI portfolio, CodeArts Agent provides intelligent coding capabilities including code generation, software development question-and-answer support and automated unit test generation.
The solution is designed for complex software projects and enterprise environments, helping developers streamline development workflows and accelerate software delivery.
For more complex development requirements, CodeArts Agent brings together several capabilities designed to support the wider software development lifecycle.
Its Agent Team consists of 16 specialised agents covering areas including requirements analysis, architecture design, coding, testing, issue resolution and code review. By simulating the collaboration of a professional engineering team, the system can autonomously plan and execute complex, long-duration development tasks.
The platform also incorporates specification-driven development capabilities and more than 30 reusable Huawei engineering skills. These are based on Huawei’s software engineering experience and are translated into AI agent capabilities for enterprise software development.
Another key capability is CodeArts Agent’s deep code understanding, which supports incremental software development.
The solution can understand and retrieve code across tens of millions of lines, giving its AI agents the project context required to extend and update existing software systems more efficiently.
This is designed to help organisations work with complex and established software environments rather than limiting AI coding tools to new or isolated development projects.
Huawei Cloud has continued to develop its cloud and AI product portfolio as enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence expands.
In July 2026, Gartner named Huawei Cloud a Leader in its 2026 Magic Quadrant for Cloud AI Infrastructure, according to Huawei. The recognition reflects Huawei Cloud’s position in the global cloud AI infrastructure market.
Huawei Cloud’s wider 2026 strategy also includes Agentic Infrastructure, Agentic MaaS and enterprise-grade agent platforms, positioning AI agents as part of a broader cloud infrastructure and software development ecosystem.
Alongside the Malaysian launch, Huawei Cloud introduced the CodeArts Agent Early Bird Programme.
Eligible enterprise users will receive three months of complimentary access to the Professional Edition. Enterprises seeking to establish AI-powered, enterprise-grade software development practices can also receive additional support, including one-to-one coaching from local experts and enablement services.
The programme is intended to give Malaysian enterprises an opportunity to explore AI-assisted software development while receiving support in incorporating the technology into their development practices.
Huawei Cloud said CodeArts Agent will continue to combine its software engineering expertise with advanced AI technologies to provide smarter, more efficient and secure development experiences.
The company aims to support developers and enterprises as they evolve their software engineering models and adopt AI more broadly across development workflows.
Huawei Cloud’s AI services and capabilities have already supported customers across Asia Pacific in moving from cloud migration towards wider AI adoption, with applications focused on improving productivity and responding to changing business needs.
As Malaysia continues to develop its AI ecosystem, Huawei Cloud said it will continue investing in AI innovation and providing a secure, stable and intelligent cloud foundation to support businesses across Asia Pacific.

title: Optics Valley Launches International Communication Alliance to Support Tech Companies’ Global Expansion
bodyText:
Optics Valley has launched the Optics Valley International Communication Alliance to help local technology companies strengthen their international communication capabilities and expand into global markets.
The alliance was inaugurated on 13 September under the theme “Chasing the Light, Connecting the World”, bringing together representatives from 13 founding member companies, including FiberHome, China Construction Third Engineering Bureau, HGTECH, YHKT Entertainment, Huakang Clean and Shenglong Electric, alongside representatives from more than 100 other Optics Valley enterprises.
Established by Optics Valley in collaboration with the News & Information Service Center of Xinhua News Agency and other partners, the alliance is designed to provide companies with access to international communication resources. Its services include overseas public opinion response and multilingual content production, supporting enterprises as they develop their brands and operations in overseas markets.
The initiative reflects Optics Valley’s growing focus on helping companies progress from “product export” to “brand export” as more of its technologies and products reach international audiences.
In recent years, Optics Valley’s innovations have gained greater visibility overseas through the international social media presence of “Optics Valley of China”. Products such as the Optics Valley Photon sky rail and driverless minibuses have also attracted international attention.
The alliance aims to build on this momentum by giving companies greater support in communicating with international audiences and responding to overseas public opinion.
Xinhua News Agency, China’s national news agency, has 184 overseas branches and established cooperative links with more than 2,000 media organisations worldwide, providing the alliance with an extensive international communication network.
According to Optics Valley, the alliance will act as a “navigator” for companies going global by helping them strengthen international branding while navigating different markets and audiences.
Li Lei, vice president of FiberHome and representative of the alliance’s founding members, highlighted the importance of combining global expansion with local operations.
FiberHome’s business currently covers more than 100 countries and regions, with wholly owned subsidiaries in 36 countries and overseas optical cable plants in Ecuador, Thailand and Hungary. At its Philippine subsidiary, locally hired employees account for more than 95 per cent of its workforce.
“We will stay committed to high-quality global expansion and to deepening localized operations, and, with the platform of the Optics Valley International Communication Alliance, we will not only export China’s advanced communication technologies and solutions, but also serve as a bridge for industrial cooperation and people-to-people connectivity between China and the rest of the world,” he said.
The alliance is therefore positioned not only as a communications platform, but also as a means of supporting companies as they build longer-term relationships in overseas markets.
Huakang Clean, another founding member, is a leading enterprise in China’s cleanroom industry and has identified international expansion as a core strategy for its 15th Five-Year Plan period.
The company has established a market presence across Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, South America and Africa, while exporting its cleanroom technology solutions.
Through the new alliance, Huakang Clean aims to deepen cross-border collaboration and strengthen its international brand building as it continues expanding overseas.
A think tank report titled Going Global, Competing Worldwide: How ‘Optics Valley of China’ Polishes Its International Calling Card in Service of Building a Strong Nation in Science and Technology — Practices and Insights was also released during the ceremony.
Produced by Reference News Press and Reference Think Tank, the report examined Optics Valley’s approach to international communication and the overseas expansion of its leading enterprises.
According to the report, leading companies represented by the “Seven Stars of Optics Valley” have recorded average annual overseas revenue growth of more than 30 per cent.
It describes Optics Valley’s international communication approach through “one strategic direction and ten keywords”, highlighting areas including central-local coordination, AI empowerment, collective overseas expansion and tailored strategies for different markets.
The report also identified several areas for Optics Valley to consider as it strengthens its international communication capabilities.
These include elevating the Optics Valley story from individual corporate activity to a broader national narrative, using AI as a global knowledge-service infrastructure for international communication, and developing communication capabilities as an industrial capability in its own right.
The report’s recommendations reflect the growing role of technology in how companies communicate with international audiences, manage their global reputation and develop brands across different markets.
A training session on overseas communication capacity building was held alongside the alliance’s inauguration.
David Wei, founder of Vision Knight Capital, and Cao Yang, deputy director of the International Communication Department of the News & Information Service Center of Xinhua News Agency, were invited to deliver lectures.
The session provided participating companies with further guidance on strengthening their overseas communication capabilities as they pursue international markets.
With the establishment of the Optics Valley International Communication Alliance, the region is seeking to give its technology companies a more structured platform for global communication, brand building and cross-border cooperation as they expand beyond China.

title: MATRADE Leads Malaysian Tech Delegation to Hangzhou for Global Digital Trade Expo
bodyText:
The Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) will lead a delegation of 11 Malaysian technology and digital enterprises to the 5th Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) in Hangzhou, China, from 21 to 25 September 2026, as Malaysia seeks to strengthen its presence in Asia’s rapidly expanding digital economy.
The Export Acceleration Mission (EAM) aims to expand Malaysia’s trade presence within China’s digital ecosystem while creating opportunities for cross-border collaboration in frontier technology sectors.
The Malaysia Pavilion at GDTE will serve as a platform for business matchmaking, technical exchange and market expansion, connecting Malaysian technology companies with potential partners and buyers in China and the wider region.
The Malaysian delegation will showcase a range of digital and frontier technology solutions aimed at supporting enterprise digital transformation.
Their offerings cover AI data integration and customer automation, industrial Internet of Things (IoT) solutions for energy and utilities, AI-enabled robotics, high-performance cloud computing and Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS).
The delegation will also feature solutions spanning PropTech ecosystems, cross-border trade platforms, Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) media tools and smart health applications.
The breadth of technologies reflects the growing range of Malaysian digital capabilities being positioned for international markets.
Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof, Chief Executive Officer of MATRADE, said participating in China’s technology ecosystem represents a strategic move for Malaysian exporters.
“Venturing into China’s dynamic technology ecosystem is a deliberate, strategic positioning move for our exporters. The 5th GDTE places Malaysian innovators directly alongside global industry leaders, empowering them to tap into high-value sourcing channels, capture joint venture opportunities, and integrate into regional technology supply chains.”
The mission takes place against the backdrop of strong trade growth between Malaysia and China, with China remaining Malaysia’s largest single trading partner for 17 consecutive years since 2009.
Trade between the two countries continued to expand in 2026. During the first eight months of the year, Malaysia-China trade rose 35.0% to RM456.68 billion compared with the corresponding period in 2025.
Malaysia’s exports to China increased 23.7% to RM148.56 billion, while imports from China grew 41.2% to RM308.12 billion.
The continued growth in bilateral trade provides a wider commercial environment for Malaysian technology companies seeking to enter or expand within the Chinese market.
Malaysia-China economic relations are also supported by regional trade frameworks, including the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area (ACFTA) 3.0 upgrade and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).
These frameworks provide enhanced rules for paperless trade and modern digital trade facilitation, alongside intellectual property protections.
For Malaysian digital exporters, these arrangements can support efforts to expand their market reach and participate in regional technology supply chains.
The combination of growing bilateral trade and deeper regional economic integration provides opportunities for Malaysian companies to explore partnerships, sourcing arrangements and technology collaboration beyond their domestic market.
Throughout the five-day GDTE, MATRADE will carry out a programme designed to generate direct commercial opportunities for the Malaysian delegation.
A key component will be curated business-to-business (B2B) matching sessions, organised in collaboration with the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) Hangzhou Branch and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC).
The sessions are intended to connect Malaysian technology companies with potential Chinese buyers, business partners and investors while exploring opportunities for market expansion.
The delegation will also participate in site visits to leading Chinese technology companies and industrial hubs across Hangzhou.
These visits will provide opportunities to explore potential research and development partnerships, technical integration and commercial channel expansion.
Through its participation at GDTE, MATRADE aims to position Malaysian technology companies closer to emerging opportunities within China’s digital economy and wider regional technology supply chains.
For the 11 participating enterprises, the mission provides a platform to showcase Malaysian digital capabilities while pursuing new sourcing channels, partnerships and opportunities for international expansion.
The initiative also forms part of Malaysia’s broader efforts to strengthen its digital exports and deepen commercial links with one of its most important trading partners.

title: Malaysia’s Trade Surges 43.4% to RM354 Billion in August 2026
bodyText:
Malaysia recorded another strong month for external trade in August 2026, with total trade, exports and imports each registering growth of more than 40% year-on-year (y-o-y), according to the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM).
Total trade increased 43.4% y-o-y to RM354.01 billion, supported by a 45.5% increase in exports to RM191.05 billion and a 41.1% rise in imports to RM162.96 billion.
Malaysia recorded a trade surplus of RM28.09 billion, extending its surplus streak to 76 consecutive months since May 2020.
The strong export performance was supported by higher shipments of manufactured and mining goods, particularly electrical and electronic (E&E) products, petroleum products, liquefied natural gas (LNG), metalliferous ores and metal scrap.
E&E products continued to be a key contributor to Malaysia’s export performance. From January to August 2026, E&E exports reached RM656.14 billion, putting the sector on track to surpass its full-year export value recorded in 2025.
Overall, Malaysia’s exports rose 45.5% y-o-y in August to RM191.05 billion. The increase was driven by stronger domestic exports as well as re-exports.
Domestic exports accounted for RM151.0 billion, or 79% of total exports, representing a 46.0% increase from a year earlier. Re-exports rose 43.3% to RM40.1 billion.
Malaysia also recorded export growth across its major trading partners in August, with shipments to ASEAN, China, the United States, Taiwan and the European Union registering robust increases.
Exports to both the US and China reached their highest monthly values thus far, highlighting continued demand from two of Malaysia’s largest trading partners.
Export expansion was also recorded across Malaysia’s free trade agreement (FTA) partners, including Hong Kong SAR, Japan, Mexico, the Republic of Korea, India, the United Kingdom, Türkiye, Pakistan, Canada, Peru and Chile.
The wider growth in shipments reflects Malaysia’s continued presence across regional and global markets.
For the first eight months of 2026, Malaysia’s external trade expanded 27.0% to RM2.514 trillion.
Exports continued to grow faster than imports, rising 31.2% to RM1.356 trillion, while imports increased 22.4% to RM1.158 trillion.
The trade surplus reached RM198.66 billion, more than double the surplus recorded during the corresponding period last year.
Trade, exports, imports and the trade surplus all recorded their highest cumulative values on record for a January-August period.
The January-August trade surplus has also already surpassed the full-year values recorded in both 2024 and 2025, highlighting the strength of Malaysia’s external trade performance so far in 2026.
Looking ahead, Malaysia will continue efforts to strengthen the foundations for sustained trade growth by widening its market presence, improving the competitiveness of strategic industries and positioning local exporters to capture emerging global opportunities.
Greater utilisation of free trade agreements (FTAs) and deeper engagement with both established and emerging markets are expected to create further avenues for export expansion.
At the same time, efforts to move towards higher-value activities are intended to strengthen Malaysia’s export base and support its longer-term position in global trade.
With external trade continuing to expand, the latest figures point to sustained demand for Malaysian products across major markets while highlighting the importance of strengthening higher-value industries and broadening the country’s international market reach.

title: She Leads. She Defends. Where Leadership, Law and Technology Meet
bodyText:
By Harriet Santhana and Natasha Isabel Saravanan
Law, Risk, Governance and Technology may once have occupied separate corners of an organisation. Today, the boundaries between them are becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish. Artificial intelligence is changing how businesses operate. Cyber attacks are becoming more sophisticated. Legal and statutory expectations are evolving alongside new technologies.  At the same time, leaders are being asked to make decisions that protect not only growth and profitability, but also trust, people and organisational resilience. These converging realities formed the foundation of the recent inaugural She Leads. She Defends—Law, Risk and Governance Forum 2026 , organised by WomenAtlas Media & Events , powered by Laurea People’s Signature and founded by Nisha Meng Mingg Li .
The event brought together women leaders and professionals from Corporate Affairs, Law, Governance, Technology, Cybersecurity, Communications, and Public Service. It explored what leadership means at a time when organisations can no longer afford to manage these issues in isolation. As the conversations unfolded throughout the day, one message consistently emerged. The future of leadership belongs to those who understand how to build trust, ask difficult questions, and prepare for risks before they become crises.

As the event Co-officiator, Rita Irina Wahab reflected on how rapidly organisations are being reshaped. “The way we work is changing. The way we communicate is changing. Technology is reshaping industries and challenging institutions,” she said, before asking, “What kind of leadership does the future look like?” Rita opined, “No organisation succeeds in strategy alone. No institution succeeds in policy alone. And no leader succeeds in expertise alone. What ultimately determines success is trust.”
Trust, she explained, connects businesses with communities, organisations with regulators and leaders with the people they serve. She distilled her message into three principles: lead with purpose, build trust deliberately and lift others. “A single decision does not create trust. It is earned through consistency, credibility, and integrity over time.”

Dalvin Kaur , the event’s Co-officiator , further emphasised the Convergence of Law, Governance, Risk, and Technology. Reflecting on the diverse professionals at the forum, she noted that their presence reflected how these areas have increasingly become interconnected. “In your organisations, Law, Risk, Governance, and Technology have all already collided into one conversation,”she said.
“This is no longer a technology problem with a legal footnote,” she said. “Cybersecurity is no longer confined to an IT department. It is unambiguously a board matter.” Dalvin urged organisations to anticipate emerging risks through stronger governance. “Good governance is the discipline of asking hard questions before you’re forced to answer them,” she said, pointing to questions around an organisation’s readiness for AI decisions, a board’s responsibilities during a cyber incident and the clarity of legal, risk and compliance roles.

The first keynote of the day turned attention to another area often underestimated in governance discussions: language. Dr Diyana Hassim, Head of Corporate Communications at Jabatan Perkhidmatan Awam , explored the relationship between words, mental health and policy in her keynote, Words Shape Policy: Communicating Mental Health with Purpose, Empathy and Impact .
“With one careless sentence, we can silence an employee. One poorly communicated policy can create fear. One dismissive response can stop someone from asking for help.” Dr Diyana encouraged leaders to consider what employees leave unsaid when fear of judgement or dismissal prevents them from speaking up. “Can your employees speak without fear?” she asked. “Or can your team say anything to you without feeling guilty?”

The panel session sought to address one of the most pressing of questions facing Malaysian organisations:  are they genuinely ready to govern AI? Moderated by Moyra Ibrahim, Co-Founder and Executive Director at ECS Malaysia, the forum “ AI Governance: Are Malaysian Organisations Really Ready? ”, brought together Dr Salasiah Abbas, Chief Executive Officer of SOVA Intelligence (M) Sdn Bhd, Wendy Lim, Founder of Wei Ling Chambers, and Cally Yau, Chief Executive Officer of PEOPLElogy Berhad.
Dr Salasiah said the biggest gap was not necessarily policy or awareness, but practice. “Come Monday morning, when everybody is busy, we use AI tools and may upload sensitive documents. As deadlines loom, and we chase profit and revenue, are we going to follow the policy? The gap lies in putting governance into practice.”
Cally Yau brought the discussion closer to everyday workplace behaviour, noting that while many people were already using tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, fewer organisations appeared to have AI handbooks or governance frameworks. She quizzed,  “How do we measure our own responsibility for AI governance that we have checked in for our day-to-day use?”
Wendy Lim emphasised that organisations should first understand their current position before building policies for the future. She recommended an AI impact assessment, describing it as “like a health check” to identify existing AI use and governance gaps across policies, employment practices, personal data and external contracts.

The fireside session In Her Own Words: Leading Through Change shifted the focus from systems and governance to the personal realities of leadership.  The session featured Farah Jaafar, Global Advisor at Straits Investment Bank; Norliana Aida Ramli, Principal at Luminar Consulting Services Sdn. Bhd.; and Hjh. Mastura Abd Manap, Chief Executive Officer at Scubatex Holding Berhad, and was moderated by Jasmin Edna Peters.
The conversation explored how leaders navigate uncertainty and take responsibility for the people behind their decisions. Norliana reflected on making high-stakes decisions during her corporate career, noting the importance of having support. Mastura , speaking from the perspective of an entrepreneur, highlighted, “As an entrepreneur, I have to make the decisions that affect the company and its people.” She shared that giving long-serving employees greater authority helped the business continue in her absence. “The trust that I’ve given to them gives them a feeling of belonging to the company,” she said. Farah offered a broader reflection on leadership, noting that while traditional corporate environments often focus on financial returns, a ‘return on care for people’ could bring more sustainable impact to businesses.

The second keynote by Dr Pin Lean Lau , Law in the Age of AI: Why Every Legal Leader Must Understand Technology , brought the discussion back to the relationship between law and technology. “Technical fluency is a currency of our legal leadership,” she said. “If you don’t understand code and how it executes policy, then how do we credibly determine what accountability might be?” she asked. She later put the argument more strongly: “Ignorance is a violation of duty,” she said.
Her keynote explored emerging legal questions surrounding AI, blockchain, virtual environments and digital assets, while also introducing the idea that “code is law”. Technology, she explained, increasingly shapes what people can access, copy, share and do online, regulating behaviour in ways similar to traditional rules and laws. Dr Pin Lean urged legal and governance professionals, particularly when dealing with data, automated decisions and AI systems to,  “anticipate [the questions] and move from reactive to being proactive.”

The forum’s discussion on the modern legal leader continued the theme of the day by examining how the traditional boundaries between legal, risk, compliance and regulatory functions are becoming increasingly blurred.
The panel, moderated by Rhaveena Shree Darhavyl, Head of Legal and Compliance at Iconix Property and Asset Management, featured Syafiqah Abdul Razak, Partner at Atiqah Syafiqah and Associates, Jiwantti G., Senior Manager of Regulatory and Compliance at YTL Communications, and Azreena Askalani, Senior Vice President and Head of Strategic and Sustainability Risk Management at Bursa Malaysia. The discussion pointed out the need for leaders to move beyond narrow functional responsibilities and understand how legal decisions affect business strategy, reputation, regulatory criteria and organisational risk.
Legal professionals increasingly need to understand business realities. Risk professionals need to understand regulatory developments. Compliance teams need to communicate effectively across the organisation. The modern leader, therefore, is not only someone with deeper expertise in one discipline, but someone who can connect disciplines and ensure important risks do not fall between organisational silos.

Cybersecurity formed the focus of the forum’s later sessions, beginning with Jane Teh’s keynote on leading digital defence . Teh emphasised that cybersecurity is a leadership responsibility, not a purely technical concern. “Doesn’t matter what size company you are. You can be an SME, you can be a Sendirian Berhad, or even a solopreneur; if you’re servicing a customer, you will be the target,” she said. The growing use of AI, she explained, has created new opportunities for both defenders and attackers.
“AI is a double-edged sword,” she said, with organisations using it to improve security and analyse threats while attackers use it to operate at greater scale and speed. Teh who is the Founder & Chief Executive Officer of VortiQ[x] , stressed the importance of governance when deploying AI systems. “If your organisation is mature enough, you should be able to have an AI to detect the attacks before it actually attacks you,” she said.
At the board level, Teh argued that cybersecurity discussions must move beyond technical jargon to focus on business risks, including “What kind of risk am I taking on? What kind of losses?” She urged organisations to align risk appetite, third-party governance and incident response in line with business goals. “In the age of AI, resilience is not only about technical achievement. You must ensure that you are able to recover, and recover fast.”

The keynote by Raihanah Abdul Razak, Deputy Public Prosecutor at the Attorney General’s Chambers of Malaysia , examined the challenges of investigating and prosecuting cyber-enabled crimes, where evidence may span devices, cloud platforms, financial systems and international jurisdictions. She stressed the value of understanding technology even inside the legal system. “ When I receive a case whereby it involves technology, I translate [it] as simply as possible,” she said, pointing out the need to explain complicated ideas in ways that courts can understand. She also emphasised the importance of acting quickly following a digital incident.
“When something happens, you have to report it as soon as possible. Then you must preserve the evidence,” she said. Digital evidence must also be authenticated with screenshots, recordings and devices which may require forensic examination. Her message reached beyond prosecutors and investigators, stressing that everyone involved in cyber investigations must develop a working understanding of technology.

From its opening ceremony to its final keynote, She Leads. She Defends. presented leadership as an ever more interconnected responsibility. AI decisions carry legal implications, cybersecurity requires governance, communication shapes trust, and leadership determines how organisations prepare for uncertainty.
For Malaysian SMEs, this makes cross-functional thinking especially important. Throughout the forum, speakers returned to the need to ask questions early, build trust deliberately and develop the confidence to engage beyond one’s traditional area of expertise.
Perhaps this was best captured in Dalvin Kaur’s challenge to the audience during the opening ceremony: “ Good governance is the discipline of asking hard questions before you’re forced to answer them. ”

title: IFC and AFFIN BANK Partner to Expand US$400 Million MSME Financing in Malaysia
bodyText:
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and AFFIN BANK have announced a partnership to expand access to finance for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) across Malaysia.
At the centre of the partnership is a US$400 million long-term financing package for AFFIN BANK, which aims to broaden access to capital for MSMEs and other underserved business segments.
The financing will prioritise women-owned businesses and enterprises operating in regions where access to finance remains constrained, with the partnership intended to support productive investment, business competitiveness and more inclusive economic development.
Under the agreed framework, AFFIN BANK will channel funding to eligible MSMEs to help businesses access capital for productive investment and growth.
The partnership comes as financial access remains an important consideration for smaller businesses seeking to expand, particularly those operating outside major urban centres.
Allen Forlemu, IFC Regional Industry Director, Financial Institutions Group, Asia Pacific, said small businesses remain an important driver of employment and economic opportunity in Malaysia.
“We estimate that this partnership could create at least 42,000 jobs across Malaysia over the next five years, while expanding access to finance for women entrepreneurs and enterprises operating outside major urban centers, especially the ones where the financing gaps are wider,” Forlemu said.
He added that IFC welcomed the opportunity to work with AFFIN BANK to support the growth of Malaysian MSMEs, including women-owned businesses, while uplifting underserved communities in areas such as Sarawak and Sabah.
A key focus of the partnership is improving financing access for women entrepreneurs and businesses operating in areas where financing gaps are more pronounced.
AFFIN Group President and Group Chief Executive Officer Datuk Wan Razly Abdullah said MSMEs are central to Malaysia’s economy, contributing to job creation, innovation and local communities.
“Through this collaboration with IFC, we are expanding our ability to support businesses that have the potential to grow, particularly women-owned enterprises and businesses in regions where access to financing remains more limited,” Wan Razly said.
He said greater access to capital could contribute to socio-economic development, strengthen local economies and create opportunities for more Malaysians to participate in the country’s growth.
The partnership therefore combines access to international development finance with AFFIN BANK’s local market presence and existing SME banking capabilities.
The agreement will also broaden AFFIN’s access to international capital and development finance expertise.
According to Wan Razly, the partnership brings together IFC’s international investor network with AFFIN’s understanding of the Malaysian market, creating opportunities to expand its customer base and deploy capital into productive sectors of the economy.
The initiative is also aligned with AFFIN’s AFFIN Axelerate 2028 (AX28) Plan, which guides the Group’s longer-term business strategy.
Wan Razly said the partnership would support AFFIN’s ambition to become the “Most Creative and Innovative Financial Company in Malaysia”.
AFFIN BANK has continued to develop its SME banking franchise through targeted propositions for start-ups, women entrepreneurs and growing businesses.
The bank was recognised as Best Bank for SMEs in Malaysia at the Asiamoney Best Bank Awards 2023.
Through the new IFC partnership, AFFIN BANK aims to further expand its capacity to serve MSMEs, particularly businesses operating in segments and regions where access to finance remains constrained.
The US$400 million financing package is expected to strengthen the flow of capital to eligible Malaysian MSMEs, supporting business investment, competitiveness and broader participation in economic growth.
For businesses outside major urban centres and women-owned enterprises in particular, the partnership places greater emphasis on addressing financing gaps and widening access to capital.

title: OCBC Extends Bank of Ningbo Alliance as ASEAN-Greater China Business Flows Accelerate
bodyText:
OCBC has extended its strategic partnership with Bank of Ningbo for another 10 years, strengthening a two-decade collaboration as business, trade, wealth and investment flows between ASEAN and Greater China continue to expand.
The new strategic cooperation agreement builds on the banks’ partnership, which began in 2006, and is intended to strengthen synergies between the two organisations as Chinese companies increasingly explore opportunities across ASEAN.
The partnership also reinforces OCBC’s role in facilitating cross-border business flows between China and Southeast Asia, supported by its regional network and China Business Offices established in ASEAN markets beyond Singapore in 2019.
The collaboration has supported strong business growth, particularly over the past decade. In 2025, OCBC recorded a 50% increase in the number of new-to-bank Chinese companies expanding into ASEAN, reaching a record high.
The broader ASEAN-Greater China corridor has also continued to strengthen. China has remained ASEAN’s largest trading partner since 2009, with bilateral trade exceeding US$1 trillion for the first time in 2025.
Against this backdrop, OCBC and Bank of Ningbo expect the corridor to present continued opportunities across cross-border trade, business expansion, wealth management and investment.
OCBC Group CEO Tan Teck Long said the partnership had generated synergies across wholesale banking and wealth management while creating value for both organisations.
“Further renewing our partnership for 10 years reflects the deep trust between both organisations and the shared conviction in the growth trajectory of the ASEAN-Greater China corridor,” Tan said.
He added that the two banks had been leveraging their complementary strengths to accelerate their cross-border growth and wealth ambitions, with plans to build further on the partnership over the next decade.
The partnership is underpinned by Bank of Ningbo’s domestic banking franchise in China and OCBC’s regional network across ASEAN and Greater China.
Bank of Ningbo is one of China’s leading commercial banks and one of the country’s 21 domestic systemically important banks. As at 11 September 2026, it was the largest city commercial bank in China by market capitalisation.
The bank recorded a net profit of RMB16.6 billion in the first half of 2026, representing a 12% increase from the same period a year earlier.
Its corporate, SME and retail businesses provide OCBC with access to a growing pool of Chinese customers seeking opportunities outside China, including in ASEAN markets.
The collaboration is therefore positioned to support Chinese companies looking to expand into Southeast Asia while connecting businesses and investors across both regions.
OCBC first invested in Ningbo Commercial Bank in 2006, acquiring a 12.2% stake before the bank was renamed Bank of Ningbo in 2007.
OCBC subsequently increased its shareholding to the maximum permitted 20% in 2014 and reaffirmed its long-term commitment through a 10-year strategic cooperation agreement in 2017.
The latest agreement extends this relationship for another decade, building on 20 years of collaboration between the two financial institutions.
OCBC Chairman Andrew Lee and Bank of Ningbo Chairman Zhuang Lingjun were present as OCBC Group CEO Tan Teck Long and Bank of Ningbo President Feng Peijiong signed the new agreement in Ningbo.
Beyond business and financial cooperation, the new agreement also renews the banks’ commitment to talent development and knowledge sharing.
OCBC will continue its US$5 million training grant, first established under the 2006 agreement. The funding supports staff training, knowledge-sharing initiatives, staff secondments and leadership exchange programmes involving OCBC and Bank of Ningbo.
More than 1,000 employees across the two banks have benefited from these initiatives to date.
The continuation of the training programme reflects the broader scope of the partnership, which combines cross-border banking and business development with efforts to strengthen expertise and leadership capabilities across both organisations.
With the new 10-year strategic cooperation agreement, OCBC and Bank of Ningbo will continue working together to capture opportunities arising from the growing economic links between China and ASEAN.
The partnership brings together Bank of Ningbo’s strong domestic presence in China with OCBC’s established regional network, providing a platform for further cooperation in cross-border business, trade, wealth management and investment.
As companies continue to explore expansion opportunities across the ASEAN-Greater China corridor, the two banks will seek to deepen their collaboration and support the evolving needs of businesses operating between the two markets.

title: Rework.com Launches Agentic OS to Help Malaysian Businesses Enter the Intelligence Age
bodyText:
Rework.com, a global technology company with more than one million users across 12,000 companies, has unveiled its Agentic Operating System (Agentic OS) for Business in Malaysia, aiming to help organisations move beyond isolated AI experiments and integrate artificial intelligence into everyday business operations.
Launched at Rework Launch 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, the platform brings people, AI agents, business data and operational workflows together within a single connected environment.
The launch comes as businesses increasingly explore how AI can move beyond individual tools and become part of how work is actually performed. Rework positions its Agentic OS around a model in which humans and AI agents can work together across interconnected business services, enabling organisations to execute tasks faster, improve operational efficiency and reuse accumulated business knowledge and context.
Traditional business software has largely been designed around the assumption that people perform the work while software stores information and organises processes. As AI becomes increasingly capable of executing tasks, Rework believes organisations will need to reconsider how responsibilities are shared between people and AI.
For Malaysian businesses, the shift comes against a backdrop of significant investment in the country’s digital economy. According to MDEC, Malaysia recorded RM87.4 billion in digital investments in 2025.
However, AI adoption remains uneven. A Strand Partners report cited by Rework found that 67% of AI adopters in Malaysia still rely primarily on basic applications such as chatbots, while only 19% have a formal strategy for scaling AI across multiple business functions.
Rework Founder and CEO Eric Pham said the challenge is not necessarily a lack of investment or access to large language models, but the absence of business infrastructure that allows AI to become embedded in everyday operations.
“Malaysian businesses’ AI adoption gap is not due to lack of investment or large language model; it is a lack of business infrastructure that lets AI move beyond isolated tools into the way work actually gets done.”
He added that Rework’s Agentic OS for Business is intended to help businesses move from fragmented AI use towards what the company describes as a truly agentic business.
As AI models and capabilities continue to advance, Rework believes AI itself may increasingly become commoditised. In this environment, the company argues that competitive advantage could depend less on access to a particular AI model and more on how effectively businesses apply AI to their own operations and knowledge.
The Agentic OS is designed to provide a shared operating environment for people and AI agents, allowing organisations to capture and reuse operating knowledge, decisions, processes, customer history and accumulated experience.
Rework refers to this accumulated knowledge as organisational intelligence.
“Agentic OS for Business provides a shared operating environment for humans and AI that allows businesses to capture and reuse their operating knowledge, decisions, processes, customer history and accumulated experience,” Pham said.
The approach is intended to allow AI agents to develop a deeper understanding of how an organisation operates rather than functioning as disconnected tools.
Rework’s Agentic OS for Business consists of two core layers: its Intelligence Architecture and Business Services.
The Intelligence Architecture forms the underlying intelligence layer connecting and powering the business. It includes centralised business outputs, compounding business knowledge and a multi-AI-agent stack spanning Service AI, AI Assistant, AI Desktop and Workflow AI.
The second layer, Business Services, consists of hundreds of interconnected, ready-to-use operating services organised around key business functions.
These include Marketing Operating Services, covering areas such as lead monitoring and nurturing, prospect engagement, customer messaging, campaign monitoring, partner management and event services.
Sales Operating Services support pipeline management, opportunity-to-revenue workflows, quotations, orders, invoicing, field sales and distribution management.
Meanwhile, Work Operating Services cover requests, projects, business processes, datasets and cross-functional work orchestration.
For human resources and employee administration, People Operating Services include employee services, leave management, timesheets and payroll.
The platform also includes Communication Services for chat, town halls, meetings and other organisation-wide communications.
Together, these layers are intended to give AI agents the context, knowledge and capabilities required to understand business operations, execute work and coordinate activities across an organisation.
Rework Co-Founder and COO Brian Trinh said businesses should be able to continuously improve how work is performed rather than simply adding new AI tools to existing software systems.
“The opportunity in the AI era is not simply to add another AI tool to an existing software stack. Businesses need to rethink how work is designed, how context is captured, and how people and AI agents operate together.”
According to Trinh, the Agentic OS is designed to provide organisations with a practical foundation for making this transition.
The platform therefore positions AI integration as an operational transformation rather than simply another layer of software. By connecting business services, organisational knowledge and AI agents, Rework aims to help companies incorporate AI into workflows across different functions.
Rework’s inaugural launch event in Malaysia brought together approximately 150 senior business leaders. The event featured keynote sessions on the intelligence age and the latest evolution of Rework, alongside product demonstrations and customer success stories.
The launch also marks the availability of Rework Agentic OS for Business in Malaysia, giving local organisations an option to explore how AI agents can be integrated across their business operations.
Interested businesses can book a demonstration and explore Rework’s AI integration options through the company’s website.

title: Retail Summit Asia 2026 Puts Customer Retention at the Heart of Sustainable Retail Growth
bodyText:
More than 400 retailers, founders, marketers and industry leaders gathered at Menara AFFIN, TRX for Retail Summit Asia 2026, exchanging practical strategies and real-world business experiences around a central question: what does it take to build a retail business that lasts?
For Malaysian brands, the retail environment has become increasingly competitive, with businesses facing stronger competition, thinner margins and rising efforts to attract new customers.
Against this backdrop, the summit highlighted the importance of putting customer relationships and experience at the heart of retail growth, rather than relying solely on acquiring new customers.
YB Ng Sze Han, Selangor State EXCO for Investment, Trade and Mobility, officiated the summit and noted that the strength of any business ultimately comes down to putting people first.
The summit challenged the familiar assumption that retail growth must always come from bringing in more customers.
Instead, experiences shared throughout the event pointed towards the value of retaining and deepening relationships with customers who have already chosen a brand.
As EasyStore Head of Product Goh Chong Xian put it, “The best customer is not always the next customer. Sometimes, it is the customer you already have.”
The idea was reflected in the experiences of Malaysian brands including Tanamera, XIXILI, Claire Organics and Bayu Somerset.
Each brand has navigated changing trends, competitors and market shifts, sharing the decisions and strategies that have helped them continue growing.
As customer acquisition becomes more costly and demanding, the second sale, the next visit and the relationship that follows can become increasingly important to a retailer’s growth.
Across the discussions, a common theme emerged: businesses that last are those that place customer experience and brand promise at the centre of their operations.
Rather than viewing every transaction as an isolated sale, retailers are increasingly looking at the entire customer journey and how each interaction can strengthen the relationship between consumer and brand.
This means creating more consistent and intentional experiences across different points of contact, whether customers are shopping online or visiting a physical store.
