Rather than an immediate return to a higher rate, the association is advocating a staggered, step-up structure beginning from a lower base and progressively adjusting upwards over five-year intervals.
MRCA said a phased approach would give businesses sufficient time to adapt while cushioning household sentiment and supporting economic stability.
The association also called for a transparent, multi-stage consumption tax system supported by a reliable refund mechanism and strict zero-rating for essential goods.
According to MRCA, such a system could help reduce the compounding costs associated with the existing Sales and Service Tax (SST), broaden the national revenue base and establish a fairer tax ecosystem for both businesses and consumers.
MRCA is also seeking measures to strengthen the competitiveness of Malaysia’s domestic retail economy.
The association has proposed eliminating sales taxes on locally manufactured goods, arguing that removing these cascading costs would enable domestic retailers to offer more competitive prices against imported products.
The measure could also support local manufacturers while encouraging domestic production and consumption.
By reducing the tax burden across the local supply chain, MRCA believes the Government can strengthen the position of Malaysian businesses and stimulate activity within the domestic economy.
Tourism is another area highlighted in MRCA’s Budget 2027 wishlist.
The association is calling for the RM1,000 domestic tourism tax relief to be extended through 2027 and for its scope to be expanded beyond specific sectors.
MRCA is proposing that the relief explicitly cover hotel accommodation as well as targeted retail shopping expenditures.
The association believes broadening the relief could maximise the economic multiplier effect of domestic tourism by encouraging Malaysians to spend on accommodation, travel and retail activities within the country.
MRCA said a stable and business-friendly policy framework would help reduce compliance costs, strengthen investor confidence and create a more sustainable operating environment for retailers.
As Malaysia prepares for Budget 2027, the association remains committed to working with the Government and providing industry insights to help shape policies that support businesses and consumers.
For MRCA, the overarching objective is to establish a fairer and more predictable economic framework that enables Malaysian retailers to remain competitive while contributing to a globally competitive and sustainable retail sector.

title: CIMB Named Malaysia’s Best Retail, Digital SME and Investment Bank by Euromoney
bodyText:
CIMB Bank Berhad and CIMB Investment Bank have been recognised for their performance, innovation and customer impact, winning three key awards at the Euromoney Awards for Excellence 2026.
CIMB was named Malaysia’s Best Retail Bank, Malaysia’s Best Digital Bank for SMEs and Malaysia’s Best Investment Bank.
The three awards reflect CIMB’s continued focus on customer-centric financial solutions, digital capabilities and market expertise across its retail, SME and investment banking businesses.
Novan Amirudin, Group Chief Executive Officer of CIMB Group, said the recognition reflected the trust of customers and the dedication of the bank’s teams.
“These recognitions are a testament to the trust of our customers and the dedication of our teams across the Bank. They reaffirm CIMB’s purpose of advancing customers and society by making financial solutions more accessible, relevant and impactful for the people and businesses we serve,” he said.
In retail banking, CIMB continued to develop its diversified franchise through personalised propositions, digitally enabled customer journeys and stronger engagement across key customer segments.
Revenue and profitability advanced during the year, supported by market share gains across auto finance, credit cards and retail deposits, alongside continued progress in digital sales and customer cross-selling.
The bank also continued to strengthen its wealth proposition through differentiated investment solutions, broader product diversity, Chief Investment Office-led advisory capabilities and enhanced digital wealth platforms.
Momentum was particularly strong within the Preferred segment, reflecting deeper engagement with affluent customers and CIMB’s focus on expanding advisory-led and relationship-based wealth capabilities.
For small and medium-sized enterprises, CIMB continued to advance digital banking through the launch of CIMB OCTO Biz.
The platform connects account opening, financing and transaction banking through an end-to-end digital journey and has onboarded more than 280,000 customers to date.
CIMB OCTO Biz provides businesses with real-time cash flow visibility alongside access to payments, foreign exchange, trade and financing services.
The bank also expanded financing access through embedded merchant financing with TNG eWallet.
Its SME FlexiCash offering provides flexible financing by using account history and transaction behaviour to determine pre-qualified limits, while linking repayments to a proportion of revenue. This is designed to better support businesses with uneven cash flows.
CIMB Investment Bank’s performance across Malaysia’s equity and debt capital markets, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and bespoke financial advisory services also contributed to its recognition as Malaysia’s Best Investment Bank.
The bank has continued to execute complex transactions across multiple products, sectors and jurisdictions.
In 2025, CIMB Investment Bank secured the number one ranking in Malaysian equity and debt capital markets by deal value and share of wallet.
It also captured the top position in ASEAN equity and debt capital markets by deal value, while its execution of cross-border transactions reinforced its position as a leading M&A and advisory house in ASEAN.
The three accolades reinforce CIMB’s brand promise, Moving You Forward, reflecting its continued focus on empowering customers and communities through accessible, inclusive and purpose-driven financial solutions.
The recognition comes as financial institutions increasingly balance traditional banking capabilities with digital innovation and more personalised customer experiences across retail, SME and corporate markets.
For more than 30 years, Euromoney’s Awards for Excellence have recognised financial institutions that set benchmarks in performance, innovation and client impact.
The Awards for Excellence programme evaluates financial institutions through Euromoney’s benchmarking framework, using comparable metrics, structured submissions and a transparent research process to assess institutions against their peers.

title: GXBank and IFC Partner to Unlock Up to US$110 Million in MSME Financing
bodyText:
GX Bank Berhad (GXBank) has partnered with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group focused on the private sector, in a landmark risk-sharing arrangement aimed at expanding financing access for Malaysia’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Under the partnership, IFC will provide up to US$4.95 million in unfunded first-loss credit protection, supporting GXBank’s lending to businesses that are underserved or have limited access to traditional financing.
The facility is expected to support a target MSME loan portfolio of up to US$110 million.
By absorbing initial default risks on uncovered assets, the arrangement complements existing local guarantee frameworks and is designed to help GXBank extend credit to “thin-file” businesses that may lack traditional financial track records or physical collateral.
The partnership also marks the first time a Malaysian digital bank has received an IFC first-loss guarantee.
The risk-sharing facility is intended to support GXBank’s technology-led approach to credit assessment, allowing the digital bank to reach businesses that may not meet conventional lending requirements.
GXBank said the partnership combines its proprietary digital underwriting capabilities with IFC’s first-loss credit protection and existing local guarantee schemes such as the Credit Guarantee Corporation Malaysia (CGC).
Kaushik Chowdhury, Chief Executive Officer of GXBank, said the partnership represents international recognition of the bank’s risk management capabilities and operational maturity.
“Micro-entrepreneurs form the foundation of Malaysia’s economy, yet traditional collateral requirements leave vast credit demand unmet.”
Chowdhury said the combination of technology-led underwriting, IFC’s first-loss protection and local guarantee schemes could allow GXBank to expand access to capital for underserved business owners while maintaining the resilience of its balance sheet.
He added that 15,000 MSMEs have opened digital accounts with GXBank, resulting in more than 5,000 loan drawdowns to date.
Beyond providing direct protection against credit losses, the partnership is also intended to improve GXBank’s capital efficiency under Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) frameworks.
With IFC providing first-loss protection, the risk-weighted capital requirements associated with the supported loans can be reduced. This could free up balance sheet capacity for GXBank to extend more automated credit to underserved entrepreneurs.
The bank said the arrangement enables it to scale lending while continuing to manage the risks associated with expanding access to financing.
The backing of a AAA-rated multilateral institution also provides additional support for GXBank’s approach to risk management and compliance.
Allen Forlemu, Regional Industry Director, Financial Institutions Group at IFC, said expanding access to finance for MSMEs is an important driver of inclusive economic growth in emerging markets.
“This collaboration demonstrates how digital innovation can help bridge financing gaps for underserved MSMEs, supporting business expansion, job creation, and stronger economic resilience in Malaysia.”
The partnership reflects a wider effort to use digital financial services and alternative approaches to credit assessment to address financing gaps faced by smaller businesses.
The IFC partnership builds on GXBank’s existing initiatives aimed at improving access to financing for Malaysian MSMEs.
According to GXBank, MSMEs account for 97.4 per cent of Malaysian businesses, highlighting the scale of the potential financing gap facing the sector.
One of its recent initiatives has involved the Credit Guarantee Corporation Malaysia (CGC).
Since March, GXBank has approved RM27 million in CGC-guaranteed facilities. Following the positive trajectory, the maximum credit limit for expanding businesses was recently increased from RM150,000 to RM350,000.
The move provides eligible businesses with greater potential access to working capital and expansion financing.
GXBank has also completed a proof-of-concept (POC) with Finory, a Malaysian fintech startup and winner of GXBank’s TeXnovasi Accelerator Programme.
The POC examined the feasibility of automating the onboarding process for micro traders using business licences issued by local authorities.
The initiative reflects GXBank’s broader focus on using technology to simplify access to financial services and reduce barriers faced by smaller businesses.
With the IFC risk-sharing facility now supporting its lending strategy, GXBank aims to further expand technology-led MSME financing while improving access to capital for Malaysian businesses that may otherwise struggle to secure conventional credit.

title: Malaysian SMEs Turn to AI as Kintone Identifies Malaysia as Southeast Asia’s High-Potential Market
bodyText:
Malaysian small and medium-sized businesses are showing growing interest in artificial intelligence (AI), but widespread adoption remains in its early stages, according to insights shared at the inaugural Kintone Day Kuala Lumpur 2026.
Held on 8 September at Zepp Kuala Lumpur, the event brought together around 600 business leaders from industries including manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and professional services.
Insights gathered from attendees showed that only one in 10 business leaders in the room were using AI agents in their operations, while between 30 and 40 per cent were using AI in simpler forms, such as prompting a chatbot.
For Kintone Southeast Asia, the figures represent an opportunity for Malaysian businesses to get ahead as AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday operations.
Kintone Southeast Asia, a subsidiary of Tokyo-listed Cybozu, Inc. (TSE: 4776), used the event to identify Malaysia as its highest-potential market in Southeast Asia.
New customer acquisition in Malaysia increased by more than 160 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026, reflecting growing demand for digitalisation among local businesses.
The company said this opportunity is supported by the strength of Malaysia’s SME ecosystem.
According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia, micro, small and medium enterprises contributed RM689.8 billion in value added in 2025, equivalent to 39.7 per cent of the country’s GDP. The sector grew 5.7 per cent, compared with national economic growth of 5.2 per cent, and employed 8.09 million people, close to half of Malaysia’s workforce.
“Every SME will be using AI before long,” said Tsubasa Nakazawa, Managing Director of Kintone Southeast Asia. “The ones that gain most from it are the ones that start while most have not, and starting no longer requires an IT department or a single programmer.”
A key focus of Kintone Day was the growing potential of agentic AI, with Kintone giving attendees an early look at capabilities currently in development.
Unlike AI tools that simply respond to individual prompts, an AI agent within the Kintone platform could carry a business process forward after a specified trigger condition is met.
Potential applications include automatically routing a closed sales opportunity to a delivery team or proposing a response when a recurring quality issue is identified.
The company said organisations would retain control over how these AI capabilities are used.
Kintone’s controls allow businesses to establish their own requirements around data safety and permission levels, including who can use AI and how far an AI agent can act. Organisations can also switch the technology off entirely.
The approach is intended to allow AI adoption to fit alongside individual company policies as well as Malaysia’s National AI Action Plan 2026–2030, which outlines the country’s ambition to become an AI Nation by 2030 through 28 initiatives covering sectors, talent, infrastructure and governance.
Despite growing interest in AI, many Malaysian SMEs continue to operate using a combination of spreadsheets, messaging applications and single-purpose software that do not necessarily communicate with one another.
This can leave employees repeatedly reconciling information manually and spending valuable time managing disconnected systems.
Kintone said that while consolidating these systems can address part of the problem, technology adoption can lose momentum after implementation, particularly among businesses without dedicated IT departments or in-house technical expertise.
“Malaysian companies are not short of ambition. They are short of IT people, time and the confidence that help will still be there after go-live,” Nakazawa said.
He added that Kintone is designed to address this gap by allowing employees closest to the work to build and modify their own systems, while the company and its partners provide continued support.
The approach also extends to AI adoption, with businesses able to decide whether or not to use AI based on the nature of the data they handle.
The growth of Kintone in Malaysia comes as its parent company, Cybozu, reports continued expansion.
For the first half of 2026, Cybozu recorded consolidated net sales of approximately US$130 million (RM532 million), representing a 16.1 per cent year-on-year increase.
Kintone was the group’s largest product line, generating approximately US$77 million (RM313 million) in sales, up 19.1 per cent year-on-year.
Kintone established its Malaysian operation in March 2022.
Yoshihisa Aono, President and CEO of Cybozu, Inc., also shared the company’s approach to building technology around people during his keynote conversation.
Speaking about Cybozu’s development, Aono said the company chose to listen to individual employees rather than rely solely on a single set of policies.
“If you have 100 people, you get 100 different answers, so we stopped writing one policy and started listening to each person,” he said.
According to Aono, the people who remained with the company played a significant role in its transition to cloud technology, after which its revenue grew more than tenfold.
Cybozu now employs more than 1,000 people, compared with three employees when the company was founded.
The experience of Malaysian food waste technology company Mentari Alam Eko (MAEKO) provided an example of how digitalisation can address operational challenges within an SME.
MAEKO designs and builds food waste conversion machines in Malaysia. Its operational needs became more complex after the company moved from selling machines to renting them.
While a sale involves a single transaction, a rental model creates ongoing requirements for maintenance, servicing and asset tracking. With around 200 to 300 machines operating nationwide, managing these processes manually became increasingly demanding.
The company previously responded by adding more people to handle paperwork.
Today, MAEKO uses Kintone to manage areas including purchase approvals, manufacturing drawings, HR records and ISO documentation, alongside smaller operational processes such as service vehicle bookings and key custody.
The company operates without an IT department or programmers, with its employees building and modifying applications internally.
For the second half of 2026, Kintone said its priority in Malaysia is to help more small and medium-sized businesses establish digital systems that they can build and maintain themselves.
As AI adoption accelerates, the company believes SMEs that begin experimenting with practical applications early could gain an advantage in productivity and competitiveness.
For Malaysian businesses, the challenge may therefore no longer be whether AI will become part of their operations, but how they can adopt it in a way that fits their people, processes and data requirements.

title: Tourism Malaysia Backs Homegrown Wellness Brand to Strengthen Malaysia’s Wellness Tourism
bodyText:
Tourism Malaysia has extended its support for efforts by homegrown wellness brand JYY Group to strengthen Malaysia’s position as a wellness tourism destination, following the opening of the brand’s flagship store at Pavilion Kuala Lumpur.
The new flagship outlet provides an additional touchpoint for international travellers and local visitors to discover Malaysian wellness products, hospitality and cultural stories while exploring one of the capital’s key tourism and shopping destinations.
The initiative forms part of Tourism Malaysia’s continued efforts under Visit Malaysia 2026–2027 (VM2026–2027) to work with homegrown Malaysian brands and bring local products and experiences to a wider audience.
The opening ceremony was officiated by Mr Mohd Akbal Setia, Deputy Director General (Promotions) and Head of the Visit Malaysia 2026–2027 Secretariat, Tourism Malaysia, together with Mr Lee Thai Hung, Deputy Director General (Promotions II), Tourism Malaysia.
Tourism Malaysia said partnerships with homegrown brands are important to VM2026–2027’s ambition of improving the overall traveller experience throughout their journey.
By placing Malaysian wellness brands within major tourism landmarks such as Pavilion Kuala Lumpur, visitors can discover local products and experiences alongside conventional tourism activities.
The approach extends the visitor journey into everyday experiences such as shopping, wellness and cultural discovery, giving both domestic and international travellers more opportunities to engage with Malaysia’s natural and cultural heritage.
Tourism Malaysia also hopes that greater visibility for homegrown wellness products will encourage travellers to explore locally inspired offerings while creating stronger connections between tourism and Malaysia’s growing wellness ecosystem.
The flagship store opening also featured Malaysian singer and actor Nicholas Teo, who brought an East Malaysian connection to the brand through its Trigona honey, which is sourced from the highlands of Malaysian Borneo.
The connection highlights the role of locally sourced ingredients in telling Malaysia’s wellness and cultural stories.
Tourism Malaysia said showcasing products rooted in Malaysia’s regions and natural biodiversity can help build greater appreciation of the country’s diverse natural heritage and its contribution to everyday wellness.
This also forms part of the broader tourism story that VM2026–2027 seeks to share with visitors, linking Malaysia’s biodiversity, locally sourced products and cultural identity with its tourism offerings.
Tourism Malaysia said its support for initiatives such as this is intended to encourage greater public engagement with homegrown wellness products that incorporate locally sourced ingredients.
These ingredients give Malaysian wellness products a distinctive local identity while encouraging brands to continue developing and showcasing locally inspired products to international audiences.
The collaboration also reflects Tourism Malaysia’s commitment to making wellness experiences more accessible and convenient for both international visitors and Malaysians throughout VM2026–2027 and beyond.
To coincide with the flagship store opening and Malaysia’s National Month celebrations, JYY Group is also offering a series of limited-time privileges across its outlets.
The promotions include discounts, special offers and complimentary items for customers.
The initiative is intended to give both local and international visitors greater access to affordable, high-quality wellness products while supporting homegrown Malaysian brands.
With the flagship store located in the heart of Kuala Lumpur, Tourism Malaysia sees the initiative as another way to incorporate wellness, shopping and local product discovery into the wider visitor experience.
Through collaborations with homegrown businesses, Tourism Malaysia aims to further strengthen Malaysia’s wellness tourism ecosystem while showcasing the country’s locally rooted products, natural resources and cultural stories to travellers from around the world.

title: Yunnan and Malaysian Women Entrepreneurs Explore New Opportunities for Cross-Border Cooperation
bodyText:
Women entrepreneurs from Yunnan and Malaysia are exploring new opportunities for economic and business cooperation following an exchange held in Kunming on 9 September 2026.
The “Women Entrepreneurs Strengthening Connectivity · Yunnan-Malaysia Working Together for Development — Yunnan-Malaysia Women Entrepreneurs Economic and Business Cooperation Exchange” was jointly organised by the Yunnan Women Entrepreneurs Association and the Women Entrepreneurs Committee of the Malaysia-China Chamber of Commerce (MCCC WEC).
The exchange aimed to strengthen connections between women entrepreneurs from both regions while promoting resource sharing and complementary strengths across trade, industry, investment and cross-border markets.
Held at the Kunming Yunan International Convention and Exhibition Hotel, the event brought together women entrepreneurs from various industries in Yunnan and Malaysia for thematic discussions, business presentations, project introductions and business matching.
Wu Tao, Director of the Women’s Development Department of the Yunnan Provincial Women’s Federation, attended and delivered remarks.
Zhang Mei, President of the Yunnan Women Entrepreneurs Association, and Jamie Tiew Yen Houng, Chairperson of the Women Entrepreneurs Committee of the Malaysia-China Chamber of Commerce, also delivered keynote addresses.
The programme featured business and project presentations from entrepreneurs on both sides, followed by economic and trade project presentations and interactive business discussions.
In her address, Jamie Tiew said leading the MCCC WEC delegation to Yunnan represented not only a business and industry study visit, but also a “return visit of friendship”.
Members of the Yunnan Women Entrepreneurs Association had previously visited Malaysia twice, with the continued exchanges and mutual visits creating a foundation for further cooperation.
Tiew noted that meaningful cooperation is not built through a one-off exchange, but through continuous interaction and connection. She also highlighted the importance of trust and mutual understanding developed through repeated engagements.
The Yunnan visit was themed “Meeting in Colourful Yunnan · Joining Forces for Shared Development”. Through site visits, industry study, business exchanges and cultural experiences, the delegation sought to strengthen friendship and understanding while identifying opportunities for industry cooperation and market expansion.
The exchange provided entrepreneurs from Malaysia and Yunnan with an opportunity to introduce their businesses, areas of expertise and potential cooperation projects.
The Yunnan side highlighted strengths across cultural tourism and wellness, wellness-oriented real estate, specialty agriculture, highland agricultural products, integrated logistics, cross-border e-commerce, intangible cultural heritage and creative industries.
Other areas included Yunnan tea and opportunities for market expansion into ASEAN.
Malaysian entrepreneurs, meanwhile, shared their experience and business opportunities in international sales, business management, legal services, real estate, finance, brand marketing, logistics, trade and cross-border market development.
Through face-to-face discussions, participants explored potential synergies across industrial chains, supply chains and market resources.
A total of 38 Chinese and Malaysian entrepreneurs and business representatives participated in the sharing sessions, comprising 17 Malaysian representatives and 21 representatives from China.
The programme subsequently continued with economic and trade project presentations, interactive discussions and the identification of potential cooperation projects.
Tiew said women entrepreneurs are an important force in driving economic development and social progress.
Since its establishment in 2018, MCCC WEC has brought women entrepreneurs together while promoting women’s entrepreneurship, business growth, international exchanges and economic and trade cooperation.
She stressed the importance of developing a longer-term, stable and practical cooperation mechanism that encourages member enterprises from both sides to pursue mutual visits, project cooperation, resource sharing, market development and industry matching.
Tiew described the significance of the exchange through four stages: “From introduction to understanding, from exchange to cooperation, from friendship to partnership, and from mutual visits to shared success.”
She also expressed hope that women entrepreneurs from Yunnan and Malaysia would continue to visit, communicate and remain connected, bringing their resources, markets and business networks closer together.
As economic and trade relations between China and Malaysia continue to deepen, both sides have opportunities to cooperate across areas including trade and investment, technological innovation, education and culture, tourism and industry.
As an important gateway connecting southwest China with South and Southeast Asia, Yunnan offers a platform for Chinese and Malaysian enterprises to explore cross-border business cooperation and access new markets.
The exchange strengthened ties between women entrepreneurs from Yunnan and Malaysia while creating conditions for future collaboration involving industries, projects, capital and markets.
The Yunnan Women Entrepreneurs Association and MCCC WEC look forward to building on the exchange as a new starting point for continued interaction and project implementation between entrepreneurs from both sides.
Through sustained engagement, both organisations aim to strengthen the “tree of friendship” and widen the “bridge of cooperation”, creating new opportunities for shared development among women entrepreneurs.
The connections established during the Kunming visit are expected to develop into further business partnerships and cooperation opportunities in the years ahead.

title: You Can Inherit a Business. But You Still Have to Earn the Right to Lead It
bodyText:
Lydia shared with MALAYSIA SME about succession, generational differences, leadership, growth, and what it means to build the next chapter of a family business without losing sight of why it was built in the first place.
1.  Please share a brief history of your family business and its founding principles?
WEBEST was founded by my father more than 30 years ago, starting in construction before moving into main contracting and, eventually, property development. Growing up in that environment shaped how I see development today. We don’t just look at a building from the perspective of selling it. We understand what it takes to build it, deliver it, and stand behind it. My father was always particular about one thing: reputation. Doing things properly, keeping commitments, delivering quality — those weren’t just business principles. They were who we were. Today, we describe our purpose as “Build Things That Matter.” The business has changed. The belief hasn’t.
2. What was your journey like? Did you always see yourself taking over?
Honestly, no. I never grew up thinking, “One day I’ll run the company.” When I did join, I wanted to start from the ground,  business development, sales, working across different parts of the business, because I didn’t want to inherit a title. I wanted to understand the business. Over time, I realised that if I was going to carry this forward, I had to make it my own responsibility. Not something I inherited. Something I chose.
3. What values from the first generation do you strive to uphold?
Three things: integrity, responsibility, and quality. My father always said reputation takes a long time to build and very little time to lose.  And coming from construction, we’ve never believed in building something just to complete it and move on. Our name stays on that building long after we’ve handed over the keys.
4. How did the leadership transition happen?
More organic than structured. There was no single day my father said, “You’re taking over now.” It happened gradually: more decisions, more responsibility, eventually making calls independently. But succession is much more than transferring ownership. The harder part is transferring trust and the ability to make decisions. That’s still a process. Leadership is something you keep earning.
5. What were the biggest challenges stepping into leadership?
The biggest was expectation. When you’re the founder’s daughter, people compare you to the person who built the company. And so did I, for a while. But eventually I realised my job wasn’t to become my father. My job is to take what he built and make it relevant for the next generation. That was the mindset shift that changed everything.
6. How did your parents prepare you for this role?
I watched how my father dealt with contractors, customers, banks, difficult situations and how he took responsibility when things went wrong. That shaped me more than any formal training. Of course, today’s environment demands different capabilities — branding, digital, governance, data. So I see my role as taking the first generation’s foundation and building new capabilities around it.
7. How do you balance their vision with your own leadership style?
I don’t think my job is to preserve everything my father did. I think my job is to understand why he did it.
The principles don’t change; integrity, quality, responsibility. But how we deliver them must evolve.
Today we are far more intentional about brand, customer experience and design. We use data. We think about long-term asset value. I’m not changing what WEBEST stands for. I’m changing how WEBEST expresses it for a different generation.
8. What changes have you implemented since taking over?
The biggest shift has been moving WEBEST from being primarily construction-led to becoming a developer with a stronger focus on product, brand and customer experience. We’ve expanded beyond Melaka into Johor, Putrajaya and Penang. We’re diversifying into hospitality with the transformation of an existing hotel into a Marriott Moxy property. But the goal was never to get bigger for its own sake. I want WEBEST to become better, stronger and more resilient. Growth has to mean something.
9. How has technology influenced your strategy?
It’s changed how we think and how fast we learn. We can measure campaign performance, track sales data, understand customer behaviour in real time, things the previous generation simply didn’t have access to.
But I don’t believe technology replaces judgement. Data tells you what is happening. You still need people to decide what to do about it.
10. What are your thoughts on innovation versus tradition?
They’re not opposites. Tradition should protect our values. Innovation should improve how we deliver them.
We should never preserve an outdated way of doing things simply because “that’s how we’ve always done it.” The world has changed. Customers have changed. If we don’t evolve, even the traditions we’re trying to protect become irrelevant.
11. What are the key challenges second-generation leaders face today?
Finding your own identity. You inherit a company with history, relationships and expectations and you have your own ideas about where it should go. There’s always a tension between respecting what was built before you and having the courage to change it. And you can’t simply say, “This is my company now.” The authority my father has, he built that over 30 years. As the second generation, you have to earn that trust in your own way, with your own track record.
12. How do you handle long-serving employees who knew the first generation?
With respect, and with clarity. They contributed to WEBEST long before I was in any leadership role. Their knowledge is genuinely valuable. But the company cannot stay exactly the same forever. So I make it clear: I’m not here to erase the past. I’m here to build the next chapter. Leadership is ultimately demonstrated through decisions and results. Over time, people will judge you on that.
13. What are the biggest opportunities in the next five years?
The market is shifting toward quality, experience and differentiation. There’s plenty of supply. Simply building another product at a price point is getting harder. Customers are asking not just “how much?” but “what am I actually getting?” For WEBEST, that means better design, better construction, stronger service and more thoughtful communities. But the biggest opportunity is the same one we’ve always had: understanding what people actually need and building something that matters.
14.  How do you separate family and business?
It takes discipline. We’re still family — but when we’re discussing business, the business comes first.
We don’t always agree. But I’ve learned that disagreement doesn’t have to become personal. You can disagree on the business without becoming disconnected personally. That’s one of the most important lessons in any family business.
15. How do you bridge generational differences in management style?
My father’s generation was relationship-driven, entrepreneurial, very hands-on. Mine has access to more information, more tools, more structured systems. We sometimes see things very differently. But I’ve stopped framing it as who’s right. The older generation gives us experience. The younger generation challenges us to think differently. You need both.
16. What advice would you give other second-generation leaders?
Don’t try to prove you’re different just for the sake of it. First — understand what made the business successful. Then identify what genuinely needs to change. And most importantly, don’t inherit the business without earning the right to lead it. Spend time on the ground. Know your people, your customers, your numbers. Eventually, you have to stop asking “what would my father do?” and start asking: “What is the right thing for the business now?” That’s when you start becoming a leader in your own right.
17.  Is sustainability a key focus?
Yes — though for us it’s broader than just environmental sustainability. We think about how long a building lasts, how it operates, how people experience it years after completion. We don’t want to build something that only looks good on launch day. Adaptive reuse is part of this thinking — our hotel transformation is a good example. Instead of demolishing an existing asset, we’re giving it new life and new purpose.
In our residential work, we emphasise greenery, lower density and spaces that encourage better living. For me, sustainable development has to make sense on three levels: commercially viable, environmentally responsible, and meaningful to the community.
18. What is your long-term vision for WEBEST?
To become a respected Malaysian boutique developer known for quality, not quantity. I don’t want WEBEST to be the company that builds the most. I want us to be the company where people say: “If WEBEST built it, I know there’s thought behind it.” Our purpose is simple: Build Things That Matter. Good buildings, yes — but also a good company, good teams, and something that continues to create value beyond my generation.
19. Would you encourage the third generation to take over?
I would never want them to feel obligated. If they have the passion and capability, I’d be proud to support them. But the choice has to be theirs. My job isn’t to hand them a company one day and say “this is yours.” My job is to build something strong enough, meaningful enough, and exciting enough that the next generation actually wants to be part of it.
20.  What has been the most rewarding part of leading the family business?
Seeing something go from an idea on paper to something people actually live in. But what’s become even more meaningful is seeing people within the organisation grow with the company. WEBEST isn’t just my family’s business anymore. There are many people and families whose lives are connected to it. That makes the responsibility bigger and the purpose much clearer.
21. If you could go back, what advice would you give yourself?
“You don’t have to have all the answers.” I used to think a leader had to know everything. I now know leadership isn’t about being the smartest person in the room. It’s about surrounding yourself with good people, asking the right questions, and taking responsibility for the outcome. I’d also tell myself: be more patient. Building a company takes time. You don’t need to win every battle. You just need to keep building.
22. What legacy do you hope to leave behind?
Not that I grew WEBEST bigger. That I made it better. My father spent more than 30 years building the foundation. My responsibility is to strengthen it and write the next chapter. I want our people to be proud to work here. Our customers to trust our name. Our partners to know we honour our commitments.
And one day, when I’m no longer running the company, I don’t want people to say “that was Lydia’s company.” I want them to say: “WEBEST has always built things that matter.” That’s the real legacy.

title: Yang Arnieda: Finding Her Voice Again — How TalentCorp’s Women-Industry Network (WIN) Helped Her Rebuild Her Confidence and Career
bodyText:
As a manufacturing engineer from Johor Bahru,  Yang Arnieda Azaman began her professional journey on factory floors where male colleagues vastly outnumbered female ones. Growing up in a household of four sisters had taught her the value of supporting women, yet stepping into the engineering world meant entering an environment where she constantly felt she had to prove herself.
Over the years, she gradually moved away from engineering and into business development, corporate communications and leadership roles. Although her career progressed steadily, there was one challenge that never quite disappeared.

“I was always more comfortable working behind the scenes,” she reflected. “I never really dared to take on leadership positions or lead major projects. I always felt like I wasn’t ready.” Yet life was about to present her with a challenge far greater than any workplace obstacle. As a single mother, her priorities changed dramatically when she realised her young daughter needed help with reading and writing.  Today, awareness of learning differences such as dyslexia is much greater. But at that time, information and support were difficult to find.
“I didn’t know where to go or who to ask. I searched online, tried to understand what she was going through, and learnt different techniques to teach her myself.” Every evening became another lesson. She coloured books by hand, enlarged letters, created her own learning materials and patiently guided her daughter through words, numbers and exercises that many parents take for granted.
While the pandemic disrupted careers across the country, she saw it differently. “I felt it was a sign from God,” she said. “I already knew my daughter needed me. The pandemic simply made the decision clearer.”
She stepped away from her career for almost two years to devote herself fully to helping her daughter build the confidence and foundational skills she would need before entering primary school.
It was a sacrifice that many people did not fully understand. Professionally, she was stepping away from a leadership role she had worked hard to earn. Personally, she was putting her daughter’s future ahead of her own career ambitions. But she never questioned the decision. “I didn’t want her to enter school feeling left behind or lose confidence in herself.”
The effort paid off. By the time her daughter entered Year One, she could read and write independently. Although she progressed at her own pace, she no longer feared being left behind. Today her daughter is twelve, and Yang has no regrets. “I thought my career needed me. But actually, my daughter needed me more.”
When the pandemic eased, she was ready to return to work. She assumed returning to the workforce would simply mean updating her résumé and attending interviews. Reality proved very different. After nearly two years away from work, she found herself questioning everything she once knew.
“When you’re away for that long, you lose confidence. You walk into meetings surrounded by people talking about new projects and experiences, and suddenly you feel small.” Even asking simple questions became intimidating. The greatest challenge was not rebuilding technical knowledge. It was rebuilding belief in herself.

While searching for ways to regain her confidence, she came across the Women Career Comeback Programme under Talentcorp’s Women-Industry Network (WIN) initiative. She applied, completed the selection process and became part of the programme’s very first cohort in 2021.
She described the experience as arriving at exactly the right time. “I didn’t just need training. I needed someone to believe in me again.” Matched with an experienced mentor for three months of one-to-one coaching, Yang found herself challenged in ways she had never experienced before.
Her mentor was direct, transparent and unafraid to point out areas she needed to improve. Instead of feeling discouraged, she found the honesty refreshing. One assignment required her to prepare and deliver presentations. For someone who had always avoided public speaking, it felt overwhelming.
So she found an unexpected audience. Her daughter. “I practised every presentation in front of her.” Without realising it, both of them were learning together. “My daughter could actually see how I was growing.”

One of the biggest mindset shifts came from simply observing the women around her. For perhaps the first time in her career, she was surrounded by accomplished female leaders who were also participating in the programme. “They were CEOs. They were leaders. But they were still themselves.”
Until then, she had unconsciously believed that becoming a leader meant becoming tougher, louder or more masculine.
WIN challenged that assumption. “It showed me that you don’t have to stop being a woman to become a leader.” That lesson transformed how she viewed leadership. Rather than trying to imitate others, she learnt to lead authentically, with EQ, confidence and her own communication style.


The difference soon became visible. After completing the programme, she accepted a new leadership opportunity within an oil and gas organisation. Just two weeks into the role, she was entrusted with preparing and presenting a major proposal to Petronas.
“If you had asked me before the programme, I couldn’t have done that.” Instead of staying in the background, she volunteered ideas, contributed confidently and eventually led major projects. Her confidence had changed not only how she viewed herself, but also how others viewed her. “People respond differently when you believe in yourself.”

That renewed confidence eventually inspired another leap. In 2024, she established Bayu Ignitra, a training and development company focused on AI, leadership, communication, safety and professional development programmes. Working with a network of trainers across different disciplines, she now designs and delivers programmes while continuing to grow the business.
Among the areas closest to her heart is a women’s empowerment programme. Having spent much of her career as “the only woman in the room,” she understands the quiet challenges many women continue to face. “There were meetings where people didn’t take my opinions seriously. Sometimes they dismissed what I said before I even finished speaking.”
Yang doesn’t let those experiences discourage her; she uses them to help other women build confidence, strengthen their voices, and develop their own leadership styles. “I don’t want women to think they need to become someone else just to succeed.”

When asked what the WIN Programme gave her, she doesn’t immediately mention presentations or networking. Instead, she speaks about something much deeper. “It helped me reconnect with my professional identity.”
The WIN programme reminded her that career breaks do not erase experience. They do not diminish capability. Nor do they define a person’s future. She encourages every woman who joins similar programmes to commit to the experience fully. “You have to embrace your weaknesses before you can discover your strengths.”
For her, the programme became far more than a return-to-work initiative. It became the bridge between the person she used to be and the leader she was capable of becoming.

title: JurisTech Named Asia’s Best Lending Solution 2026 by Euromoney
bodyText:
Malaysia-founded lending and recovery technology company, globally recognised for connecting the credit lifecycle and demonstrating measurable impact from AI in lending operations.
The award was presented under Euromoney’s Awards for Excellence 2026, an established awards programme for the banking and financial services industry, recognises JurisTech’s approach to transforming the credit lifecycle by connecting infrastructure, decisions and workflows behind lending to address fragmentation within the lifecycle.
In a statement released by Euromoney, JurisTech stood out for the breadth and operational impact of its credit management technology.
“For institutions looking for a vendor with the entire lending platform, we support the journey from the moment a customer initiates a loan. We are best of a 360 AI Lending Technology.”


Lending is rarely a single-system problem. Retail loans, SME facilities, commercial lending, automotive finance and leasing involve different workflows, documentation requirements and risk controls. Financial institutions may need to modernise one part of the technology stack or connect a broader lending ecosystem. JurisTech supports both approaches.
Its platform covers the lending journey from first customer contact through to recovery, with capabilities for digital onboarding, lead management, credit decisioning, financial analysis, origination, credit administration, loan management, collateral, collections and recovery. Individual components can be deployed within an institution’s existing architecture or combined into a more complete end-to-end environment.
“We connect the surrounding systems and ensure the entire ecosystem works together. Regardless of the operating model you have, we can support it with an end-to-end solution,” See said.

A significant element of JurisTech’s lending technology strategy is applying AI directly to operational financial workflows to improve speed, accuracy and efficiency. For a government-backed SME lender, JurisTech deployed AI-powered document intelligence through Juris AICraft, its agentic AI platform, alongside Juris Analyst, its financial analysis solution for extracting and structuring financial data.
The implementation reduced credit analysis turnaround time by 94% and manual financial spreading effort by 85%. The system now handles more than 3,000 pages each month as part of the lender’s document-intensive SME and commercial credit analysis process, helping reduce processing time from two days to under two hours while improving data accuracy from around 60% to 85%.
“A lot of banks now are asking us to create AI agents,” See said. “Many still have large teams reviewing documents manually to check whether they match. Even for financial spreading, people are still keying in balance sheets manually. That no longer makes sense.”

At Alliance Bank Malaysia Berhad, a banking group in Malaysia serving consumer, SME, commercial, corporate and Islamic banking customers, JurisTech implemented an AI-enabled origination framework combining digital onboarding, lead management, configurable rule-based scoring, origination workflows and credit administration.
The deployment delivered 30% faster application turnaround and a 30% increase in staff productivity. Personal loan disbursement was reduced from three days to one day, mortgage processing from seven days to three days, and same-day credit card approvals were enabled.
The results demonstrate the operational value of connecting onboarding, decisioning, workflow and administration across the lending journey.


JurisTech’s lending platform runs on containerised, cloud-native infrastructure, to enable traditional virtual-machine environments to containerised deployment. The architecture is designed to support horizontal scalability, automated deployment, resilience and more efficient infrastructure use.
The company has also moved towards microservices, product-level ownership and API-based integration, to make its software increasingly componentised and extensible as AI becomes more embedded in product development and operations.
“We transformed ourselves so every product unit can run on microservices and scale up,” said See. “We made our software API-based, so even our collection system can talk to our decisioning services, contract management and other systems.”



JurisTech’s roots are in Malaysia, where the company was founded in 2003. Its experience has since extended beyond its home market, including expansion into Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, with demand from banks, multi-finance companies, leasing firms, digital banks, government-backed lenders and non-bank financial institutions.
In emerging and fast-growing credit markets, lending transformation requires strong process discipline. See shared, “Sometimes the priority is digitalisation before AI transformation.” she added, “Ultimately, policies, transparency, auditability and security have to be embedded. We focus on fixing the root cause of what is slowing the process down.”


Euromoney highlighted that JurisTech stood out because it addressed the harder layer of lending transformation. Not the application screen, but the machinery behind it: onboarding, data extraction, financial spreading, policy rules, approvals, documentation, servicing and recovery.
Its platform has breadth across the credit lifecycle, but the stronger point is how those components work together. AI is embedded into document handling, underwriting support and decision workflows, alongside configurable rules and governance controls.
In a crowded lending technology market, JurisTech showed that credit transformation must come from connecting the whole process, then making it faster, more automated and more controlled at the same time.

title: Malaysia’s Labour Market Remains Resilient, but Skills Mismatch Persists
bodyText:
Malaysia’s labour market remains broadly resilient, with employment continuing to grow in July while the unemployment rate remained unchanged from the previous month at 3.0%.
While the latest labour market figures point to continued employment growth, Jobstreet by SEEK Malaysia’s platform data offers a closer look at the types of jobs being advertised and the candidates seeking opportunities.
The data highlights a potential skills mismatch between available jobs and the experience and classifications represented among registered candidates.
Manufacturing, transport and logistics accounted for the largest share of advertised jobs on Jobstreet by SEEK, representing 12.9% of hiring activity.
Retail and consumer products followed with 8.4% of advertised roles.
This broadly corresponds with findings from the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), which showed that employment continued to expand in manufacturing and across the services sector.
However, the areas where employers are advertising vacancies and where candidates are looking for work do not always align.
Retail and consumer products accounted for 8.4% of advertised roles, but only 5.3% of registered candidate classifications. Conversely, administration and office support represented 11.3% of registered candidates, compared with 7.0% of advertised roles.
As Malaysia’s labour force grew by 0.1% to 17.37 million people in July, the figures point to an important challenge beneath the positive headline numbers.
Greater labour force participation and continued employment growth do not automatically mean that candidates’ existing experience matches the areas where job opportunities are concentrated.
According to Nicholas Lam, Managing Director of Jobstreet by SEEK Malaysia, the next challenge for the labour market is therefore not simply supporting employment growth, but helping workers keep pace with changing demand.
A resilient labour market requires stronger connections between the skills available among jobseekers and the capabilities businesses need as Malaysia’s economy evolves.
For jobseekers, particularly those earlier in their careers who may have less professional experience to draw on, targeted upskilling can help bridge this gap.
Building transferable skills that are relevant across different roles and industries can give candidates more ways to access available opportunities, rather than limiting their job searches to positions that correspond exactly with their previous experience.
As hiring demand shifts across sectors, developing capabilities that can be applied in multiple environments could help workers remain adaptable and competitive in Malaysia’s changing labour market.
Employers, meanwhile, have an opportunity to reconsider how they assess talent.
Placing greater emphasis on skills and potential, alongside clearer pathways for training and professional development, can help businesses reach candidates whose previous experience may not be an exact match but who have the capabilities to grow into a role.
Broadening recruitment criteria in this way could allow employers to tap into a wider pool of potential talent while giving jobseekers greater opportunities to transition between roles and industries.
Malaysia’s resilient labour market is not only one that creates employment opportunities, but one that helps people move towards them.
Improving the connection between available jobs and potential talent will require both jobseekers and employers to look beyond exact experience matches and recognise how skills can transfer across Malaysia’s changing economy.
As hiring needs continue to evolve, stronger investment in upskilling, transferable skills and skills-based recruitment could help ensure that employment growth translates into more accessible and sustainable career opportunities for Malaysian workers.

title: Selangor Triple Accelerator Programme 2026 Names Top 24 Finalists
bodyText:
The Selangor Information Technology & Digital Economy Corporation (Sidec) has announced the Top 24 finalists of the Selangor Triple Accelerator Programme 2026, following three days of live pitching and exhibitions during its Showcase Days.
The finalists were selected from 511 applications, with 90 startups chosen to participate across three accelerator tracks: Token-X, Deep-X and Retail-X.
Participants presented their businesses and solutions during the Showcase Days held from 18 to 20 August 2026 at Menara Affin, TRX, Kuala Lumpur. Eight startups from each track subsequently advanced to the Grand Final.
The Top 24 finalists were unveiled at a dedicated announcement event at Sidec’s office in Puchong, following a series of sessions involving programme participants, delivery partners and alumni.
The event opened with POWER-UP: Charging Forward, an introduction by Salman Ahmad, Head of Startup & Digitalisation at Sidec.
This was followed by POWER-UP: From Acceleration to Opportunity, a panel session featuring the programme’s delivery partners, including Aizat Rahim, Chief Executive Officer of Borong (Dropee), and Fiona Chin Quant Lynn, Co-Founder of Ominent Sdn Bhd (IGL Coatings).
Participants from all three tracks also took part in POWER-UP: The Cohort Conversation, while programme alumni shared their experiences during POWER-UP: Life After Acceleration.
The event concluded with the announcement of the Top 8 finalists from each track.
The eight finalists for Deep-X are:
The eight Retail-X finalists are:
The eight Token-X finalists are:
Yong Kai Ping, Chief Executive Officer of Sidec, said reaching the Top 24 reflected the progress, commitment and growth demonstrated by the participating founders throughout the programme.
“Reaching the Top 24 reflects the progress, commitment and growth these founders have shown throughout the programme. They’ve refined their strategies, sharpened their investment readiness, and built the confidence to take their ventures to the next stage. We look forward to seeing them showcase that growth at the final Demo Day,” he said.
The 24 finalists will compete at the Grand Final Demo Day on 14 October 2026 at the Plenary Theatre, Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre (KLCC), as part of the AI & Semiconductor Summit (AiSEM@Selangor).
At the Grand Final, the startups will present their businesses and solutions to a panel of judges and industry stakeholders, with the final round determining the Champion of each accelerator track.
A total of 12 winners will be recognised across Token-X, Deep-X and Retail-X.
Each track will award four Top winners, including one Champion. All winners will receive a trophy and certificate, alongside an opportunity to participate in an international trip providing exposure to regional markets, industry ecosystems and investment opportunities.
The international experience will include curated business and investor matching, industry visits and strategic connections designed to support regional expansion and business growth.
In addition, the Champion of each track will receive an RM20,000 cash prize.
Since 2015, Sidec has worked with more than 447 startups and SMEs, giving the organisation first-hand insight into the challenges businesses face as they grow and scale.
The impact of its accelerator programmes can also be seen among past alumni.
IGL Coatings, for example, secured new distributors in Bahrain and Bangladesh and launched a Petronas Graphene Advanced Technology in Las Vegas.
Meanwhile, Eartheories founder Fadz Subari was named one of the Top 10 CEOs in Malaysia for retail and e-commerce by CEO Insight Asia 2025.
These outcomes reflect Sidec’s broader focus on supporting businesses beyond their participation in an accelerator programme.
The programme has received support from a range of industry and ecosystem partners.
AFFIN Group serves as the Strategic Banking Partner, supporting Malaysian SMEs and startups through financial solutions, business insights and opportunities related to growth and investment readiness.
Fiuu, the Strategic Payment Partner, has supported participants through digital payment solutions and insights aimed at strengthening their digital commerce capabilities.
Sidec’s Global Partners, Plug and Play APAC and Endeavor, contributed global speakers, industry insights and international networks to provide founders with greater exposure to global markets and expansion opportunities.
MRANTI, the Strategic Innovation Partner, supported the programme through its innovation ecosystem, industry connections and platforms focused on the development and commercialisation of emerging technologies.
Cradle, Malaysia’s national agency supporting the startup ecosystem, also contributed to strengthening ecosystem linkages and supporting the growth and development of local startups.
The programme was further supported by 13 venture capital partners, including 500 Global, GenAI Fund, The Hive, PNSB, Gobi Partners, Vynn Capital, AppWorks and Artem Ventures.
These VC partners shared investment expertise and market insights, provided strategic guidance to founders and explored potential investment opportunities with participating startups.
Collectively, the partnerships give participating founders access to global exposure, industry expertise, investor perspectives and pathways for business growth, strengthening their opportunities to scale in Malaysia and beyond.
